speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That section twenty-seven of the Civil Service Superannuation and Retirement
Act, Chapter seventeen of the Revised Statutes of 1906, be amended to provide that the rate of interest computed on all sums to the credit of the Retirement Fund, whether principal or interest, be increased from four to five per centum per annum, that the Governor in Council shall have power to reduce the said rate of interest, but not below four per cent per annum, and that the proposed amendments shall be deemed to have come into force and effect on and from the first day of January, 1920.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPERANNUATION AND RETIREMENT ACT AMENDMENT.-RATE OF INTEREST.
speechtext: This resolution speaks pretty well for itself. I would point out that I am withdrawing resolution No. 5 on the Order Paper dealing with the same subject matter as this resolution. The object of the resolution before the Committee is to increase from four to five per cent the rate of interest on the percentage that is taken compulsorily from the salaries of civil servants, and the aggregate of which is paid over to them on their retirement. In view of the higher rate of interest now prevailing it has been thought but just to grant this increased rate.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
maintopic: SUPERANNUATION AND RETIREMENT ACT AMENDMENT.-RATE OF INTEREST.
speechtext: When this Act was passed, the rate of 4 per cent allowed on these savings was considered to be rather a generous one, because the Government were then borrowing at 3 per cent or less. I quite agree that in view of the changed conditions of the money market, 5 per cent is not too high to-day, and I quite approve the action of the minister. It suggests,,however, the point to which I drew attention the other day, that we are increasing the rate of interest on nearly everything except savings bank deposits. I mention the matter merely for the reflection of my hon. friend Sir Henry Drayton.

maintopic: SUPERANNUATION AND RETIREMENT ACT AMENDMENT.-RATE OF INTEREST.
speechtext: I see that provision is made to raise the rate of interest from four to five per cent, but the Governor General in Council is given power to reduce it, not below four per cent. It seems to me that some explanation is needed in regard to this provision. Why should thait power rest in the Governor in Council? I think that if a year hence, or at any other time in the future, circumstances were found to justify the reduction of ithe rate the minister might come to Parliament and obtain its sanction for that reduction.

maintopic: SUPERANNUATION AND RETIREMENT ACT AMENDMENT.-RATE OF INTEREST.
speechtext:
I think it is well, in
increasing the rate of interest, to give notice that this is due to the general higher value of money, and that if a change takes place the rate may have to be reduced. But even if the 5 per cent rate were continued it would not be too generous.

maintopic: SUPERANNUATION AND RETIREMENT ACT AMENDMENT.-RATE OF INTEREST.
speechtext: I am quite aware that in 1898 a change was made in the superannuation law giving an option to a great many civil servants to retain their status under the old Act or to come under the new Act. I should like to know from the minister how many civil servants are now entitled to the benefit of superannuation, and how many are entitled to that under the fund with which we are now dealing. Does it apply to the Civil Service generally? An explanation from the minister would be greatly appreciated by the country, as there is at present some confusion in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPERANNUATION AND RETIREMENT ACT AMENDMENT.-RATE OF INTEREST.
speechtext: I regret that 1 have not the definite statistics here, but, as I understand the matter, with the legislation of 1898 the former superannuation system ended. The result is that only those who were employed in the service prior to 1898 are still entitled to the old superannuation fund, which was not and is not a selfsupporting fund, and towards which, I think, the country has contributed something like $11,000,000. That is altogether stopped now, except as regards those who had an interest in it at the time that legislation was passed. The present arrangement applies, I understand, to all civil servants who, apart from the change in the law stopping the superannuation, would have been entitled to that superannuation. The great difference between the two funds is that the present retiring allowance is supplied entirely by the employee himself, his salary being arbitrarily reduced by five per cent.

maintopic: SUPERANNUATION AND RETIREMENT ACT AMENDMENT.-RATE OF INTEREST.
speechtext:
An option was given to the civil servants to determine whether they would remain under the old Act or take advantage of the benefit-if it was a benefit- of the new Act. I think a few old officials came to the conclusion that they would avail themselves of the option, and I know of one notable instance in which an old public official who had contributed a great deal of money, and to whom in the natural order of things nothing would be due at the time of death, took the option and agreed to come under the retirement fund. He died a few weeks afterwards and his heirs got many thousands from the public treasury.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time, and concurred in.
Sir HENRY DRAYTON thereupon moved for leave, to introduce Bill No. 17, founded on the resolution.

On the motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance), Bill No. 15, to amend the Currency Act, 1910, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On Section 1-Standard for gold and silver coins-
Will the minister please inform the House what the . old standard-was?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The change made here is in connection with silver coinage. The old standard was 925 parts fine, and the reduction is to 800 parts.

I take this opportunity of calling the attention of the minister to an article that appeared in the Boston Post a few days ago, regarding our exchange. In the debate on the Address I made some remarks that seem to have been regarded as being inconsistent with the general ideas concerning exchange, and I received a great deal of cheap advertisement throughout the country. The Boston Post published an editorial on my observations in which it said that Canadians could not expect anything else in regard to their money if they continued to grind it out simply in the press instead of digging it out of the ground in the form of gold. If it be the case that our exchange is what it is by reason of the fact that we have too much paper and not enough gold, when are we going to make an honest effort to get back to gold conditions and to a proper ratio between our paper money and our gold reserves so that our dollar will be worth one hundred cents as it was not so many years ago?
And get the good opinion of the Boston paper.

Get the good opinion of those who are selling goods and get a good opinion of our dollar. We know that our dollar is perfectly good and legal tender everywhere. I never heard of a paper dollar issued in Canada for which payment was refused in- gold when it came back to the proper quarters. There is some prejudice against our money in the United States which is not justified. If it be true, as this paper says, that we have too much paper and not enough gold, whenever an opportunity presents itself to bring this matter to the notice of the Minister of Finance, I think we should do so. I do not profess to be an authority on these things but it

does not require very much sense to know that when you present your dollar in any of the hotels in Boston it is only worth eighty-five cents. I want to bring back the old conditions when it was worth one hundred cents on the dollar. It is all very well to say that we do not scientifically understand these things. I think I am justified in bringing it to the notice of the Government and to those who are supposed to have scientific knowledge. I want to know whether there is anything in the argument of the Boston Post or not.

Mr. Chairman, what is the business before the House? We have absolutely no knowledge of what is going on. We might as well be sitting looking at a moving picture show. I would like the members, when they are addressing the House, to turn in this direction so that we will have some slight knowledge of what is going on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are considering clause 1 of Bill No. 15.
Thank you very much. I would like to have a copy of the Bill. We do not know what the Bill refers to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Bill has been distributed and ought to be on the hon. member's file.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid it would take some time to properly answer the question of the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). Perhaps it will be enough to say that Canada's currency stands well and compares favourably, taking any standard of comparison, with any other currency in the world. It is absolutely an ill-founded statement to say that the declension in one particular matter, brought about by the exigencies of trade and the movements of money both as shown in trade balances which are apparent and those which are not so apparent is owing to the fact that the Canadian dollar is not sound. It is sound and not only compares well, hut, compares very favourable with any other currency.
On Section 2 : Silver coins ; schedule amended.
Mr. MeMASTER: May I ask the minister to explain what "remedy allowance" and "millesimal fineness" mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They mean that you are getting the fineness down to a very small point. This "remedy" which is spoken of refers to the standard of fineness that every coin ought to have. For example, it is impossible to get every single
coin absolutely perfect to the fraction of a grain and this is the standard of remedy which is fixed. The standard may be within that very small margin which is allowed. Our standard of remedy is exceedingly severe and more severe than the standard of remedy which is applied in the United States.
How is that remedy applied? Are deficient coins called in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Deficient coinage is rejected. There is a machine which tests each accurately and any coin not coming up to the standard is at once rejected.
I do not think the minister understood my qusetion. When coins in circulation get below this standard, is there any machinery for calling them in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This particular clause of the Bill does not refer to that; it refers to minting. Of course, coins which are below standard are called in.
On -Section 3: Silver coins heretofore struck to continue current.
I would like to ask the minister how this will compare with American coin and whether the change will not"make our coins pass for less than they do at the present day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member's question I would say that a silver coin, ordinarily and properly, is a token coin. iSo long as the country stands behind the silver token, and stands for the obligation, it does not make any difference whatever as to what the contents of the token are. We have been getting into an abnormal condition, in so far as silver is concerned, owing to the unprecedented rise in the price of silver, a matter that was discussed when the motion was introduced. The price has risen, during the last year, from 80 cents to $1.41 an ounce, so that at one time we were coining silver at a loss. Of course, just as soon as you have your token coin containing enough currency to be worth the increased amount-that is the amount a coin as a token coin is worth -then the coin is more than a token and there is actual value in it apart from the token. But the function of silver coinage is token coinage, and it could have no effect upon the value of our silver currency as a token.

At the present time I understand our coins are worth about one-twelfth less in actual value of silver than American coins. What I want to get at now is,

what will be their relationship with this change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The fineness oi the American token is 900. Our old token was 25 points above the American token, but although it was 25 points better that did not help it in the American market. I might say, for the information of the hon. member, that the British Parliament, at the present time, is considering reducing the fineness of silver coinage to 500, and that the American authorities are now considering reducing the fineness of their coinage to 800.

The minister has not
answered my question: What would be the proportion now between the actual value of the American silver and ours?
(Sir HENRY DRAYTON: As eight to nine.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

On the motion of Sir Henry Drayton, Bill No. 16, to amend the Government Annuities Act, 1908, was read a second time and the House went into committee thereon -(Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-sale of annuities to persons resident in Canada:
Will the minister explain the meaning of the change proposed here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The purpose of the change is to remove from the officers looking after the sale of Government annuities the obligation of seeing that a man is domiciled in Canada. It renders it more easy for them to do business, more easy for Government annuities to be placed readily at the disposal of people living in Canada. No one entertains any idea looking towards leaving Canada for the purpose of pressing the sale of annuities; this provision simply enables the officials to deal with those Canadian residents who come to do business with the department without first finding out whether they are legally domiciled here.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-limit of amount increased from $1,000 to $5,000:
Mr. CAHILlL: Will the minister kindly explain the purpose of this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under the old clause no annuity could he sold for a greater amount than $1,000. This provision allows annuities to be purchased from the

Government for as large an amount as $5,000.
Mr. CAlHILL: What was the reason for the Government's desire to increase the amount from $1,000 to $5,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Requests have been made from time to time, from residents of Canada, who were anxious to make provision either for themselves or for their children and who found an annuity of $1,000 was not sufficient for that purpose.

The reason is that he wants the money?
Sir HEN-RY DRAYTON: I think that is quite right; that is an additional reason.

The House would like to know whether the Government sale of annuities has been a good paying business -what the record of the Annuities Branch has been since its inception, up to the present time. The Annuities Branch is not a very old institution in Canada. It commenced its operations, I think, in 1910, and some changes were brought about with respect to it in either 1912 or 1913. I can recall that when the former Postmaster-General, now Judge Pelletier, was in the House, we had lengthy explanations from him with respect to the annuities, and I think it is only fair to ask now if the business has been a paying one. We are paying out annuities from time to time and receiving certain contributions from the people, who are preparing themselves for the receipt of those annuities. Has the business been a paying one?
iSir HENRY DRAYTON: I have not the exact figures showing how the operations of the department have worked out, but if the hon. gentleman desires I will be very pleased to obtain them for him. The real trouble in the past has been that we have not done very much business. Now, in so far as to whether the sale of annuities has been a paying business or not, the complaint has been made that in the past the Government has been making too much money out of them. A general complaint has been made that we have not been generous enough to the public, having regard to the table on which the annuities were based, rather than that the Government was losing money on them. The real trouble with the situation, I think, is that owing to the limitations that we are now trying to get rid of, there has not been as satisfactory a volume of business in the department as could have been desired. It is hoped that with the removal of these

restrictions a far better volume of business will be transacted, and satisfactory profits made.
Would the minister instruct his officials to give us a fair idea of-how the business stands as to outgoings and incomings from its inception up to the present time?
A report is laid on the table each year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.	.
On section 3-Age when annuity payable:

Mr. Chairman,
there is very great difficulty in following the discussion from this end of the Chamber. I have only just learned that clause 3 relates to Bill No. 16 to amend the Government Annuities Act of 1908. I did not hear the reason given by the Finance Minister for the amendment; consequently I am not able to properly answer something that I could not possibly understand. Speaking in this direction (towards hon. members opposite) section 3 appears to be all right, but I have a great deal of objection to it for the reason that I do not know the number of the section to be repealed. It has not been produced before the House, that I am aware,, and-
Louder.

What I am saying, Mr. Chairman, is that section 3, repealing subsection 3 of section 8 is rather difficult to understand when the Act to be repealed is not before the House. I would like to have a full explanation of just what that section means by the Finance Minister addressing the Chairman first in this direction, so that hon. members at this end of the House may hear him, and then in the opposite direction so that other hon. members may hear as well.
It becomes a perfect absurdity and brings the House into disrepute when the public business is proceeding with only one half of the members able to hear what is being discussed. A conversational tone is,accepted I believe, in some deliberative assemblies as being a highly ornamental method to disseminate knowledge, but it is not to be recommended for adoption in this Chamber. 1 notice the pressmen with their hands to their ears in an attempt to understand what is being said-and they are quite close to the ministers. Every member is entitled to the courtesy of those gentlemen who are a little further away using their best efforts to state plainly the matter that is before the
House so that public business will be intelligible to every one; but we cannot hope for any improvement while the present conversational tone is maintained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have much pleasure in answering the question of the hon. gentleman, and I hope he can hear me now. We are striking out, as the hon. gentleman observes, sub-section 3 of section 8 of the old Act, which reads as follows:
Except upon the occurrence of invalidity oi disablement of an annuitant, no annuity shall be payable or paid to any annuitant, unless he has reached the age of fifty-five years.
The amendment will enable annuities to be sold so that they become effective before the age of fifty-five years is reached.
Does any age limit apply now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There will be no age limit at all. The rates of pay, however, provide a very effective age limit, because if a man wants to get an annuity at an unusually early age the charge becomes prohibitive.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-rate of interest increased:
What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The change here is merely to provide that the rate of interest which is payable to the estate of a man who would have become an annuitant if he had lived long enough shall be at four per cent instead of three. There are really three classes of annuities: (1) Where a guaranteed number of payments is made either to the man if he lives long enough or to his estate if he dies; (2) where all premiums paid on account of the annuity shall fail unless the annuitant lives for the specified period; and (3) the intermediate class where if the annuitant dies his estate does not lose the benefit of the payments which he has made, but is entitled to a return of those payments plus interest, which used to be at three percent but we now make it four percent .
Section 4 agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Resuming the adjourned debate on the proposed resolution of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Hon. Mr. Rowell) respecting the Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers and Bulgaria:

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: STATUS OF CANADA AS A NATION.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before speaking to the resolution I should like to ask my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Rowell) whether in the resolution itself the word " plenipotentiaries" is correct, or whether the word "plenipotentiary" should be used. I notice the resolution states that the Treaty has been signed "on behalf of His Majesty, acting for Canada, by the plenipotentiaries therein named." But on referring to the Treaty itself I find there is only one plenipotentiary mentioned for the Dominion of Canada, the Hon. Sir George Perley-unless it is to be understood that the other British representatives named are also signing on behalf of the Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATUS OF CANADA AS A NATION.
speechtext:
It should be
" plenipotentiary." In this case only one representative signed on behalf of Canada; in the other case there were two Canadian ministers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: STATUS OF CANADA AS A NATION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while listening to my hon. friend, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in introducing this resolution I could not help feeling that he himself in asking Parliament for the approval of this Treaty was doing so simply as a matter of form. There was really nothing in his argument in the way of a substantial reason why this Parliament should approve of the Treaty so far as the relations between Canada and Bulgaria are concerned. This is a Treaty between the Allied and Associated Powers and Bulgaria, and we as a Canadian Parliament are being asked to give our approval to it. One would assume that, the Canadian Parliament being asked to approve the Treaty, we would find in it somewhere something relating to the Dominion of Canada. One would also have expected that there would be a possibility of an opinion of this Parliament influencing the judgment of those who have to do with the final ratification of the Treaty. But looking at the Treaty, one sees that it was signed by the different powers at Neuilly-sur-Seine on November 27, 1919, and I am very sure my hon. friend will agree that anything that this Parliament may do in the nature of approving or disapproving the Treaty will not affect the dotting of a single "i" or the crossing of a single "t" in a single clause of the Treaty from beginning to end. It is for that reason I say, it seems to me, that the approval of this Parliament is being asked for simply as a matter of form.
LSir Henry Drayton.]
But while the hon. member has given us no substantial reasons why this Parliament should approve the Treaty, he has given reasons why it would be unwise for us not to approve the Treaty. In drawing attention to its different clauses, he pointed out that practically everything that we are asked to approve here was approved last year when we had before us the Treaty between the Allied and Associated Powers and Germany. Therefore, not to approve this Treaty at this time would be to have it appear that in the interval something had arisen which had caused this Parliament to take a different attitude towards the Treaties of Peace which are being signed in Europe from that which was taken at the last session. I am not aware that anything of the kind has arisen, and for that reason, I think it would be unwise for Parliament not to take, in the matter of approving the Treaty, the same action as it took in the matter of approving the Treaty between the Allied and Associated Powers and Germany.
But I want to point out just what are the grounds upon which my hon. friend has asked this Parliament to approve the Treaty. The grounds are broadly comprised under two headings. My hon. friend has mentioned one particular in which the Treaty has "special inteiest" to Canada, and it is the only particular in which he has specified any special interest to Canada as regards this Treaty. My hon. friend says that the provisions relating to debts and financial matters are of special interest to Canada in view of the fact that there are a number of Bulgarian Nationals living in Canada, and that there is a certain amount of enemy property in this country. It sounds very serious that there should be Bulgarian Nationals living in Canada, and that there should be a certain amount of enemy property in this country; but would any one consider for a moment that that was a reason serious enough to present to this Parliament for approving a particular Treaty? Yet, as I said, that was the only mention my hon. friend made in his speech of the particular interest this Treaty has with respect to Canadian affairs. In the same connection he pointed out that the provisions the Treaty contains respecting debts and financial matters are on all fours with similar provisions in the German Treaty which was approved last session.
My hon. friend went on to give another ground which he said made the matter of "most immediate concern" to Canada. It may be summed up in his own words as follows:

To go back to the two groups of clauses in the Treaty which are of most immediate oon-cern to Canada, should like for a few minutes to speak in reference to the' League of Nations and to the labour clauses of the Treaty.
In other words, we are being asked to approve this Treaty at the present time because of what it contains in reference to the League of Nations and the labour clauses of the Treaty. This Parliament has already approved the League of Nations' Covenant; it has already approved the labour clauses of the Treaty. Why should the time of Parliament be taken up in approving a second or a third time these particular matters? There has been no difference of view between us as to these clauses. I am not aware, when they were being debated in connection with the German Treaty, that a single exception was taken by any member of the House to the clauses relating to the League of Nations, and, in particular, to the labour clauses. Therefore, the reasons which my hon. friend has urged, are more in the nature of excuses for bringing this particular Treaty before the House, than they are good and substantial reasons for asking the approval of Parliament of this Treaty. I have said that they are excuses. I think, if my hon. friend would tell the House exactly what was in his thoughts, he would admit that his reason foT asking the House to approve the Treaty was 4 p.m. largely that he might repeat at this session what he said in Parliament at the last session and what he has since been saying on a good many platforms in regard to the League of Nations' Covenant and the labour clauses of the Treaty. I think that is the main reason for the introduction of this measure at this time.
My hon. friend, however, in addition to the two statements which I have quoted, has said that the adoption of the resolution involves the acceptance of certain principles which he has set forth. It is important that we should consider what my hon. friend has said in that connection. It affords the reason why, it seems to me, it would.be inadvisable for this House not to approve the Treaty. These statements of principle might be made as separate substantial motions in this House; they might be made in reference to almost any other Treaty as well as this particular one. But should this House, in view of the statement which my hon. friend has made, refuse to approve the Treaty, then it would be immediately said, or the impression would be conveyed, that in some way or another 30
this House was unwilling to accept the statements of principle which my hon. friend set forth.
Let me take up these statements of principle, one by one, and see whether there is any difference of opinion between members on both sides of the House in reference to them. They are all in the nature either of recognitions of something which is already conceded, or of reaffirmations of something which has already been affirmed. The first is the recognition of democratic control of foreign policy, and that Canada should not, without the consent of its Parliament, be finally committed to important international engagements such as are embodied in this Treaty. I venture .tp say there is not an hon. member who for one moment will take exception to the desirability of democratic control of foreign affairs. If we are to have an increased measure of foreign policy as a part of the business of this Parliament, it becomes increasingly important that we should have some effective democratic control of it; but the first example my hon. friend has given of democratic control by Parliament of foreign affairs is a somewhat unfortunate one inasmuch as he brings here for our approval a Treaty that was signed several months ago, the contents of which were not made known to a single member of this House until within the last two or three days, and a document which, I am sure my hon. friend himself will say, cannot be altered one way or another by anything which this House may do at the present time. But that is not the only example which my hon. friend has given to the House of his view of democratic control in regard to these matters	of foreign policy.
On the first of March my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Rowell) laid upon the Table of the House copies of other treaties:
The Czecho-Slovak Minorities Treaty, a treaty between the Principal Allied and Associated Powers and Czecho-Slavia, signed at Saint Ger-main-en-Laye, September 10, 1919. Ratification on behalf of Canada authorized by Order in Council of December 1, 1919.
Note those words " ratification on behalf of Canada authorized by Order in Council of December 1, 1919." Mr. Chairman, is ratification of a treaty by Order in Council an evidence of democratic control on the part of the Parliament of Canada? That is exactly the line of action which hon. gentlemen opposite have been taking in so many matters of all-important concern during recent years-and that we have been pro-



testing against. Instead of submitting these matters to Parliament for consideration, they have taken action upon them by Order in Council.
Copy of another treaty was also laid on the Table by my hon. friend on March 1:
The Serb-Croat-Slovent Minorities Treaty, a Treaty between the Principal Allied and Associated Powers and the Serb-Croat-Slovene State, signed at Saint Germain-en-Laye, September 10, 1919. Ratification on behalf of Canada authorized by Order in Council of December 1, 1919.
Here again is more ratification by Order in Council instead of by Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, let me repeat, we on this side of the House are strongly in favour of democratic control of all these matters of foreign policy. I think we would be willing to go so far as to say that we would like to have an expression of opinion of this House to the effect that Canada should not be bound by any treaty or agreement in matters of external relations, of which Parliament has not been fully informed in a way of which all of us could take cognizance. That would be helping along the democratic control of foreign relations, and when we have that principle carried out we shall have a sense of security which at present we do not feel in the matter of our external and inter-imperial relations.
The next reason that my hon. friend has given is that the adoption of the resolution will involve:
A recognition that in any war in which the British Empire is engaged and in which Canada has taken part is a matter ot concern to the people of Canada; that the terms of the Treaty of Peace bringing such a war to an end are also a matter of concern to the people of Canada, and that such a Treaty should not be ratified by His Majesty until it has been approved by Canada as of the five nations of the British Commonwealth.
There can be no difference of opinion on that matter. Every one in this country will admit that any war in which the British Empire is engaged and in which Canada has taken part is a matter of the greatest possible concern to Canada. Every one will be fully prepared to admit also that the terms of the treaty of peace bringing such a war to an end are also a matter of concern to the people of Canada, and that such a treaty snould not be ratified-I think the word " not " has been left out of Hansard by mistake-until it has been approved by Canada as one of the five nations of the British Commonwealth. I am not sure that my hon. friend would not have been more consistent if he had inserted after the word "treaty" in the phrase "such a treaty" the words "in so far as Canada is concerned." 
I just interject that point for his consideration.
Those are two recognitions or declarations of policy, or whatever one may choose to call them, upon which I think all hon. members of this House are thoroughly agreed. The remaining three are not recognitions of accepted policy, but are reaffirmations of positions this House has already accepted. First there is
A reaffirmation by Parliament of its approval of the creation and maintenance of a League of Nations for the promotion of international co-operation and the achievements of international peace and security by the methods set forth in the Covenant of the League.
As I mentioned a moment ago, this Parliament has approved of the creation and maintenance of a League of Nations for the promotion of international co-operation and the achievement of international peace and security by the methods set forth in the Covenant of the League. We have approved that over and over again, and why should our approval of it be asked for again in this connection? Is that a reason why this particular treaty with Bulgaria should be brought before the House for its approval at this time?
The fourth reason given toy my hon. friend is that the approval of the treaty will mean:
A reaffirmation by Parliament of its approval of the Labour Clauses; and of the creation and maintenance of the International Labour Organization under Its provisions.
How often have we to be asked, Mr. Speaker, to state what we have already stated time and time again in this House as to our views upon the Labour Clauses of the Covenant of the League of Nations? it may be that my hon. friend has some doubt as to the position some of his supporters may take towards those Labour Clauses, but let me tell him, speaking for those of us who are members of the Liberal party on this side of the House, that before the House took action one way or the other in regard to the Labour Clauses of the Covenant of the League of Nation^, the National Liberal Convention, composed of lepresentatives of the Liberal party from the Atlantic to the Pacific, made as one of the planks of its platform a full acceptance of the Labour Clauses in the spirit in which they were framed as part of the Covenant of the League of Nations. So that there may be no doubt as to the position which we pn this side of the House have taken as to the Labour Clauses of the League of Nations, let me read the following from a

resolution which was adopted in August last year by the National Liberal Convention:
Resolved that the Committee recommends that the National Liberal Convention accept in their entirety as a part of the Liberal platform, in the spirit in which they have been framed and in so far as the special circumstances of the country will permit, the terms of the Labour Convention and general principles associated with the League of Nations and incorporated in the conditions of peace.
Unless hon. gentlemen opposite entertain a different view of the significance of these Labour Clauses, I cannot see why this Parliament should again be asked to approve them under the guise of expressing its approval of a treaty between Bulgaria and the Allied Powers. So far as the League of Nations is concerned, I believe there is only one opinion in this House and in this country. We all recognize that the League of Nations is in a formative stage, that its constitution is more or less nebulous at the present time, but that it has in it promise of great good for humanity and for mankind. We all desire to see the League of Nations made a success, and we cannot by approval after approval in this House make our position better known than it is!
Now I come to the last reason which my hon. friend gave as to why we should approve this Treaty. He says its adoption involves:
A reaffirmation by Parliament of its approval of the position and status accorded to Canada in the League of Nations and in the International Labour Organization and of its determination to maintain that status.
Well, Mr. Speaker, who has questioned the status which Canada has attained in the League of Nations in any way that calls for a further approval by this Parliament of the status which we already have? Some question has been raised in the House and outside of the House as to whether the status is in any way the new thing which my hon. friend would lead us to believe it is; ivhether it is not a recognition of something that was achieved long before the Administration, of which he is a member, had anything to do with the matter one way or another. I think we are all agreed, Sir, that whatever status we have we desire to maintain. There is not a man in Canada who would cede one inch of ground on the question of the status which Canada has as a nation, and I do not think there is any difference of view between any of us on that point. Yet my hon. friend seizes this opportunity to bring up this question of Canada's status as a nation. As I have 30}
listened to his remarks in this Chamber and read his speeches delivered outside oi the House, it has seemed to me that whether he intends to do so or not, he is seeking to convey the impression that we have a new status which we have never had before, and that it has in some mysterious way come about through some action of the Administration with which he is connected. I would be the last one to deny the Administration any credit to which I think it is entitled in regard to the service which it has rendered Canada in helping to maintain and clearly define a status which we have and which has long been admitted. But I think we are allowing full credit to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and those associated with him, my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Doherty) and my right hon. friend the Secretary of State (Hon. A. L. Sifton) for their service to this Dominion in standing firm on the question of its status, when we give them credit for having dene their duty in a manner satisfactory to the people of the country.
Let me say at once that this whole question of Canada's position as a nation, when it comes to debating the matter, turns very largely on the meaning that we attach to the use of words. Hon. gentlemen opposite, on one or two occasions, have sought to make it appear that gentlemen on this side of the House, were, in some way or other, little Canadians who were endeavouring to minimize the status of their country, because they were unwilling to admit that, from certain points of view, strictly legal, or technical if you will, Canada was a nation with sovereign powers. Now, Mr. Speaker, no good purpose can be served by a contention of that kind. What is needed above everything else is clear and precise thinking on questions of this nature. Let me direct my, hon. friend's attention to his own language in order to illustrate my meaning. My hon. friend says that in approving this resolution we are endorsing the following principle:
The recognition that in any war in which the British Empire is engaged and in which Canada has taken part is a matter of concern to the people of Canada; that the terms of the Treaty of Peace bringing such a war to an end are also a matter of concern to the people of Canada and that such a treaty should not be ratified by His Majesty until it has been approved by Canada as of the five nations of the British Commonwealth.
My hon. friend will observe that in the first part of the paragraph he speaks of any war in which the British " Empire " is engaged and in which Canada takes part, while

in the last part of the clause he speaks of the five nations of the British "Commonwealth." In other words, we go into war as part of the British Empire and emerge from it as part of the British Commonwealth. My hon. friend knows as well as any one here that, according to one meaning of the term, you cannot say that an empire is a commonwealth; although, according to another meaning, the two terms are more or less identical. It is exactly the same in regard to the use of the word, " nation." If you wish to emphasize and lay particular stress on a certain legal technical point, then it cannot be said that Canada has all the rights, the privileges, and the attributes of a sovereign nation. But if, instead of looking merely at the letter of the word you look at the spirit of it, I think that everyone will be prepared to concede that, with the self-governing status which we have, we are to. all intents and purposes a nation. Now that is the point I would direct to the attention of my hon. friend. There is in Holy Writ a familiar passage which says: " The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life;" and that is as true in reference to the interpretation of constitutional documents as it is in reference to the Scriptures. If you rigidly follow the letter you kill what is real in the relationship between the different nations that comprise the Empire. If, on the other hand, you take the spirit of that relationship, then we distinctly have five nations forming a part of the British Empire or Commonwealth, by whichever name you choose to designate it. I should like to have that point made perfectly clear, and I trust I have done so in a way which will satisfy my hon. friend.
What, then, is the difference which exists between us and my hon. friend, or any of those associated with him, in regard to this question of the status of Canada? So far as I can see, we have no difference on what is fundamental as respects our status. Our difference is that hon. gentlemen opposite, and in particular my hon. friend, would have it appear, as I have already said, that our status is something newly acquired; that in some way or other which is inexplicable to us there has been a change within the last few years, and that we stand in a position now, from the legal and constitutional viewpoint, which we did not have before. We on this side of the House maintain that while there has been a clearer defining of the status of Canada, and while there has been unquestionably, and above all else, in the eyes of the world and from the international point of view, a recogni-

tion of the status of Canada through the splendid services of her armies overseas, and by reason of the valiant part they played in the great war, all these circumstances have served to emphasize and strengthen and make permanent a status which we already had and which we intend to maintain. If my hon. friend has any doubt at all on this point, I hope his mind will be disabused of any misgivings before I conclude.
By way of illustration of the point which I have been seeking to make clear, let me draw the attention of the House to the first Government^ notice of motion which appears on the Order Paper. In the name of my right hon. friend, the Minister of Justice, there appears the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that a humble address be presented to His Most Excellent Majesty, the King, in the following words:
To the King's Most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Tour Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the Commons of Canada, in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that you may graciously be pleased to give your consent to submit a measure to the Parliament of the United Kingdom, to amend the British North America Act 1867, in the manner following, or to the following effect- etc., etc.,	'
Note the words in that resolution. The prayer from this Parliament is not to the King to assent to an amendment of the British North America Act. It is to His Majesty to submit a measure to the Parliament of the United Kingdom to amend the British North America Act. If you take the letter of the Constitution alone will any one for one moment contend that this country is a sovereign nation to the degree of having all the rights and privileges which the British Parliament has when we have to go to the British Parliament to ask for an amendment to our Constitution? If you construe the Constitution according to the letter, you kill the spirit immediately because we know, as my hon. friend pointed out the other day, that if we ask the British Parliament to amend the Constitution according to the constitutional practice, it is almost certain to do so and, since it is almost certain to do so, we have to all intents and purposes the full rights and privileges of a sovereign people in reference to our own Constitution. But I would like to submit to my hon. friends opposite that perhaps it would be more in accord with the status which Canada has as a self-governing dominion or nation within the British Empire if, instead of presenting an address to His Majesty to ask

His Majesty's consent to the Parliament of the United Kingdom amending the British North America Act in the two particulars mentioned, the Government should consider the advisability of an address being presented to His Majesty to have powers given to the Parliament of Canada, subject to the concurrence of the several provinces of the Dominion, to amend the Constitution of Canada in such particulars as may be agreed upon as a result of conference between the provincial and federal authorities and approved by this Parliament and the legislatures of the different provinces.
T have here a copy of the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Australia and of the Dominion of New Zealand. Both Australia and New Zealand have the right to amend their own constitutions in the particulars mentioned therein. Why should this Parliament not have the same powers to amend its own Constitution, subject to the safeguards that are necessary to comply with the spirit of the Act of Confederation, as have these other nations within the British Empire?
As I have said, our difference with hon. members opposite is not at all upon the question of Canada's being a nation but upon the inference which they would convey that national status, or to put it in the phraseology of the minister, equality of status with the other nations of the British Empire, is something newly acquired, something to be credited to the present Administration. What we say is that Canada's status as a nation from the constitutional point of view was established long before the present Administration was formed and in spite of the opposition of some of its own members and their associates in the past. If any one doubts this I will quote my hon. friend an authority which he will not question. Indeed, I am prepared to leave the question of Canada's status as between hon. gentlemen opposite and gentlemen on this side of the House to the testimony of my hon. friend himself.
I have in my hand a copy of a splendid address-one of the many splendid addresses which my hon. friend has delivered. It was not delivered since the war, or since the present Administration of which he is a member was formed, but it was delivered in Montreal on November 11,	1912-nearly
eight years ago. The address is entitled:
A Short History of the Beginning and Growth
of Constitutional Government in Canada.
In it my hon. friend has set forth the constitutional development of this country and to whom the credit should be given in
that connection. Let me, without quoting too many extracts, just read a few that are significant as showing the position which we on this side of the House are prepared not only to maintain but which we are glad to have the opportunity of advocating and of furthering to the extent of our ability. My hon. friend started in by saying:
In all discussions of the relations of Canada to Great Britain and the other parts of the Empirei three questions (appear to (be uppermost in the public mind: Our political relations, our trade arrangements, and the defence of the Empire.
I am glad we have with us this evening a descendant of Papineau, a man, who, in the early history of our country, struggled to secure for the people of jhis province what William Lyon Mackenzie was struggling to secure for the people of Upper Canada-the right to manage their own affairs; and while we may not agree with the methods either pursued, we must agree that they were fighting against grave abuses and were struggling to redress serious injustice to the mass of the people of the two provinces.
The Rebellion of 1837, and the exceedingly able report of Lord Durham on the political conditions in Canada which followed the Rebellion constitute a convenient starting point for our discussion. Permit me to recall to your minds the records of the two political parties in this country from the Rebellion of 1837 down to the year 1911 on the three questions I have mentioned.
I am not going to quote at any great length, but just let me give one or two sentences.

subtopic: STATUS OF CANADA AS A NATION.
speechtext: Whose speech is that?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: STATUS OF CANADA AS A NATION.
speechtext:
It is the speech of my hon. friend the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Rowell): He says:
The four main events in the development of our political relations during this period were: (1) the struggle for and securing of responsible government: (2) Canadian Confederation, including the purchase of the Northwest Territories; (3) the evolution of Canada from the position of a colony of Great Britain to that of one of the free self-governing nations of the Empire; (4) the creation of a truly Imperial organization under the name of "The Imperial Conference."
I wish to remind hon. members that this is an address which was delivered on the 11th of November, 1912. The Armistice was signed on November 11, 1918. It was in 1912 that my hon. friend was speaking. After mentioning the great fight for responsible government, he says:
Around this issue the battle waged for years, Baldwin and Lafontaine leading the Liberal forces,	.
What further does my hon. friend say? He says:

The Conservative party in Great Britain clung just as tenaciously to government by Downing Street as did the Conservatives in this country.
Then he goes on:
The only party that believed in responsible government as being essential to the progress and prosperity of Canada, and that the granting of this right of self-government would not only not weaken but strengthen our loyalty to the Crown and the Mother Country, was the Liberal party in Canada.
My hon. friend makes the position clearer when he declares:
The result of the Conservative policy was the Family Compact, the Rebellion of 1837, and the long and bitter struggle which retarded the progress and development of Canada, and divided the people of Canada into two hostile camps. The result of the Liberal policy was the securing for Canada-
Listen to this:
-and ultimately not only for Canada but the other colonies of the Empire-of the right to manage their own affairs, and with that right the peace and progress of the country and a great increase in affection for and the desire to maintain British connections.
Then my hon. friend says:
This great discovery of colonial self-government, which, according to Sir Herbert Samuel, is one of the two great contributions in the sphere of Government which the British people have given to the world, was made, was wrought out and secured by the Liberal party in Canada.
My hon. friend goes on to say:
Their labour has made the Empire as it exists to-day possible.
I shall pass over what my hon. friend has had to say about the question of Confederation and the part played by the two parties in this country in that connection, and what he has said about the acquirement of the Northwest territory. He concluded, however, that part of his address by saying:
Here again it was the policy of the Liberal leader and the Liberal party which forced this great question to the front, and was so largely instrumental in securing these territories for Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, lest it might appear that we were getting away from this all important question of the status of Canada, and Canada's status as a nation within the British Empire, I am pleased to see that my hon. friend has devoted a considerable part of his address to that one particular subject. " The changed status of Canada," he calls it. Now let me read what he says in that connection:
When Sir Wilfrid Laurier went to England to attend the Diamond Jubilee of Queen Victoria-
That was in 1897, 23_ years ago-

In one of his very first public utterances he took the position that Canada was no longer a colony but a nation. He said:	" The authority
of the Queen does not rest on military force, but from the Pacific to the Atlantic rests on the cheerful allegiance of five million people who feel themselves a nation. The feeling dominating Canada is one of pride in her local autonomy and legislative liberty connected with Imperial unity."
That is the end of the quotation from Sir Wilfrid Laurier's speech and my hon. friend goes on:
Throughout his stay in Great Britain Sir Wilfrid consistently maintained the position that Canada had reached the status of a nation. When he returned to the city of Montreal, and the citizens extended such a memorable welcome to him he again emphasized that position. He said:	He had longed to live to
see the day when Canada would no longer be a colony, but would be a free nation within the Empire, and he was glad to be able to say he had lived to see that day.
Mr. Speaker, whatever doubt there may be on the other side of the House, as to Canada's status, there can be no doubt as to the position which we of the Liberal party of Canada have had in regard thereto. My hon. friend has stated it accurately, he has stated it truly, and as he has stated it here every one of us is prepared to see that it is maintained along those lines. But what was the position-and here I should like to point out there are times and seasons for all things-of hon. gentlemen opposite? To-day they are saying a great deal about Canada being a nation. They are able to do so, why? Because the struggle which the Liberal party maintained for a quarter of a century in this country has at last, through the great service of our men overseas, come before the world in its true and bold form. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said: "Let us have the attributes of a nation and when the time of stress comes Canada will respond and do her duty by the Empire." Was not his prophesy fully fulfilled? Was it not because we had the status of a nation, because we believed we had the status of a nation, that Canada played the part which she played in this great war? I think one of the most significant things in the history not only of Canada but of the world is the fact that when this war came on, so far as I am aware, the British Government asked nothing of this Dominion; that everything that was done was done voluntarily and freely by the people of Canada through their Government. How did that come about? It came about as a consequence of Canada recognizing that she had the status of a nation, that she had said: "Recognize our status as
