speechtext:
a nation and we will do our part." Had she been held in a colonial position is it possible to believe that she would have responded as she did at that time?
But, as I have said, it is one thing to proclaim Canada a nation to-day; it was another thing to proclaim Canada a nation twenty-five years ago in the heart of the British Empire across the seas, and that is what Sir Wilfrid Laurier did. He did not wait, he spoke, he blazed the way. There at the Queen's Jubilee when all the nations were looking on he took that position and from that time he fought steadily to see that it was maintained in every particular. I might quote not only the address my hon. friend has referred to, but also a speech which Sir Wilfrid Laurier made at the constitutional club in London, England, on July 7, 1902. I have in my hand a report which appeared in the London Times on the day following and what is the expression used there? Every member of the House will recall the expression and the occasion of its use. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
You may search the annal3 of history so far as the human eye can pierce into them, and you shall not find a parallel to the spectacle of which you are to-day the witness. The Empire of Rome in the heyday of her splendid power never reached that level of moral attitude. And the reason is obvious. The Empire of Rome was composed of slave states; the British Empire is a galaxy of free nations.
That is where we get for the first time the expression of the British Empire as a group of free nations. Sir Wilfrid Laurier used the striking, the poetic phrase "a galaxy of free nations." Hon. gentlemen opposite to-day use the expression "A community of free nations," or "A cluster of free nations," or " A family of free nations." Call it by any name you like the essence of the whole relationship is in the phrase Sir Wilfrid Laurier used, " A galaxy of free nations," and from that moment up to the present time we have sought to maintain that position-that is, all of us who have fought for Liberal tradition and sought to maintain it.
Now, what was the attitude of the Conservative press towards Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he took that stand? What was the attitude of some of those who belong to the party opposite? My hon. friend the 'Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Rowell) has told the country. He says in this address:
What was the attitude of the Conservative press in regard to this? They charged Sir Wilfrid with being a separatist.
He goes on to quote from the Mail and Empire and he mentions that other Conservative journals and leaders of the Conservative party took the same position and indulged in the same criticism. He adds:
They failed to perceive that which Sir Wilfrid Laurier and those who shared his views saw, that there can be no permanent basis of union and no permanent plan for co-operation between the peoples of the Empire with a dominant race living in one country to which those living in a self-governing Dominion would be more or less subject; that the future of the Empire as well as its strength, and stability depended upon a frank recognition of equality in the status of the people in the selfgoverning Dominions with those of the Mother Country.
Note those words. I imagine my hon. friend might be tempted to say that while we had sought to maintain a certain status, we had not equality of status as we have it to-day. But here are his own words: either he spoke what was true then, or he did not speak what was true then. I think my hon. friend will say that he believes he was speaking the truth then as he believes he is speaking the truth to-day and at that time (1912) he said:	Sir Wilfrid
Laurier took the position that the strength of the British Empire and its stability depended upon a frank recognition of equality in the status of the people in the selfgoverning Dominions with those of the Mother Country. My hon. friend says further:
This assertion of our national status was necessary for the people of Canada to develop our own national self-consciousness and our own self-respect. It was necessary for the people of Great Britain in order that they might realize that they were dealing not with subjects but with fellow citizens. That this is our position, and that we are now a nation, is not only recognized by the statesmen of Canada but by the statesmen of the Mother Country.
The other day my hon. friend asked permission of the House to place on record certain excerpts from speeches delivered by the Right Hon. Arthur Balfour, the Right Hon. Lord Milner and by General Smuts. He told the House that the reason he wished to place these particular extracts on Hansard was to make it perfectly plain that not only was the status of Canada recognized here among Canadians, but that it was also recognized by the great leaders of thought and opinion overseas. Well, my hon. friend adopted exactly the same method in 1912, and he placed on record then in the course of his address before the Montreal Reform Club quotations from British statesmen to precisely the same effect. I shall not take the time of the House to read

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
them, but instead of quoting General Smuts he quoted Sir Frederick Pollock. He also quoted Mr. Balfour and Mr. Asquith. He quoted all these gentlemen, for what purpose? To show that our position as a nation was not only recognized by the statesmen of Canada, but was equally recognized by the statesmen of the Mother Country. He said:
Nowhere have I seen this changed relationship more clearly stated than in an article on the Imperial Conference written by the editor of the Round Table. Referring to the resolution passed by the Colonial Conference in 1907, establishing the Imperial Conference, this writer says:
" This resolution"-
-that is, a resolution passed in 1907, when, I think, my hon. friend for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was present-
-" established the status of the Dominions as national entities, entirely distinct from that which inhabited the British Isles. It recognized that the basis of Imperial organisation was the co-operation of live nations, not the centralization of power in the hands of the British Government as an Imperial Parliament. It finally destroyed the older conception of Imperial development, as a gradual re-union of the colonies with the Mother Country through representatives in either of the British Houses of Parliament." .
But, Mr. Speaker, there are two or three more clauses that I wish to read. These are, I think, perhaps the most conclusive of any of the utterances cxf my hon. friend-and I again remind the House that these statements were made in the city of Montreal on November 11, 1912:
Some of the most important changes in our British constitutional system were not brought about by any Act of Parliament or legislature, but by the demand on the one hand for new or enlarged rights and powers, and the recognition of these rights and powers on the other. This momentous change from a colony of Great Britain to that of one of the free nations of the Empire did not require any Act of Parliament -British or Canadian-for its consummation It simply required a demand on our part for a new status and the acceptance and recognition of that new status on the part of Great Britain
I venture to suggest-
It gives me, Mr. Speaker, particular pleasure to read these words at this time and iir this place-
I venture to suggest that when the history of our constitutional development ds written among the great things that Sir Wilfrid Laurier has done none will appear greater than his perception of the fact that the status of Canada must be changed and that this change must be brought about, not by legislative enactment, but by the demand on our part for a new status, persisted' in until the people of Canada were convinced of its necessity; persisted in until the statesmen of Great Britain were convinced that it was right. By this great achievement Sir Wilfrid has enlarged the liberties and

improved the status of every Canadian citizen, and what he has done for Canada he has done for all the self-governing Dominions.
My hon. friend uttered those words while Sir Wilfrid Laurier was alive. I ask him: Will he not be the first to say that they are equally true now that Sir Wilfrid Laurier is jio longer here?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does my hon. friend want an answer?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should be pleased to receive an answer.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say undoubtedly they are true. And what is true of Sir Wilfrid Laurier is equally true of Sir Robert Borden in connection with the work of the Peace Conference and the League of Nations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon.
friend's statement just made in such a straightforward and honourable way is interesting not only in regard to the meed of praise which he is prepared to concede to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but also because of his reference to Sir Robert Borden.
Let me repeat here, Mr. Speaker, that my purpose in quoting my hon. friend is not in any way to belittle the work of Sir Robert Borden or of the hon. gentlemen who were associated with him. I would say frankly that Sir Robert Borden and his colleagues stood firm for the maintenance of Canada's status-they did their duty by Canada in that regard. If they had done less they would have been derelict in their duty and would have been liable to the censure of this Parliament. Having done their duty, and done it well, they are entitled to the thanks of this Parliament and of this country.
But, Sir, let me add this from the words of my hon. friend in regard to what Sir Robert Borden and his colleagues have been able to achieve. They are the very next words that appear in the speech from which I have been quoting:
The welcome which Mr. Borden and his colleagues received last June was only made possible because of the work Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his colleagues had done for Canada.
I will ask my hon. friend if those words are not equally true?
'Mr. ROWELL: If my hon. friend wishes an answer I am quite prepared to give it. I believe those words are equally true. I am prepared to give credit to whom it is due, and I think the other side should be just as ready to give credit ro Sir Robert Borden and his colleagues too.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I hope we are.
I should like to make it perfectly clear that in this matter we are not seeking for honours; all we wish is to have the position made clear and plainly stated. As between us, if you will, honours may be evenly divided. What I wish to make perfectly plain is what my hon. friend himself has emphasized, namely that the welcome which Sir Robert Borden subsequently received was only made possible because of the work that Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his colleagues had done for Canada.
This is the next paragraph:
To-day-this was 1912-we stand in our relationships and in our negotiations, both in the mind of the people of the mother country and in the mind of the people of the other selfgoverning dominions, as one of the five free nations that go to make up the Empire. It is again the work of Liberal leaders and the triumph of the Liberal policy which has laid the broad foundation upon which alone the future strength and security of the Empire can rest.
Just one word in regard to the development of" an Imperial organization. My hon. friend went on to say:
Some of our Conservative friends are very fond of talking about Imperial organization, they are fond of talking about representation in some Imperial body, they are talking about Canada having some voice in Imperial affairs.
I think this will interest particularly my hon. friend for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding):
While they have been talking and dreaming the Liberal leaders of Canada and the Liberal leaders of Great Britain and of the other Dominions, have been creating a truly Imperial organization for dealing with Imperial affairs.
We have in the Imperial Conference a truly representative body which, up to the present time, has proved itself capable of dealing with all important matters of Imperial concern ....
It is important for us to bear in mind some of the characteristics of this Conference. It recognizes the national status of the Dominio'ns, as distinct from the mother country; it is truly representative in its character, being composed of the Prime Ministers of the mother country and self-governing Dominions; it is responsible in that each Prime Minister has back of him a parliamentary majority, and therefore has the power to implement the resolutions to which he gives assent; it recognizes the autonomy of all the governments and no resolution affecting any particular government can become effective unless assented to by it.
And this further word:
But Sir Wilfrid's contribution towards securing for us a safe and effective Imperial organization is not limited to a suggestion as to the form and work of the Imperial Conference. He has also done good work for Canada and the Empire in assisting to defeat proposals for Imperial organization which would have seriously impaired our rights of
self-government. In so doing, he was not only fighting for Canada, but he was fighting for the whole British Empire. '
That leads me to conclude by referring to the concluding remarks of my hon. friend the other day. After he had spoken at considerable length of the status of Canada, he said something to the effect that the choice to-day was between remaining part of the group of free nations comprising the British Empire and, on the one hand, either reverting to the old Colonial status, or, on the other, going in for complete independence. All of us will agree that it is unthinkable to speak about any return to the old colonial status; but my hon. friend did not put his hand on the real danger when he spoke .about the alternative being complete independence. The thing about which we on this side of the House are alarmed is not independence or the maintenance of the status which we have as one of the nations comprising the British Empire. The thing we are concerned about and what we fear is the danger of swinging to the other extreme and developing a form of centralised Imperialism which we think would be thoroughly objectionable so far as the interests of tins country are concerned. It is not to any status of Canada as one of the nations within the British Empire that we take exception. We wish :o see that position maintained and strengthened; but we do not wish to see, through any insidious or other method, a condition of affairs brought about whereby the full autonomy of this country and o' this Parliament will in any way be lessened or impaired by any scheme of Imperialism which will lead to a centralisation of the control of the British Empire, instead of the maintenance of the free self-governing position which we are privileged to enjoy at the present time.
We believe that position can be maintained by holding to the attitude of conference and consultation which was developed under the old Liberal administration; that it is possible for the British Empire to become, as regards the League of Nations, a league within a league, if you like, for the preservation of freedom amongst the different nations of the world. That position will be maintained by the attitude of conference and co-operation; it will not be maintained by a development which will lead to the loss of either of those features through any centralising tend-
5 p.m. ency one way or another. So, to make plain the position that we on this side take in regard to the question of status and what has happened in the last few
m

years, we would say that the change that has taken place in Canada's status as a result of the war-and there has been in the last few years an emphasis which there had not been for many years previously-has not been any change in the nature of our status, but has been, as regards the British Empire and relations within the British Empire, a clearer defining of a status already existing. As regards the world, there has been an international recognition of that status such as never existed hitherto in the history of the British Empire, and for that international recognition we are first and last, and shall always be most indebted to the services of Canada's armies across the seas. That is where the credit belongs for the international recognition which has come; and as I have already said, as regards the clearer definition of the status, we are prepared and are glad to concede to the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and his colleagues that they have done their duty well in maintaining that status firmly.
So long as, in the last analysis, all matters pertaining to Canada in her external or inter-imperial relations are made subject to the approval of this Parliament, so long as no action can be taken of which the Parliament of Canada does not have ample opportunity to approve, we shall feel that to all intents and purposes, we are a nation in the true sense of the word. But let the sovereignty of this Parliament be impaired as respects anything that concerns Canada in either her inter-imperial or international relations, and we shall feel that the position of Canada as a nation has been menaced to that extent.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall have occasion to say, with regard tp what the hon. gentleman (Mr. King) has said, some words that will, unfortunately, not be words of congratulation. I hasten, therefore, at the very outset, to offer him some words of congratulation for which I think his speech calls. I congratulate him for permitting us to listen to a different tale from what we .listened to at the last session of this House when we spoke about Canada's status as a nation. I have not time to quarrel with the hon. gentleman about his reservations;
I have not time to quarrel with him with regard to the question as to what particular Canadian or Canadians we owe the fact of Canada's status as a nation. I am content to congratulate him and to congratulate this country that he, as the leader of the great Liberal party-and at the last session we expected that the leaders of the great
	.
Liberal party would have taken the attitude that he took, but we were disappointed- with, as I say, certain reservations which he thought necessary to make for fear that somebody who never claimed any credit, might get it, has recognized, speaking for his party, that Canada has achieved the status of a nation within the great British Commonwealth-if he will permit me that word, as he does not seem to like it-and a nation standing on a footing of equality with the other nations of the Commonwealth. I congratulate him that he has agreed with us on that. We were amazed when people did not agree with us on that. We are gratified now to find that, on second thought and under a second leader, the Liberal party, as represented in this House, does agree with us.	.
I shall have occasion to refer to that-portion of the hon. gentleman's address in which he belittled the importance of that by thinking it worth while to enter into a discussion as to who got it for us, as though it were not manifest to all of- us, and as though any Canadian with heart and head large enough to be worthy to call himself a Canadian, were not prepared to recognize the obvious fact that that status was the result of a growth, a growth to which succeeding statesmen, one after another, contributed. Let me say at once, that I take off my hat without hesitation in respect to the memory of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the great contribution that he made to that growth. All that surprises me is that the hon. gentleman (Mr. King) should have thought it necessary to quarrel with some imaginary person who had .set up a claim that in the twinkling of an eye Canada had been made a nation, and made a nation by some one individual yesterday or the day before. If he would have taken the pains to read what was said in this House at the last session, he would have seen that no such contention was ever made. I ask him now, whether by or on behalf of anybody who had the honour to represent Canada at the Conference in Paris, any such claim was made as that we had made Canada a nation. Mr. Speaker, I shall have occasion to refer later to that very long and very laboured part of the hon. gentleman's address.
Let me go back to the beginning and take up some of the things that lamentably call for answer, if it be merely for the purpose of giving information to the hon. gentleman about some things that he does not know. The hon. gentleman said that this Treaty was brought before this House

merely as an excuse- for the making of a speech, and he -asked why there was any need to -bring the Treaty before the House, because in the first -place, he said, there was nothing in it that related particularly to the Dominion of Canada, and in the second place, nothing that this Parliament might say about it -could have the slightest effect upon the binding nature of that Treaty or alter its provisions by one iota,- by the dotting of an "i" or the crossing of a "t," I think he said. He said that this Parliament could do nothing in the matter because the Treaty was signed some months ago, and signed not only on behalf of the other nations of the British Empire, but on behalf of Canada, and he -asked, "What are you going to do about it?"
The hon. gentleman does not know that treaties do not bind until they are ratified. The hon. gentleman who has talked -so eloquently -about- our status as one of the nations of the British Empire apparently does not know that this Treaty was signed by the British Empire. He does not know that when you want the signature of the British Empire you get the -signatures of all the nations that constitute the British Empire. The hon. gentleman does not know that, just as he does not know what a most elementary knowledge of international law would have taught him, that treaties -do not bind until they -are ratified. He does not know that when the British Empire proceeds to ratify a treaty it takes the whole British Empire to do it. Why, the hon. gentleman whom I -have congratulated on -sharing our views on Canada's national status, has not quite fully grasped what it means. He still imagines, as other hon. gentlemen opposite who spoke on this matter at the last session of the House evidently imagined, that-thereisa something somewhere which i-s the British Empire and which makes treaties, and that there is a Canada standing off on the side, and that the British Empire is making and ratifying treaties, or refusing to ratify treaties while Canada stands on the side not interested in the slightest degree.

Does my hon. friend mean to say that if this Treaty be not approved by the Parliament of Canada it will -not be binding on -the whole British Empire just the same, having been approved by His Majesty the King?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Treaty has not as yet been ratified by His Majesty the King. His Majesty the King, as the constitutional sovereign of Canada just as much as he is the constitutional -sovereign of the United
Kingdom, has adopted as his guide of action that he will not ratify -a treaty binding upon the entire Empire until he has had the advice of the Governments o-f each and every one of the self-governing nations that make up -the Empire. His Majesty the King does not sign on behalf of the Empire because the United Kingdom tells him to do so.
My hon. friend has hardly met my question. Is -the approval of this Treaty by this Dominion essential to the binding effect of the Treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. In order that the Treaty shall bind the British Empire it is necessary that it -shall be executed with the approval of all the self-governing nations of the British Empire, and Canada it one of them.
And if this Parliament -should for -any reason not approve, this Bulgarian Treaty would have no effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not -saying it would have no effect, but it would have no effect so far as Canada is concerned. It would not bind the British Empire. It would bind, -if you will, -such par-ts of the British Empire as chose to ratify it, but it would not bind the whole British Empire. Have hon. gentlemen read -the Treaty?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not surprised then.
There is not an hon. member of this House who has read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Much is now clear to me.-Hon. gentlemen -have not read the Treaty.
Does my hon. friend say he has read it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have read it and reread it, and I did not get very -far into it until I found out that one of the parties to the Treaty is the British Empire.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Did my hon. friend find any -mention o-f Canada in the Treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly I did. In the very opening paragraphs of the Treaty His Majesty -the King of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British Dominions overseas -and as Emperor of India,-acting in those capacities for the entire Empire- when he came to tell for whom and through whom he acted thought it worth while to mention Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My right hon. friend has not answered the question I asked. He says he read the Treaty through and I have asked him to be kind enough to inform the House whether on any page of that Treaty there is any mention whatever of Canada, not in the signatures but in the text of the Treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend wish to know whether there was some special thing that was provided for Canada?	.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No; that is not the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There was no mention cf Canada because we were not looking for anything special. But, Mr. Speaker, it is significant that this question should be asked by the hon. gentleman who boasts of his pride in Canada's status as a nation standing on a footing of equality. What is the tacit suggestion of his question? It is virtually this: Unless we wanted some particular thing for Canada, this great nation, of which he is so proud, should not have had anything to do with the Treaty. My hon. friend said he did not read the Treaty. Let me point out to him-
Will the minister pardon me? It was I who said that I had not read the Treaty. I tried to do so, but I may confess that I did not read every line, for I found it too arduous a task.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not care to go further than to point out who are parties to the Treaty and how they are constituted. The party for whom His Majesty is acting is the British Empire, but His Majesty knows what it is that constitutes the Empire and he therefore informed those with whom he was contracting that when he contracted for the British Empire he did so on behalf of the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India, etc. He made it clear that he contracted for Canada, Australia and the other Dominions through their plenipotentiaries, and what constituted the signature of the British Empire was the combination of all those signatures. That is why I say that if you strike off one of those signatures, or if ratification fails on the part of one of those nations, you cannot have the signature nor the ratification of the entire British Empire. About that there seems to be no room for question. It is for them who made the contract to ratify it. If the contract could not be made without the participation of all the constituent nations of the Empire, how, I ask, is it to

be ratified without similar participation on the part of'those nations? This is one of those things which to me seem so obvious that I can only wonder that people do not perceive it.

I dare say the minister remembers that Lord Milner, speaking for the Crown authorities of Great Britain, submitted an opinion to the Canadian Government in regard to the signing of the German Treaty in which he told us that our ratification of that Treaty was not necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Taking, for example the German Treaty, suppose that four or five nations of the British Empire had given their assent to the ratification and one had refused that assent, what, in the opinion of the minister, would have been the action of His Majesty?	t

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is perhaps rash foi
me to answer a question based upon the hypothesis which the hon. gentleman puts. I cannot tell what His Majesty would have done. That is something that I would not like to take upon myself to say but I do venture this expression of opinion-I might say conviction-that whatever His Majesty did in the absence of the assent of one of the self-governing nations of the Empire, would not constitutionally be binding upon the entire Empire and more particularly would not he binding upon that nation of the Empire which had withheld its assent. What would be the effect upon the existence of the Empire of a divergence of that kind is another question. What would be the necessary consequence of such a situation arising is something the discussion of which I would not like to enter upon at the present moment. My impression is that the consequence might he very grave indeed. But this after all is only a consequence of the fact that the great thing that holds this Empire together is that we have so far found it possible to get together on the great, vital and important questions, and for my part I have abundant confidence that for years, and years,

and years-I might venture to say centuries -we shall continue in that happy position. It is not necessary for me to undertake to prophesy what will happen after the nations of the British Empire disappear. All I am concerned with is to point out that in order to get the evidence of their agreement you must have the action of all of them.
The hon. gentleman, in dilating upon the entire absence of reason for bringing this Treaty here, intimated that at the last session of Parliament there had been no dif-fence of opinion about the League of Nations. He seemed to have entirely forgotten that the hon. gentleman who sits next to him (Mr. Fielding) had proposed to amend the League of Nations and to put in a reservation to one of its provisions.

Is it not true that the reservation proposed by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) last year was almost identical with the interpretation of clause 10 given by the Minister of Justice himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not criticising the amendment which was proposed. I am only pointing out that the hon. gentleman says that there was no difference of opinion upon it when as a matter of fact there was, in the opinion of the hon. gentleman, a sufficient substantial difference of opinion that he thought it necessary to divide the House upon it. Now they tell us that they took up the time of the House with a division about something that did not differ materially from what the Minister of Justice thought.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Just for the sake of accuracy in the matter, as I recollect the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) it was to the effect that in so far as military service was concerned, nothing Parliament was doing in approving the Treaty would countenance Canada's taking part in future wars excepting with the approval of the Parliament of Canada. That was the substance of the amendment and that is practically what we are contending for to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. gentleman has quite accurately analysed the effect of the amendment proposed but I do not believe we would gain anything by threshing out what the amendment was or whether it should have been adopted or not. I only mentioned it to show that there was something or other that arose in connection with the League of Nations which necessitated dividing this House and that did not seem to be quite consistent with

the statement that there had been no difference of opinion in connection with the provisions of the League of Nations. The hon. gentleman also dealt with some observations of the President of the Privy Council in which he had reiterated our views in regard to the League of Nations, the Labour clauses, and other provisions. It may be that it was not absolutely necessary to do that but after all it was very eloquently and effectively done and I think this House will quite forgive the President of the Privy Council for having impressed these things not only upon the House and the public of Canada but upon a public that is wider than the public of Canada. The same thing might be said in this connection in reference to matters in regard to which the position of Canada was reaffirmed in the speech of the hon. gentleman.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. King) also dilated upon the possible distinction between what we meant when we said that Canada was a nation and something else that might be considered essential to Canada's ^being a nation. I do not grasp what the distinction is that the hon. gentleman is seeking to make. I do not realize that there may be respects in which Canada is not an absolutely sovereign state, but I confess I know of no national attribute of which Canada is not possessed. It does pot prevent Canada's being a nation that she should be joined and associated with other nations, acting in co-operation with them in the partnership that we call either the British Empire or the British Commonwealth, as you will. As to the meaning to ,be attached to either of these words, I think if you applied the technical meaning to the word " Empire," the old-fashioned meaning which implied dominating over o'ther powers, it would be incorrect to talk about the British Empire. The domination feature has long since disappeared, and certainly so far as the nations that compose that Empire are concerned, to state that we are all now on a footing of equality, would describe our relation to each other, and the term " Empire" is not perhaps the one to apply to a combination of nations so constituted. From my own part I think that " Commonwealth " is a most excellent word, but I would not quarrel with the words employed, anyway.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am afraid that my right hon. friend has misunderstood what I said. I was not taking exception to the word " Commonwealth in fact, I prefer the use of the word " Commonwealth " to the use of the word " Empire." What I was endeavouring to point

out was that the question of determining the status of Canada as a nation depends entirely upon the meaning to be attached to the term made use of. According to the way in which the word " Empire " is used, it may mean an excellent thing, or it may mean the very opposite. The same with regard to the word " Nation."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think there is a distinction to be made between a sovereign state and a nation. The latter may be a nation and not a full sovereign state. I do not propose to enter into the question of whether or not Canada is entitled to, or claims to be a full sovereign state. The hon. gentleman has discussed the question of Canada's status, and here I want to be careful; I am not claiming anything for anybody; I am only stating a fact. At the conference of 1917 we had the catagorical announcement by the United Kingdom, and assented to of course by all the Dominions, that the status of Canada, and of the Dominions within the Empire, was the status of nations standing on a footing of equality. We got this much further, and I should not say that, because the one thing I want to avoid is the evoking of discussion on the ground of what we are claiming for ourselves. We are happy to rejoice over what Canada has got, and let the glory go to anybody who thinks it is worth while to hunt out and claim that glory for himself. So long as Canada has the great substantial benefit accruing from that status our hearts are rejoiced and are proud for Canada's sake. What did happen that was made manifest to the world was this: We had been clearly and unmistakably acknowledged to he in the family circle in the resolution of 1917. There remained for us, if I may use the expression, to be taken out and introduced into the society of nations as a nation among the other nations. The old Mother Nation took us up and presented us to the other nations and said: These are the nations of my family; we will not stop to talk about definitions, I am bringing them into the society of nations; that is the society they are corning into. That is what happened. And that I contend is of very great value, not as making us a nation, but as giving evidence that the world recognizes.
The hon. gentleman referred to a couple of resolutions which were upon the Order Paper as indicating in some way a lack of completeness in respect of national status on our part. Now nobody has ever disputed that legally the legislative power is supreme in the Parliament of the United Kingdom
and it follows that the British North America Act-though in reality and in substance a compact between the provinces is in form an act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom. Such being the case when that Act has to be modified we have to go through the form of addressing ourselves to that Parliament of the United Kingdom. But to suggest 'that that throws any doubt upon our constitutional status as a nation within this Empire I think only implies a confusion between what may be the requirements of law and what, side by side with those requirements of law, may be the constitutional rights of the nations or peoples within the Empire. We have the two things, we have the law and the constitution, and they do not always agree-sometimes they are in absolute contradiction.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That was
exactly my position.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
went on to say, apropos of this condition, that what we ought to have, instead of what we are asking in these resolutions, is a power in this Parliament, subject to the concurrence of the provinces, to amend our own constitution. In that I am most heartily at one with the hon. gentleman. I am not quite certain how the idea came to him but it does happen to be a fact that before the hon. gentleman made the suggestion, before this matter arose in the House at all, I had taken up that very question with the attorneys general of the several provinces and in discussing these resolutions on the Order Paper with some gentlemen upon the opposite side of the House, I so informed them. I do not know whether that was the way the idea came back to the hon. gentleman or not; but if it should not he so it only shows how great minds naturally converge upon the same idea.
The leader of the Opposition spoke to me about it last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am glad that the hon. gentleman (Mr. King) has given due reflection to the subject but the fact is as I have stated. I rather inferred, therefore, that the way I have explained. is the way it came about. At all events I am glad to be confirmed now in my own view. I am all the more glad to find that I was confirmed in advance by the leader of the Opposition. We will have the opportunity, I hope, to co-operate in bringing about the desired result and we will not stop to quar-

rel about who is entitled to the credit of having thought about it first.
I was going to say one or two words with regard to the question as to what party did most to make Canada a nation. It is discouraging, it makes one wonder whether we have reached a national size after all when we cannot venture to congratulate each other and advance in our national status without at once falling into a bickering dispute as to who did the most to bring it about. I might go back to the past and claim for the men of the Conservative party-for the men of the Liberal-Conservative party at all events-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -the party of Cartier and Macdonald, who did so much to build up this Confederation,-I might claim that .they at the outset, accomplished perhaps as much as my friend's distinguished ancestor, (William Lyon .Mackenzie) and Lodis Joseph Papineau, by their readiness to stand up for the national status of Canada in those days.
They did not take the same chances.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Sir George Cartier took his share in the movement, and his name to-day stands high in the regard of all Canadians.
The hon. gentleman cited from the speech of the President of the Privy Council that one of the great steps in the building up of this nation was Confederation. I had an idea that John A. Macdonald had something to do with Confederation.
He opposed it to the very last; George Brown brought about Confederation

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I had the idea that
Macdonald and Cartier and many of their followers were Conservatives. And yet the hon. gentleman cites from a speech that recognizes, and rightly recognizes, what an immense step in the building up of our national edifice was Confederation, and then he says, "The Liberal party did it all."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member can only interrupt the Minister of Justice for the purpose of asking a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I have fallen into an error I shall be glad to be set right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I merely rise to correct a mis-statement. My hon. friend

asserted that I had said that, the Liberal party did it all. If certain names were not mentioned in what I quoted, it is not my fault; I was simply quoting from the speech of the President of the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At all events, my hon. friend impressed upon this House that the President of the. Privy Council had at some time taken that attitude. Well, the President of the Privy Council is a very eloquent advocate of the causes in which he believes, and I do not want to criticize what he may have said in earlier days. We all can recognize in him, at all events, the capacity for appreciating the light as it becomes brighter and more widespread,-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-and I have not any doubt that to-day he will find a place for the men I have mentioned among those who contributed to the building up of this nation.
I might cite speeches of Sir Robert Borden and of certain of his colleagues in the course of the Naval Debate of 1910, and I might also cite his speeches made at the very centre of the Empire in 1912 in which he stated in no uncertain tones that Canada would not be the adjunct of any nation whatsoever, nay, not even an adjunct of the British Empire.
Gentlemen, let us be fair all round. Let us recognize that there is a Canada in which we all have a share; let us recognize that part of our great inheritance as Canadians is the distinguished men that Canada has given us in the past,-and some of whom remain with us to the present day; let us recognize that those men are the pride and the glory of the Canada that in its entirety is the country of each one of us, and let us try to recall what they have done rather than say, "It was I; it was not you." Let us say: "That is what Canadians in the past did, and it is by deeds of that kind that this Canadian nation has been built up." And allow me to add a word-in which I am only joining with the hon. gentleman, -let us never forget that in rendering comparatively easy the fruition of that work the coping stone that confirmed the status we all rejoice in was laid by the soldiers who proved, as by no other means it could be proved, that Canadians had in them the stuff that made them worthy to have their country recognized as a nation, so that Canada could take her place in bearing the burdens of the world, and that having so taken her place, without counting the cost or the sacrifice, she was entitled to the open, ample and ungrudging recognition of

the world that she stood as a nation among nations, entitled to be heard not only concerning matters that interested her immediately, but to be heard in council when the Great Nations gathered together to devise what was best for the world and best for *mafikind. Let us see if from now on we cannot start out with one subject upon which we can be jn agreement.
As I have said, I would willingly admit that all of the credit belongs to the predecessors in title of the Liberals who sit opposite to me. If it is necessary I will say that, happily, all the credit to-day belongs to the gentlemen who sit upon the other side of the House. But after I have said that 1 shall still rejoice for that fact which stands out beyond peradventure, that when the nations gathered together there was a place for the Canadian nation. And I am sure that on both sides of this House we can, after all, appreciate the fact of how little importance it is whether at one time men who called themselves Liberals and at another time men who called themselves Conservatives were doing the work.
In regard to the question of our national status, we might well (take a leaf out of the book of the Mother Country, where they recognize that the relations of the country with the outside world, in other words, its foreign policy, is not a matter for party politics, but is carried on by government after government on well defined consistent lines, each successive administration profiting by the wisdom of its predecessor, and anxious to hand on in its turn some additional principle that may be availed of by its successor. Surely on this common ground of "Canada a Nation,'' we can stand together and rejoice together in the work of all those great Canadians who have helped to build up Canada, to all of whom without discrimination we are so grateful, and of all of whom without discrimination we are so proud.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution submitted for our approval is in all respects identical with the one that was presented for our consideration at the last session of Parliament, which session was called especially that we might give our assent to the Treaty with Germany. In the course of his remarks the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) made to this side of the House 31	f |	{
what one might call a supplication that we should be unanimous with regard to this resolution. I do not rise for the purpose of offering factious opposition to the resolution; but it appears somewhat strange that Canada should be requested on this occasion to assent to a Treaty between the Allied and Associated Foyers and Bulgaria, and that seemingly with the object of permitting His Majesty the King of England to ratify it. The man in the street, little conversant as he is with the affairs of the Balkan Peninsula, will undoubtedly be somewhat startled when he is made aware of the necessity for this Parliament to give its assent to such a Treaty, and the question will inevitably be asked whether it is true that such a radical and fundamental change in the political or international status, of Canada has taken place. Last year the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), and again this year the President of the Council, in periods pregnant with eloquence, repeatedly assured us of a powerful evolution, almost a revolution, in our political status which has brought Canada to the fore as a full-fledged nation in the councils of the world. No man in Canada is prouder than myself to see my country attain the status to which it is entitled by its economic development, by its almost inexhaustible natural resources in land, forest, fisheries, minerals and water-powers; by its ever-increasing manufacturing industries; by its geographical situation as between two great oceans; by its sturdy, thrifty, vigorous and labour-loving population, and last, but not least, b.y the heroic deeds of Canada's sons on the battlefields of Europe. These efforts of our soldiers were directed towards preventing the world from falling a victim to militaristic domination; but I fail to see in what-extraordinary degree Canada is gaining nationally or inter, nationally. The words "Canada's status," "Canada a nation," have been resounding in our ears from the treasury benches, during last session and also during this session; but since the days when Sir Wilfrid Laurier returned from the Imperial Conferences of 1897, 1902, 1907, 1909, with what I would call complete autonomy in matters commercial, in matters of immigration and in matters naval and military, a sentiment of national pride has pervaded the mind and soul of every man in Canada. That Canada is a nation is no new discovery. Canada was recognized as an autonomous nation many years before the war; but whilst up to the war Canada had inter-



national obligations commensurate -with her national status, to-day the indications are that the equilibrium is destroyed by the predominance of international obligations over the political international advantages.
Let not my words, however, be construed as meaning that I offer any opposition to the creation or establishment of a League of Nations. There is, I think, a unanimous sentiment in this country in favour of the establishment of suoh a League which will doubtless proVe to be an effective instrument for the maintenance of peace in the world. But Canada is not an independent nation; Canada is not a sovereign nation; and one has only to travel a few miles on the European continent or even in Great Britain to become fully aware of that fact. If I desired to prolong my remarks, I could quote many instances when, during my last trip to Europe, I was confronted with situations that made it perfectly plain and clear to me that Canada was not a sovereign nation and was not enjoying the same status as the United Kingdom, although the contrary has been affirmed and reaffirmed time - and again in this House.
Moreover, a suggestion was made this afternoon by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) that we must be at one with the other nations of the Empire; to differ with the other four nations of the Empire would be fraught with the gravest consequences. Here is a Treaty to which we are asked to assent, though our plenipotentiaries were breathing the pure air of Canada when its provisions were discussed, and drafted, and signed. It is true our good friend the High Commissioner for Canada in London has affixed his signature to this Treaty; but who will doubt for one moment that Sir George Perley crossed the Channel only for a few hours; that on a cool, bracing, beautiful morning of last autumn he took an automobile ride to this delightful little town called Neuilly-sur-Seine, that he signed the Treaty, undoubtedly without reading it, and that a few hours afterwards he re-entered the capital of France only to rush across the Channel again to his absorbing duties in London, and the next morning or perhaps the same day the news w'as flashed across the ocean that Canada had signed the Treaty of Peace? And Canada has signed the Treaty. We may take it for granted that at the time this perfunctory act was discharged by Sir George Perley, not one of our ministers, surely not the members of this Parliament and the people of this country knew or had the remotest idea of some of the provisions of this
