Treaty. Would you think, Sir, for instance, that the President of the Council, or my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster), who leads the House, kneiw anything about a certain point 1295 situated about 18 kilometres west of Kuchuk-Derbend, as a part of the boundary between Greece and Serbia? Or anything about the apex of a salient formed by the frontier of the Treaty of Sofia, 1915, about 10 kilometres east southeast of Jisr Mustafa Pasha? It is a matter of history, however, that Sir George Perley has signed this Treaty without a smile.
The contention has been made in this House that Canada has attained a new starus, a position that she did not enjoy and oi which she could not boast before the war. We all recall the pathetic picture which was drawn of the struggle made by the representatives of Canada at the door of the Peace Conference. To use a phrase' that was used in this House once by the late Mr. Israel Tarte, our representatives "fought like blazes" -to gain admittance into the room. I do not want to minimize the honour or the advantage accruing to Canada by participation in the Peace Conference, but I say that no struggle should have been necessary on the part of our representatives to enter the Peace Conference. Canada had supplied 500,000 men, 69,000 of whom had fallen for the cause of the allied countries, and when the representatives of the allied countries got together in conference to settle the terms of peace I submit that no objection whatever should have been offered to the presence of the Canadian representatives.
Of the League of Nations, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to say anything because I do not want to prolong my remarks, except to attempt to correct what I consider is a wrong impression conveyed, not intentionally I am sure, by some hon. ministers regarding the voting power of Canada. In Article 4 of the Covenant it is provided that a nation that is interested in a dispute under consideration and which is not a member of the council may be invited to send a representative to sit in the council. It has been claimed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and also by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) that sitting in the council in that way, as an invited guest, as it were, Canada would have the power to register a vote. But a perusal of subsequent clauses of the Covenant shows clearly that whenever Canada, or indeed any nation that is a member of the League, is interested in a dispute she is precluded from voting.

That the League of Nations will render immense services to mankind we cannot doubt. We need only recall the effects that the enactment of the Industrial Disputes Act has had in Canada, and if we may compare a big thing with a small thing we may expect that the League of Nations will at least render to the nations of the earth the service that has been rendered to this country by the Industrial Disputes Act.
Now, what is the new status of Canada within the Empire? No one so far has been able to draw from the Government the particulars of the new situation, if there is a new situation. It is true we have been told that Canada is one of five equal nations in the Empire, but when in the course of a debate last year my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council was invited by my hon. friend from Chambly and Ver-cheres (Mr. Archambault) to name the nations that constitute the British Empfre he replied that the British nation was composed of five nations equal in status, namely, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. The claim has been made repeatedly that they are all on an absolutely equal footing in matters Imperial, and, I take it, also in matters international. Now let us see whether the claim [DOT] is well founded. In order to ascertain whether the contention is just we must proceed by way of illustration. Surely the Parliament of Canada has no more extensive powers than the Parliament of the United Kingdom. That, I think, will be accepted as gospel by my friends on the other side. Last year we had some very interesting declarations from the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), whom I am sorry not tp see in this House at the present moment. He made the declaration that if Canada refused to assent to the German Treaty, His Majesty the King would not ratify it. Have I represented faithfully the declaration of the Prime Minister? If my hon. friends do not object, then I shall go on;-this is becoming more and more interesting as we proceed. For, if the British Empire is composed of five equal nations all enjoying an equal share of autonomy and power and discretion, it is only natural to presume that in some instances one of those nations will differ from the others. We might have a case, for instance, where the United Kingdom differed from the four other nations. Now, in order to enable the House to reach a clear comprehension of what is described as ''Canada's new political and 31J
international status," 1 would request the Government to inform the House what course would be adopted by the Sovereign in case the Parliament of the United Kingdom refused, to approve this Treaty with Bulgaria after the four other nations of the Empire had given their assent to it. Would ratification take place? Would His Majesty the King yield to the wishes of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and refuse to ratify? Or would he yield to the will of the parliaments of these four other nations of the Empire and sign the Treaty? Whichever cojirse he took, the consequences would be formidable for the United Kingdom. If the United Kingdom as one of five equal nations of the Empire refused to assent to a treaty accepted by the other four nations, there would be only one course open to the United Kingdom, and that would be to drop out of the British Empire. In other words, if one of the five nations refuses to assent to a treaty, then ipso facto a severance of that nation from the Empire takes place. I submit that this proposition, so preposterous, so impossible, so absurd and ridiculous as it appears, has its confirmation from no less an authority than the Prime Minister himself. During the consideration last year of the German Treaty, the right hon. gentleman, in presenting the resolution to the House, was subjected to a number of questions from hon. gentlemen on this side, and I shall read a passage from Hansard in which he makes a definite statement in reply to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). At page 22 of Volume 1, 1919, (Special Session) this question is put to the Prime Minister:
What difference does it make to us, the Empire, or the world, if we never ratify the Treaty at all?
In answer the Prime Minister said:
It makes this difference. Canada would stand out of and apart from the rest of the Empire ratifying the Treaty. It would virtually, I think, commit Canada to such absolutely independent action that she could not be regarded in the future as acting in co-operation with the other nations' of the Empire.
, So that in the event of the United Kingdom refusing to give her assent to a treaty to which the four other nations had assented, the United Kingdom would have to drop out of the British Empire! This, surely, would be a very grave occurrence. Whatever, therefore, may be the Canadian national interest in regard to the provisions of any given treaty, if we dared to disagree we would ipso facto be wiped out of the Britannic Commonwealth-that is,


if the explanation and interpretations given by the members of the Government iare to he relied upon. The Minister of Justice, has sat, I am sure, on very many occasions on a court of revision in the province of Quebec, and I feel satisfied that in filling that oflioe, in the able manner in which he has always performed his duties, some instances have arisen in which he ^differed from the two other judges. Yet he was not thrown out of the court; he remained in the court and the judgment was rendered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend not realize the difference between the two things? In the court you have a provision of law which enables the majority to render judgment. In the present instance you have five nations constituting one Empire, and if the assent of that Empire is needed there .is no provision by which the majority or any one of them can overrule any of the constituent nations. There is a manifest distinction between the two cases, I think.

I see the distinction perfectly, but I should like to know how it comes that there is no such provision in this matter. There should be a provision by which, if one of the nations differed, it should not be read out of the British Empire because of that difference; and if this provision is lacking I say that the whole responsibility rests upon the shoulders of ,my hon. friend. Until the Constitutional Conference which is to be held in London has taken place, no man amongst ordinary mortals can definitely state whether Canada has~ advanced or receded in recent times. This state of the proceedings is very nebu-4ous lindeed, It has been affirmed that Canada has undergone an organic change of political status. We have been told that three courses were open to us; ,First, to fall back into the colonial state; second, to develop as a free nation within the Empire; and third, to declare our independence. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) makes the emphatic protestation that he refuses to recede to the colonial state. So do we. The hon, minister rejects with indignation any suggestion of 'the severance of British connection. So do we. The middle course, that is, the development of Canadian autonomy within the Empire, he embraces passionately. So (io we. I will add, however, 'that this has been the policy of the Liberal party since the year 1896; hut there may be a different appreciation of what constitutes progress in the direction of enlarging national status. And I say, with the leader of the Opposition,

that if the development .contemplated is to surrender to an Imperial Cabinet the autonomy we now enjoy in naval and military questions, and in questions concerning (participation in wars and expenditures in connection therewith-and there are signs of this surrender on the horizon-then I say .we are retrogressing and not advancing. I would warn 'the Government, if they will .accept my warning, that in shaping the pew political edifice which is in the vision .of some imperialistic genius of England ,we should not start at the roof, the imperial cabinet. The edifice would undoubtedly be an imperial parliament, which would be founded on the desire of all parliaments within the Empire to be consulted. If those parliaments were consulted, judging by what I hear all over this country, you would not find any response to your call if you wanted to concentrate and centralize in London the administration of this Dominion. I can only repeat what .was so ably said the other day, and at the conclusion of the last session, ,by my hon. friend, the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). He adequately represented the opinion of the Canadian people'when he requested that this Parliament and this country be consulted before any scheme of Imperial Federation be launched, or indeed before any step is taken to alter the present status of Canada.
As far as I am concerned, I wish Godspeed to the nations of the Balkan peninsula. As to Bulgaria, I hope she may be happy; the Peace Conference has paid a great deal of attention to the welfare of the different races that may "inhabit that country. The Treaty which is submitted to us contains a whole section-section 4-in the political .clauses, devoted to the protection of minorities. This is certainly the section of the Treaty that appeals to me the most. Reading this section, and the political clauses of the Treaty generally, we are apt to wonder how in the world it is possible that we Canadians should have entered a conflict raging some three thousand miles away from us for the vindication of certain principles, when the very principles for which we have struggled, fought and vanquished, for which we have lost 60,000 of the flower and youth of this country, may not be upheld in certain important sections of Canada itself. The reflection comes to the mind of the casual observer that the minorities of the vanquished nations have profited more than the minorities of the victorious nations. For, if we turn to the Treaty, and in particular

to the clauses I have referred to, we find that it contains an enunciation of the principles which are deeply rooted in and in. separable from the heart and soul of every free man. I refer to the privileges guaranteed to linguistic and religious minorities. Nothing is more closely related to the love of God than religious creed, and nothing is more intimately associated with maternal love than the language learned at the knee of the dear parent. That these sacred and fundamental principles should have^-a place in the Treaty of Peace is an indication to me, Mr. Speaker, that they must have been ignored or disregarded and that the necessity of their public and solemn recognition is imperative.
In this respect the Treaty of Peace appeals to me more than in any other respect. It is a proclamation to the world at large that these principles should be upheld by all countries, and that this is undoubtedly the wish of the five Great Powers. Let me quote a few sentences by way of illustration. When you come , to page 24 of the Treaty you are right in the heart of the clauses that deal with the protection of minorities. Here is article 53. I shall read a paragraph:
All Bulgarian nationals shall he equal before the law and shall enjoy the same civil and political rights without distinction as to race, language or religion.
Let us go one step further-Article 54:
Bulgarian nationals who belong to racial, religious or linguistic minorities shall enjoy the same treatment and security in law and in fact as the other Bulgarian nationals.
Article 55:
Bulgaria will provide in the public educational system in towns and districts in which a considerable proportion of Bulgarian nationals of other than Bulgarian speech are resident, adequate facilities

Adequate facilities.

for ensuring that in the primary schools
the instruction shall be given to the children of such Bulgarian nationals through the medium of their own language.
And the last paragraph:
In towns and districts where there is a considerable proportion of Bulgarian nationals belonging to racial, religious or linguistic minorities, these minorities shall be assured an equitable share in the enjoyment and application of sums which may be provided out of public funds under the State, municipal or other budgets, for educational, religious or charitable purposes.
The nine articles of section 4 are in themselves a code of tolerance.
Resuming my seat, let me say that we concur in the resolution which is submitted
to us. We have only to reaffirm the position taken last year as to the supremacy and sovereignfy of the Canadian Parliament in the matter of participating in war as involved in Article 10. We are in accord with the Treaty because it embodies those principles of tolerance and justice which should be spread throughout the length and breadth of this country, for they constitute the foundation of a united Canada.
Right Hon. Sir GEORGE E. FOSTER (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I had no idea of speaking on this phase of the discussion which has been carried on in reference to the approval of the Bulgarian Treaty, and I disclaim any idea of making a speech at the present timei I would not have been on my feet had it not been for one remark made by the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), and reiterated by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Beland). I have been, if the House will allow me to say so, pleased with the spirit of the discussion which has taken place upon this Treaty.
In fact I might go a little further and say that I have been pleased with the tone of discussions in this House since the opening of the present session of Parliament; and I indulge the hope, as I most certainly cherish the desire, that we who begin our parliamentary work of this session in these new, artistic and ample surroundings, will express the spirit of this great edifice in its harmony of purpose, in its spiritualization of stone and wood into ideas and sentiments, and that it will have a restraining influence on all of us to be more kindly in our treatment of each other as partisans taking different angles of view, and will temper somewhat, and I hope greatly, what is apt in the best of us to degenerate sometimes into a mischievous, if not a malicious, baiting and hurting of one another.
For instance there is my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau). I meet him in the corridor, and I sit with him in the club once in a while. We converse together, and he thinks I am a very fair type of humanity. And, without any stretch of imagination or any great compulsion put upon me, I am making up my mind that, taken altogether, he is a pretty good sort of a fellow. We find that our ideas run pretty nearly parallel to each other, and as we sit and talk he would not try to make me feel that he thought I was a thief, a dishonest man, corrupt, over-extravagant, and everything of that kind. Now, when we leave our social converse, where we meet man to man, and separate oqrselves

on two sides of the House, the spirit of the aggregate gets into us, the spirit of the party, and when we get on our feet we look at each other through somewhat different glasses from those through which we see one another socially. But we are just as good men sitting opposite each other here as we were sitting side by side socially outside; and in the heart of each of us, no matter what he may be impelled to say in the heat and strife of party polities, we think the same of each other individually here as we did outside. Out of the Chamber we go back again to our social converse and we relapse into about the same relative attitude one to another.
Say that in French.

Well, what I
hope is that as we grow older and more experienced we will try and keep that softened and human spirit even in our strongest and bitterest debates and so make them less strong in that sense and less bitter. How often I think of things that I have said a long time ago, when I was more vigorous than I 4am now, and wish maybe that I had not said quite all I did say; and sometimes I feel that the same thought has come to others who have said things about me. Well, we grow wiser as we grow older, but we cannot try any too much along the line of keeping with us that human kindliness even in our party debates and our partisan discussions.
Now that is not in the way of a lecture; it is just in the way of a word by a man who has been a long time in politics, party and otherwise and who, looking over the past and the present and a little towards the future, feels that we might have done more if we had been less partisan and had thiown all the best of us into the treasury of the common good for the benefit of the country.
A great deal is said about our national status. I am not sure but that we have talked nearly enough about it for a while. It seems to me as if now we had pretty well " sturdied " ourselves, if there is such a word. We know where we are and there is not any difference between us as it seems. Suppose we take it for granted that we have an improved status-and let it go at that for a little while.
Having come to a point of virtual agreement, that is a good point for us to start from. And, having a common opinion with reference to what we are and just how great and how strong we are, let us put that greatness and strength into the push

forward for the development and betterment of our common country. We all know this is necessary. We have different points of view and these different points- of view will grade our expressions, grade our feelings ; but at heart we love our country equally, and we aie equally anxious that our country shall get the best that is in us for its betterment and development.
I have found that some of the things that I have got most praise for-and I have never got a great deal of praise for anything I have done, from hon. gentlemen opposite anyway-were things that fell into my lap, things that I could not help but be for when they came to fruition. But the fruit was not my fruit; it was the development of years and years before, which, under proper cultivation long continued, proper sunlight, and proper atmosphere, just at that particular time came to the period of its fruition, and the man who happened to be at the head of affairs, who happened to have taken that line and who therefore foresaw that development-and which had come out as a sort of fulfilment of the prophesy of his own-got the credit of it when the most part of that credit did not belong to him at all. Happily for him fruition came in his time. So, when we talk about Laurier founding a nation, or if we talk of others having founded and made the status of a nation within a certain time, let us be modest about it; for this nationhood that is given to us is the growth of centuries and has had its gradual evolution. We never would have had the nation and the status we have to-day if we had not first had Confederation. That was the forming point, the foundation; our after-greatness aggregated and developed upon that foundation. We never would have had Confederation if we had not had the earnest, honest, straightforward laborious struggle and work of the explorers, the voyageurs, the colonizers and the developers of earlier days.
Confederation came as a fruit of the effort and development that preceded it, and in that work all had a share as in Confederation all had a share. And so what has developed since Confederation has been an evolution from within outward-and happy are we on each side of the House that we have been connected with that evolution and have worked in conformity with its spirit, and consequently, aided by it, have also aided in the result by our own efforts. I say this as, for myself, I have often found it a good thing to think that we all owe so much to the spirit that is about

us, which develops without our efforts, with which we are consonant and with which we sympathize, and with which, to a certain extent, we work, but without which we ourselves would have been powerless to bring about the results.
Now, I had no thought of speaking' in this line at all, but I want to say a word or two about a remark made by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat. He reiterated what we stood for on this side, and he reaffirmed his belief in those things. He agrees with us; we all agree with hijn with reference to that. But the leader of the Opposition made a remark which I would rather not have heard made, although he may think it proper to make it,- and maybe it is; I am not criticising it harshly. He said, " I fear,"-and when he said what he feared I wished in my heart that he had sat down before he voiced his fear, because he rather spoiled the effect of his speech. He said: I agree with what has been done in the matter of our status, its evolution, its strengthening, its gradual extension, its present position; but I fear Imperial centralization. If my hon. friends on the other side have-I will not call it a simulated fear-if they have an honest fear in that respect, it is their duty to voice it and to guard against that fear being realized. But what strikes me is that their fear is groundless in so far as Canada is concerned. 'Canada is the mistress of her own fortunes. It is not what an isolated man in England may have as a vision of some form of centralization that is going to affect Canada that ought to give us cause for alarm. We should have that sturdy reliance upon our own set purpose and our strength to carry it out, to treat such a thing as an idle fear, because it can have' no place in Canada itself. As I said before, we are the masters of our own fortunes.
What are the grounds for that fear? I have been searching for them after having heard them reiterated now and again in the country and sometimes in this House. I have failed to see them. If I did see them anywhere, I was utterly unable to see them in Canada itself. Therefore I am unmoved by them. Again let me say, we are masters of our own fortunes, and I do not know any one in this country who is in for a game of Imperial centralization which will sap to the slightest degree the autonomy and the rights and privileges that Canada to-day exercises, and means to exercise.
If there are no well-founded grounds for that fear, are we doing much of a service to our country and to the Empire to raise
it into prominence, to give it, as far as we can, a body, and a threatening body, and send it out to our people raising prejudices and suspicions with reference to our relations with the Mother Country and with the other parts of the Empire? I do not think that is the best service for us to perform. But every man must be guided by his own light, and if any one thinks that there is enough in it to justify him in arousing the country against that fear-which I think is imaginary-then his responsibility is with himself,
There is no harm done.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
-and I would not be unduly harsh in criticising what he says along that line. But for myself, I do not think it is needed, and if it is not needed I do not think it wise to throw that in among the many contentious things that we already have to cope with. Surely we have enough of realities to fight without putting up these eventualities or figments, of the imagination.
I think I have had pretty nearly as wide an acquaintance with the public men of Great Britain as most hon. members here. My hon. and valued friend (Mr. Fielding) who sits opposite to me may have had a more extensive acquaintance, but I have had a fairly large acquaintance with public men in Great Britain of all political shades of opinion, and for the last twenty to twenty-five yeftrs I have had the privilege of being side by side with them in a great -many different capacities and of learning their hopes, their desires, their plans with reference to the development of the British Empire. I must say, as a result of my experience, that it is not possible for me to put my hand upon any organized effort amongst the public men of Great Britain looking in the least degree towards a centralization of empire which would harm to the slightest hair's weight the automony and freedom and privileges that the overseas dominions to-day enjoy,-and which they enjoy with the good-will and perfect unanimity of the people of Great Britain.
I am not going to say that there are not cranks and extremists and faddists in Great Britain, just the same as there are in Canada. But here is where we are apt to make a mistake, in that we take the voice of some one who gets the ear of the newspapers or of the public and makes his voice widely heard-we are apt to take that as being an indication of the sentiments of the nation to which he belongs. We must be discriminating in that respect. We can take that lesson to ourselves right here in

Canada; my hon. friends can take it to themselves; my hon. friend who just sat down can take it to himself. You can take it on the language question, on the school question-you can take it on any question about which there are differences of opinion in this country. We do not get rid of the differences by saying nothing about them; at the same time, we do not get rid of them by saying too much about them, or if our statements are ill-advised and rash and reckless. But the trouble is that some extreme man in one section of the country makes a statement which is galling, rasping, unjust,-insulting if you like; and immediately, under present conditions, this is distributed to every part of the country, and it reaches that section where it hurts, where it arouses harsh feeling, and the tendency is to translate that statement as the voice of the province or of the section of the country from which its author hails. That is the chief trouble. If we could put all that class of utterance under our feet for a single decade, the unity and good feeling in this country of ours would be advanced one hundred per cent. But you *cannot put it under foot. In a democratic country, how are you going to stop a man's mouth? How are you going to stop a newspaper's ink and printing press work? So long as you have those ideas and men who hold them, you will have those ideas floating about, and the injury, and the insult, and the slur will go from one and be returned by the other. If we cannot stop those individual utterances of extreme people, then, as sensible men, and not as children, we must ignore them, and not, like children, feel that we have been insulted by a whole people when one man says of us a thing that is unjust and harsh.. We must be careful not to translate those sayings on the one side or the other into a general expression of the people. to whom they are directed or from whom they are directed. That is the point which occurs to me. After all, I am of the opinion that there is a substantial, widespread, deep and profound unity in this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Except at election times.

At election times -there is' where we get foolish, very often get very foolish; and if we see on the outside edge of the crowd half a dozen people whom we think we can influence by a sling, or a jeer, or a slur, or a prejudice stirred up, it is human nature not to let the opportunity pass. The arrow goes; but that is an argument against the man who sends the

I am digressing somewhat from my point as to this Imperial centralization, and I go back to it again, and I give it as my opinion, for what that may be worth, that neither in Canada, nor in the British Empire, nor in the outlying Dominions, is there anything to be feared from undue *centralization, because that can never be made a fact in this British Empire. We have proceeded from the first on the line of conference, better knowledge of each other, co-operation; and the result has been splendid when you measure it up over a course of twenty-five years. I can go back thirty or thirty-five years, and I was, from my youth up, an Imperialist in that I wanted the British dominions and races and countries to work together, feel together, have the same heart, the same throbbing pulses, and the same hopes, ambitions and ideals, and to work out, on the plane of their love of justice and of freedom and their constitutional power of organization, one of the best machineries for the development and civilization of the world. Always I have had that in view. I have travelled in all those overseas dominions and I have met their men, and I have yet to find, in Australia, or South Africa, or New Zealand, or India, men who are working for an Imperial centralization. Everywhere they feel as we feel here; but there is one thing that I stand for-and I believe my hon. friends on the other side stand for it also-and that is this, that this British Empire has within its borders resources, mentality, morale, spirit of enterprise, power of organization, and ideals which, if they are combined in co-operative effort, will build up this great Empire as a unity and thereby make a force amongst the internationals of the world-a force for freedom, peace, justice, and true democracy. There is the line along which, I think, we ought to abate no effort, to leave nothing undone by conference, by co-operation. Go fifty years back and see how we have advanced by conference, by co-operation. Look forward fifty years, and if we proceed on the same lines wisely, our liberties will be broadened rather than curtailed, our politicians will

have visions wider than our politicians have to-day. Our internal development, the spirit of our people, the cultivation of that which is honest and right and the putting up before us and the world of the ideals for which our Empire has stood from the first, will be a great guiding point, a star by which others will steer in their courses across the troubled seas of world development. Whilst we grow stronger ourselves, that strength will infuse itself into the world around us and be an uplifter and a developer for all other countries as well as our own. A strong nation is for the good of the world as a whole. A strong nation founded on the principles of this nation of ours is an untold good and blessing to the world. Do not let us be carried away by these imaginery ideas of somebody wanting to chuck us all into one Imperial group and take away all our liberties. That is absurd, nobody is thinking about it who has power to carry it into operation. Anyway, we are strong enough to let anybody who wants to think that way, think that way. As I said before,-we have our fortunes in our own hands.

That is practically the position we are ready to assume in Canada. We say that we are a nation, that we are a nation among the nations of the world, that of the forty-two nations that signed the Treaty, we are just as good as any. When we asked for seven thousand or eight thousand troops for all Canada, " Militarism " is shouted at us; when we ask for a few small boats to keep our coasts, it is said that we aspire to lbe a great naval power; when we ask for an air force it is said that we are going to squander money on war armaments. We will hear of that, and a great deal more than we have ever done before, if we are going to uphold our position that we assume in this League of Nations. It is going to be an immense responsibility, and I ask hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House to look it squarely in the face. I have appealed, on two different occasions and not merely today, in the discussion of this Treaty, and I again appeal to the leaders on this and the other side of the House to tell us what our responsibilities are, and what we are going to do when trouble comes. It is all very well to say that the sun is shining now and that it is always going, to shine. I believe it is the part of good policy to look ahead. I do not expect that there will always be sunshine, that there will always

be peace in the world or that we will have just the conditions that we would like to have. If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, we ought to look the whole situation over and we ought to have'a statement from one of the leaders of the House as to what our position will be when the call comes. On what basis is it going to be settled? Is it on the basis of population, or is it on thq basis of the area to be defended? On what basis is Canada, one of the five sister nations of the British Empire, to pay her share, or fight her share, with the rest of the world? That is what we will have to do. The United States Senate has balked for eighteen months over it, although we seem to be ready to take it down at one gulp and make no inquiry whatever as to what our responsibilities are in regard to it. I trust before the debate closes that we will have an authoritative statement from some quarter telling us how these troops are going to be raised, how the levy is to be made, how it is going to be paid for, and who settles the responsibility for it.
Heretofore when the British Empire has been at war we have been at liberty practically to do what we wished to help the Mother Country and in most of her wars we have wished to do nothing. In the last war, I am glad to say, Canada has taken her full share and perhaps more than her full share amongst the nations but is she prepared to take part in quarrels that she thinks do not concern her very much because some of these quarrels may be in the Balkan states, Arabia, Mesopotamia, Palestine and those countries and we may not feel like laying down the tools of peace and devoting ourselves again to armaments. If we are not prepared to do that, somebody has to do our .share for us and if somebody does our share for us-we have to pay for the share that is being done. That is the way I see it, that is the way it reads in Article 10, and the American people not only read it in the same way but they are not prepared to sacrifice the constitution of the United States in this regard to the extent of handing over to the League of Nations the right to say what they shall do, when they shall do it and how they shall do it. That is what we are doing. We are practically, when signing this Treaty, signing away our independence, not in relation to Britain but signing away our independence to the extent that we became subservient to the directions of the League of Nations. The League of Nations c'an say to Canada with a population of 8,000,000: You provide 100,000 men, ten ships and fifty or

a hundred units of the air force. That may be the levy and it may not be a very large war at that. What provision is there for finding a force of that kind? That is a part of the Treaty, that is a responsibility that may come to us sooner or later, and if it comes how are we to meet it? I think that instead of glorifying ourselves as being a nation among the nations of the world and pointing to the fact that we. have obtained a status that we had never thought of before, we should inquire, if we are going to be a man of the world, how much it will cost; are we able-.to carry the load; are we prepared to sustain the burden; are we prepared as citizens of Canada to provide the army, the navy and the air force to enable us to take our place amongst the nations of the world whenever they are called for? As I understand it that will be the final necessity of the case when we have entered into this League of Nations because it will apply with binding force to all those who sign the Covenant and in my judgment we will have to pay the piper later. If we do not recognize that now, when the assessment is made by the Council of the League of Nations, which is competent to do it, we will have to do what they ask us to do whether we like it or not, or else we will have to ignominiously drop out. altogether. If I interpret the Treaty right, if any member fails to carry out the obligation placed upon it by the Council of the League of Nations, it automatically ceases t6 be a member of the League. If that is is so it will be up to Canada, when the call comes, to contribute in the way I have suggested and in a measure commensurate with her population, resources and the area that we have and which must be defended.

to make a few -remarks on the important question which engages our attention, I cannot deny myself the privilege of offering to my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George E. Foster) my congratulations upon the address which he delivered and with which, with very little exception, we on this side of the House entirely agree. I am sure that the appeal he made to the members on both sides of the "House as to the spirit in which we should discuss not only this but all questions will be responded to all round. I listened to his address with great pleasure and I am unwilling to let it pass without this remark from myself.
I am exceedingly glad to find my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) drawing attention to the responsibilities of Canada under these treaties and under the League of Nations. He is right when he says that too little attention has been paid to that important question. I think-in fact I know-that many hon. members on both sides have become enamoured of this notion of the higher status that Canada is said to have attained. They are fascinated with the idea of having a place in the League of Nations. We are getting to be a jigger boy than we formerly were and there is a disposition to see something to congratulate somebody upon. I think that when the sober-minded hard-headed people of Canada come to fully understand this question-when they understand the cost of this whole arrangement and the obligations that are being taken upon us-they will have a different impression, and I desire that the people shall understand what this thing is costing us at present. Some of these days we shall have the pleasure, I suppose, of getting at the inside history of this claim of Canada to a separate position. The thing seems to me to be so profoundly foolish that I am unwilling to place the responsibility entirely upon the Canadian Government. I have a notion that this thing originated in the mind of some fussy person from some other section of the Empire, and that the worst than can be said of the Canadian Government is that they were not strong-minded enough to resist the movement. I believe that some of the sober-minded Ministers of the Crown- clear-headed, hard-headed men; they are not all dreamers, they are not all faddists- I cannot help believing that their loyalty to colleagues and courtesy to their party surroundings obliged them to be silent on the question. I am' satisfied, as I know these men, that they must entertain a mute protest against this foolish attempt for Canada to mix itself up in the foreign affairs of the world. I think that Canada's part in this matter has been largely a farce,- I hope it is not unkind to say that. A farce, of course, is an amusing thing. I think it was farcical last year when we undertook to represent to the people of Canada that it was necessary that Canada, through its Parliament, should approve of the German Treaty. No constitutional authority of repute would claim that it was necessary that Canada through its Parliament should approve of that Treaty. The Prime Minister himself did not say that. When the question was put squarely to him the most

he could say was: Oh well, if you do not approve of it the Government will have to resign. But it is clear, I think, to the mind of any constitutional authority in Canada that if we had never passed any motion regarding the German Treaty .that Treaty would have gone into operation just the same. And if it was a farce to deal with the German Treaty that way last year it is an even greater farce to deal in the same way with this Bulgarian Treaty. My hon. friend (Mr. Beland) gave us a picture of our respected friend, Sir George Perley, rushing down to the coast, crossing the channel, going down to the charming little French village, and hurrying in and affixing his signature to a document which he probably never read. I do not believe there are half a dozen members in this House who have read this Treaty. I do not believe the members of the Government have all read it. The Minister of Justice to-day said he had read it, and I am bound to believe him. He asked me if I had read the Treaty and I was frank enough to say no. I tried to read it, but it is a document of one hundred or more pages. I read the most of it, but I honestly confess I was unable to complete my reading. Still I am convinced that I read five times as much as most hon. gentlemen. Why, the thing is a joke. It is a joke as described by my hon. friend (Mr. Beland) if Sir George Perley went and signed the Treaty in the way described. It would be more of a joke if we could imagine Sir George Perley solemnly sitting down in Council, in judgment, on the condition of affairs to be arranged between Bulgaria and the Balkan States and the' civilized world. We cannot imagine a more ludicrous thing than to suppose for a single moment, that Sir George Perley has the qualifications-and I say this without any disrespect for that gentleman; that he has the knowledge and qualifications-to sit down and consider the matter and deliver a judgment in the form of this Blue Book. The whole thing, Mr. Speaker, is ridiculous. And it is a costly bit of folly for the people of Canada. Just what it cost for our ministers to go to Paris I do not know, nor am I interested in inquiring. Whatever we may say regarding the status of Canada we will all agree that when our Ministers of the Grown go abroad they have a status to maintain and we. would expect them to do it with dignity; and if the cost in [DOT] that respect was a large and generous one I at least will find no fault with them. The country will not begrudge any expense of that kind when the money 
is expended for the purpose of the public business of Canada. Of course, the misfortune is in that case, whatever the expenditure was, it was to no purpose, because there was no public business of Canada before the Conference. Now information was laid before this House, official information I believe, to show that the Canadian ministers over there had exceedingly little to do and that, practically speaking, our participation in that Treaty was very largely a sham. That is perhaps too harsh a word, but at all events they did little or' nothing, not because they were not able to do things, but because there was nothing for them to do. You can take the whole Treaty, and take this Treaty, and read them from cover to cover, and you will find nothing in them from beginning to end that has a direct bearing upon the affairs of the people of Canada. Therefore I say there was no need of their dealing with the matter in that way.
I again come to the question of the expense. It was stated the other day that we have paid $65,000 already for our share of the expenses of the League of Nations for the first year. I do not know by what authority or out of what appropriation that money was paid. That of course we will ascertain in due course. But there was another item that we paid in connection with this matter. Not only did the Government bring forward this pretence- that it was necessary for Canada to approve of the Treaty through her. Parliament, bht they went further and said that it was so necessary and so urgent that they had to have a special session of Parliament in Canada for that purpose. Now, I have already declared, and I am not sure but that I am the only member who did so, that it was wanton waste of the public money to call that special session of Parliament, and I do not hesitate to repeat the statement to-night. If you would say "That is a partisan opinion," if you would say "that is a statement that only some partisan Grit would make," I am going to * give you the opinion of a supporter of the Government which my Conservative friends will freely accept as having some weight. At the time that special session of Parliament was proposed the Montreal Gazette, a most influential journal of the Conservative party, had an article on the subject in which it said:
An autumn session of Parliament would be nothing short of profligacy.
That is a very harsh term, but it is not my word, it is the word of the Conservative Montreal Gazette.

No one reason worthy a moment's consideration has been given why a session should be held, while there are a score of reasons on the other side. A million and a half dollars is a tidy sum of money even in these days when men tialk familiarly of a hundred millions and do not pale when a billion is mentioned. A session of Parliament lasting only thirty days will cost the country a million and a half, and for this considerable price what can be gained? The ratification of the Peace Treaty three months earlier than in normal course! One might almost infer that an awe-struck world stands in fear and trembling lest the Canadian Parliament reject the Covenant, and so precipitate another war. It is nonsense to pretend that it makes a shadow of difference whether the Parliament of Canada, or tlje Parliament of any other country, for that matter, approves the Treaty in October or in January.
That is the opinion of the Montreal Gazette. I might put along side it the opinion of a journal that the Minister of Finance will have great confidence in, for I remember, though I have not the paper at hand, that it quoted the Gazette with approval, and that is the Conservative Kingston Standard. So that when I charge upon the Government this waste of the public .money amounting to probably a million dollars at least-I asked a question about it the other day but we have not yet the official information, but I fear the cost will be a million dollars-when I charge upon the Government this wanton waste of a million dollars in order to carry out its claim about the necessity of Parliament having to approve of the Treaty, I am simply saying that which sober-minded Conservative people, as represented by the Montreal Gazette and the Kingston Standard, have said. So I think if the people' of Canada come ito understand the expense that this thing has cost them already-and Heaven knows how much it is going to cost them in the future-this glamour about CUnada having a seat at the Peace Conference, will, in all probability, take on another colour.
Now, I must not be misunderstood. If any man says that I am willing to have the affairs of Canada disposed of by people who do not represent Canada he will state that for which there is no foundation. I insist that whenever Canada has a particular business requiring attention that business shall be attended to by the representatives of the Canadian people. That I would make quite clear. But if occasionally there are matters pending of only remote interest to Canada-the kind of interest that a man has out in the South sea islands if he is a Britisher; that a negro has in the West Indies; in fact, the interest which a Britisher has everywhere in the. wide world-if there is only that kind of interest, then I say there is no particular reason why Canada should insist upon representation, because it ought to be sufficient for us that the interests of Canada will be safe in the hands of those who represent the British Empire.
So I do claim, Mr. Speaker, that this pretence that it is necessary that Canada, for the protection of her interests, should have representation at the Peace Conference is an entire delusion. There is no need of any hesitation on our part iff claiming our right to deal with the affairs of Canada in the way I have described; there is no new status or power required for that purpose. There was a time many years ago when the affairs of the Dominions, or the colonies as they were then called, were disposed of by the British Government and the British Parliament without any reference to us. I suppose those would be what we call "the old colonial days." Unless it be between those times and the present, I do not know where you are going to draw the line as to what are referred to as "the old colonial days."
But those days are a thing of the remote past. For the last forty years at least there has been a recognition on the part of the British Government that wherever the interests of Canada were concerned, Canada must be either directly represented or she must be protected by a reservation in the Treaty that it is not to apply to her until it has received the approval of her Parliament. Our interests in that respect have been fully protected in the past, and it did not need any Conference at Paris or any League of Nations to give us that protection.
Although I may be peculiar in this respect-and I am careful to say that I speak for myself only-1 regret to say that I regard the step taken by the Dominions generally in claiming seats at the Paris Conference as a grave mistake. I say it is a mistake to separate Canada from the rest of the Empire in international affairs, and it is a mistake which will work harm in the future. Within the British Empire we should stand for our rights, we should be willing, as my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) said to-day, at any conference with the ' Imperial authorities to see that wherever it is necessary the interests of Canada are protected. But when you come to deal with foreign affairs I claim that we should deal with them as a unit, as an Empire. And when you say,

I want to say a word with regard to what my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) stated concerning the position of Canada in the League of Nations. The League is composed of a Council and an Assembly. As a matter of fact the Council is the really important body; the Assembly is a larger body which meets only occasionally, the real work being done by the Council. On the Council Canada has no representative, and I do not hesitate to say that she cannot have a representation. It is true there is nothing in the League constitution which says she will not have a representation, and the Prime Minister, for some strange reason, took the trouble to obtain from Mr. Clemenceau, from Mr. Lloyd George and from Mr. Wilson a declaration that the Dominions were not precluded from having a seat on the Council. .
But that does not prove anything. The Council is composed of the representatives of five Great Powers: Great Britain, France, Italy, the United States, and Japan. Each of these Great Powers is a member of the Council by right, and then four others are to be chosen by the Assembly. Now, when you consider that there will be perhaps fifty or more nations having seats in the Assembly, many of them seeking to get to the Council, is there any reasonable probability that, Great Britain already having one member, these other nations will give the British Empire a second member in the shape of a seat for Canada.
None whatever.

It is unreasonable, it is preposterous. We will have no seat on the Council, and it is the Council that is important.	-

Mr. White explained how the British self-governing dominions, demanded of Great Britain her support of their claims to the right of independent representation, and how they would protest and oppose any effort by this country to disfranchise them. That is what the Lenroot reservation would do, in Mr. White's opinion.
He indicated that the British Government was not particularly concerned over this reservation on its own account,

And remember that the writer of the article is reporting his conversation:

but that the colonies raised such a
clamour about it that Premier Lloyd George had been forced to take cognizance of their position, and to support it, as he did in his recent speech in the House of Commons.
Mr. White confirmed previous reports that there is little concern in Europe, particularly in France, concerning other American reservations, but the Lenroot provision is much more formidable as a bar to compromise than the Article X reservation, in his opinion.
So we have the claim of Canada a source of trouble between Canada and the United States, and this clearly shows that it is a source of trouble between Canada and the Mother Country. For these reasons, it is to be regretted that we ever made the claim for a seat in the Assembly which would be no good to us if we had it and which, I think, would not be in any way to the advantage of Canada.
It may be thought that it is only in Canada that dissent is expressed from this claim. I happen, however, to have found in my reading of the public press that the unwisdom-I do not think the word is too strong-of the Dominions making the claim has made an impression elsewhere. I hold in my hand a clipping from Wellington, New Zealand, which reads:
The Wellington Times urges that the Dominions should declare unequivocally against an apparently indefensible position which is not wanted and which those to whom it does injustice object. Such a declaration would splendidly disavow a policy of " grab all."
Another New Zealand paper, The Post,
says:



Actually there is little cause of quarrel, since the real power of the League is vested in the Council where Great Britain and America have equal votes, without the Dominions' interference. The Dominions abandoned the substance for the shadow when they accepted votes in the Assembly instead of insisting upon an effective voice in the Council where the real work will be done. The Post urges that the Dominions should reconsider the matter, which is exceptionally delicate and difficult for the Imperial authorities, compelling them to defend a position which is not of their devising, which is formally indefensible and which gives the opponents of the Treaty a powerful handle while, as usual, not the Dominions, but Great Britain must bear the brunt.
Therefore, this claim of Canada has had the effect of creating trouble in many quarters, and trouble to no good end. I regret for those reasons that the minister has attached so much importance to it. I do not think there is anything in the situation which warrants us in getting up a row with the Americans on this question.
The President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) told us that we must do one of two things- shall I say? one of three things: We must recede to the old colonial condition, (although if he were asked to define the day on which that colonial condition ceased and some new condition came into \existence, he would have difficulty in doing so); or we must go towards independence; or we must do something else which I have difficulty in defining. With regard to receding to the old colonial condition, nobody proposes anything of the kind. With regard to independence, my hon. friend says-and I am quite sure he is speaking sincerely-that he has no sympathy with the move for independence, and I am in hearty accord with him in that regard. I have said so before, and I hold that view now. But I must tell him that since Canada put forward a claim to a position in the Conference separate and apart from the British Empire, from that day there began to be a discussion in regard to independence in Canada. It is this assertion of a right, separate and apart from Great Britain, that has led men to-day to talk of separation and independence who did not talk about that subject before. I am afraid the matter goes further; I am afraid there is talk of. treating Canada as a party separate from the British nation in her authority and power, and I am afraid it leads to wider talk of worse evils even than independence. With regard to the colonial condition of the past, we know that nobody wants it. With regard to independence, I have no sympathy with it; I am heartily against it; but I can at all events understand what it means, and I can go even so far as to admire the man who argues ]Mr. Fielding.[
in favour of it as there is legitimate ground for his argument. But I do not know what my hon. friend means when he speaks about our going forward in a line of some constitutional development; I do not know what he wants, and we have the right to ask him what he means. I do not know of any grievances that Canada has.
I do not know what wi have to complain of. If my hon. friend knows of any grievance that Canada has which needs a remedy he ought to bring it forward in this House. Half a dozen hon. members in this debate have said to the Government that before they go to any Imperial Conference they should receive a mandate from this House. Well, we have had no motion made in that direction by the ministers, and I do not indulge the hope that they will give us the opportunity for giving any mandate in this matter. I do not think they will bring anything forward, for the good reason that they do not know themselves what they want. There is no grievance, nothing that we want to remedy. I do say that when hon. gentlemen talk about some great change which is to be brought about by the coming Imperial Conference I cannot understand what they mean, and I think that before we go any further in this matter we ought to have, perhaps not at this moment in the debate, some declaration from the ministers as to what change they want, and what they are prepared to recommend to the coming Imperial Conference.
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council): May I first express my appreciation of the action of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in placing upon Hansard to-day so large a portion of an address which I delivered in the city of Montreal a few years ago? I desire to express not only my appreciation of the fact that he has placed that upon Hansard, but my still greater appreciation of his statement that not only he but all his followers heartily agree with the sentiments of that address. We have therefore, Mr. Speaker, the statement of the leader of the Opposition that he spoke not only for himself but for all the men on the other side of the House when he said that the statements I then made, and which I have repeated in the course of this debate, with reference to Canada's status had the unanimous support of the Liberals who are back of him. They certainly have the unanimous support of the Liberals on this side of the House as well as of the Conservatives. I am therefore in the happy position of being able to voice the unanimous sentiment of

the whole House on this important question. My hon. friend in quoting from that address referred to it as an address upon our constitutional development. The address -my hon. friend has a copy in his hand-is an address on " Liberals and the Empire." It was a review of the part the Liberal party had taken in various important events in connection with the Empire. It is true that when it was issued by the Reform Association Publicity Branch, they put upon the face of it that it was a constitutional review, but the title of the address, which indicates its character, was " Liberals and the Empire," and it only professes to trace the share that Liberals had taken in our constitutional development. The address did not attempt to review the part taken by both parties in these great events, but in dealing with the history of Confederatioh I did refer to the great work of Sir John Macdonald. My hon. friend entirely omitted this reference in his quotations to-day.
It is not my intention to follow my hon. friend through the course of his address. I shall make only one or two further observations with regard to it, and shall then refer to the remarks of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). With ^he Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) I jnust confess that we on this side of the House could not but feel profoundly gratified at the stand taken by the leader of the Opposition to-day. It was a complete reversal of the stand taken by the leaders of the Opposition when the German Treaty came before the House. It is true that my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's in his speech to-night has harped back to the same old position that he took before, differing therein very markedly from the leader of the Opposition; but so far as the leader of the Opposition is concerned, he took entirely different ground from that taken by hon. gentlemen opposite when the German Treaty was debated last September, and if the address I delivered some seven years ago has contributed to the conversion of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition and the members on the other side of the House to a recognition of the status of Canada within the Empire, it has proved one of the most effective addresses I have ever delivered. I am proud of the result. My hon. friend this afternoon instead of taking the position which was taken in the debate last September, that we were not a nation, said, " Oh, yes, we are a nation, but we became a nation many years ago. Sir Wilfrid Laurier made us a nation." Now if he will turn to the 321
address I delivered in this House on the Treaty last September and to the one I delivered here last Thursday, he will see that I drew attention to the fact that Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1897 had claimed for Canada the status of a nation. I emphasized that in September as I emphasized it on Thursday last
Not very loudly.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-to show not only my appreciation of his great work but also how far my hon. friends on the other side had backslidden from the position which Sir Wilfrid Laurier took. I emphasized it in the hope that they might be brought up to date on this question, or at least as far as the position taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier fifteen or twenty years ago. This is not ,a question of who is or who is not entitled ,to credit for our present position, and 1, shall not discuss it from that standpoint. We are considering a great fact in our country's history, and I think it is important enough to give all parties who have contributed to the, result some share of the credit in connection with it. One cannot but contrast the position taken by the leader of the Opposition this afternoon with the position taken by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition paid a tribute this afternoon to the work of the Prime Minister and his colleagues at the Peace Conference. He said they had carried for-word the work of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that they had maintained Canada's position, and maintained it magnificently, and he added that if they had not done so, they would lhave been derelict in their duty. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's rose in his place and said:	The whole
thing was a farce, the Prime Minister and his colleagues should not have gone over to Paris.
What is the position of my hon. friends opposite on this Treaty? Do they stand for Canada and her rights as a nation, not outside but within the British Empire, or do they take the position of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's who, while he is opposed to centralization, proposes to leave the handling of our affairs in vital matters to the Government of Great Britain.
He never said so.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then, what did he say? He said that being present at the Conference was a farce, that Canada had no special interest there, and that the Prime Minister and his colleagues had no right to

be there. My hon. friend will not question that I am fairly stating his position.

I would not say they had no right to be there. I said it was no good to have them there, and was a disadvantage to Canada.
Mr. ROWELL; Then, it was a disadvantage to Canada to have them there, there was nothing of vital interest to Canada there? Well, Mr. Speaker, if the events in Europe were of such importance , that Canada raised 600,000 men to help-

Oh, let up on that.
Mr; ROWELL:	My hon. friend says:
" Let up on that." Perhaps he does not like to hear about it.
If my hon. friend is alluding to me, and will allow me-

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, my hon. friend may keep his seat and not interrupt. I was answering the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's who said it was not a matter of interest to Canada to have the Prime Minister and his colleagues at the Peace Conference. I say that if the issues in that war were of sufficient interest to Canada to call upon us to raise 600,000 men and to leave 60,000 lying buried in France and Flanders, they were important enough for Canada to be represented at the Conference in an effort to secure a just and satisfactory settlement.
It is my desire to take issue with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's in the most clear and emphatic manner on his whole conception of Canada's position and status in the British Empire and in matters that are of vital concern to Canada. I agree with the leader of the Opposition that not only would the Prime Minister and his colleagues have been derelict in their duty if they had not maintained our position, but they would have been even more derelict if they had wholly failed to attend the Peace Conference when matters of such vast importance to Canada were under consideration. Did not my hon. friend from Queen's and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) to-night speak of the obligations imposed on Canada under this Treaty? And my hon. friend the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) drew the attention of the House to the matter of our obligations under the Treaty. I shall not at present discuss these obligations, but if they are anything like as important as the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne has suggested to-night, was it not the duty of the Prime Minister and his colleagues to be at

the conference with a view to protecting the interests of Canada? Undoubtedly it was, and they were there in pursuance of that duty. My hon. friend says that this question of Canada's status .in the League is of no importance to Canada. He says that it is of no importance to her to have a voice in the Assembly, and that she will never have any chance of being elected to the Council. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not to-night intend entering upon a discussion as to the chances of Canada's being elected to the Council of the League. My hon. friend has characterized as absurd the idea that she might be elected. I shall only say that our position in regard to the governing body of the International Labour Organizations is precisely the same as that in connection with the Council of the League. There were eight powers named who were entitled to nominate members of the governing body and only four other nations were to ,be dhosen and elected from all the nations of the world to name the remaining four members; Canada, at the very first meeting of the conference was elected as one df the nations entitled to name a member to the governing body. Therefore, notwithstanding any suggestions which my hon. friend may make to the contrary, there is no absurdity whatever in the idea that Canada might some day be elected to the Council of the League, the election of Canada at the Washington Conference indicates the fine standing which this country enjoys among the nations of the world. My hon. friend has referred to the discussions that are going on in Washington, and has been good enough to suggest that the remarks which I have made have not contributed to a good understanding between Canada and the United States. I beg respectfully to differ from him, they were made to avoid misunderstandings and to maintain a good understanding. I doubt very much whether the remarks which that hon. gentleman made either in the discussion of the Treaty with Germany last September or in the present debate will contribute to a good understanding between the two nations, or will aid in securing just recognition of Canada's position in the United States. I hold in my hand the Congressional Record of the Senate debates of the present week, and I find quoted therein a statement made by my hon. friend when this question was under discussion in September last. I find it quoted by the opponents in the Senate of jOanada's position and as a justification for ,their action. In the course of the discussion, (as appears on page 4307, of the Congressional

Record of Monday, March 8, the following statement appears, by Mr. McCormick:

Mr. President, let me ask the Senator one more question. Does he recall. the speech in the Canadian House of Commons of Mr. Fielding, for 16 years a Minister of the Crown, In which he stated explicitly that logic was on the side of the contention of those in this country who insisted upon an equality of representation, in which he said that New York was more important to this Republic than the Dominion to the Empire? Surely the Senator will recall that speech.
If my hon. friend was right there would be no ground of criticism of his position. But I say he is not right, and it is just such speeches as that which he made in September and the speech he has made to-night that will be used against Canada in her effort to retain her position in the League. My hon. friend employed an illustration which is also quoted in the American senate; He compared Canada with the State of New York. It is very easy for our friends in the United States to fall into an error in connection with the situation, and I think their attitude in some respects is due to a misunderstanding-a misunderstanding materially contributed to by my hon. friend and others in reviewing the situation. Every one realizes that the British Empire bears no relation in its constitution to the United States of America. In the United States there is one government, the federal government, that conscripts men, levies taxation and carries on war. The edicts of that government run through every state in the American Union. It is the only government within the limits of the United States that has any authority to exercise these great powers. There is but one central government in the United States that wages war and makes peace. There can be only one member of the League and therefore only one vote. What is the situation in the British Empire? It is wholly different. No one government in the Empire wages war, conscripts men, levies taxation and negotiates peace. In the British Empire half a dozen governments exercise these functions. Canada did not act by reason of any law or edict of the Imperial 'Government, but on her own authority by the action of this Parliament, just as freely as the United States Congress and Senate acted when they undertook participation in the war. And I say it tends to mislead, not only the people of the United States but the people of Canada, to make any such comparison as my hon. friend made. As there are several selfgoverning nations in the British Empire each is a member of the League and each is entitled to a vote. I was also surprised
at the remarks of my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Belaud) in his reference to the terms of the Treaty and certain matters in connection with the boundary, remarks which met with the approval of the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne. I do not suppose that any statesman present at the conference other than the representatives of the Balkan States, would be able to form any definite opinion in regard to the exact boundary, hut the representatives of Canada would know just as much about the subject as the representatives of the United States. It is not a question whether they knew the exact boundaries or not. It is a question of making peace with a country with which wfe were at war. My hon. friend has referred to the Balkans as if it were a place in which we were not interested. Well, the Balkans do appear to be remote from us, hut it was trouble there in June and July of 1914 that set the world aflame and called forth the troops of Canada and other parts of the Empire to Europe to wage war. And unless the Balkan situation .is cleared up on a basis of justice and equity, by the best solution that the nations can devise, who can tell how soon trouble in the Balkans may again produce the same results and call forth our troops once more? I desire to dissent absolutely from the position and attitude of my hon. friend that a controversy which called Canada's sons to war and may do so again, is not a matter in the wise and sane solution of which the people of Canada are interested. My hon. friend from Beauce- and this also touches the point raised by the hon. member for Brantford-spoke of the provisions of the Treaty and stated that it was quite clear that Canada would not be entitled to be present and have a vote in [DOT]the Council of the League in the event of the question of military contribution being under consideration. My hon. friend from Brantford wanted to know how the question of a military contribution would be settled. I desire to direct his attention to two important provisions of the Treaty.
In Article 16 this clause appears:
It shall be the duty of the Council dn such case to recommend to the several governments concerned what effective military, naval or air force the members of the Deague shall severally contribute to the armed forces to he used to protect the Covenants of the League.
It is the duty of the Council to recommend to the several governments. If my hon. friend will turn to Article 4 of the League, he will find this provision:
Any member of the League not represented on the Council shall be invited to send a re-

presentative to sit as a member at any meeting of the Council during the consideration of matters specially affecting the interests of that member of the League.
It is set forth in language so plain that no one could mistake it that if the Council is called upon to consider a matter affecting the interest of any member of the League, that member must be present and is entitled to a seat. I should not have thought that the matter was open to argument at all. But in order to remove any doubt or apprehension from the mind of my hon. friend, I would like to draw his attention to a commentary on the Covenant of the League of Nations contained in an official document issued by the Government of Great Britain. This official commentary wTas prepared by the Rt. Hon. Lord Robert Cecil, K.C.M.G. and Lieut. General the Rt. Hon. Ian Christian Smuts, K.C., the two men, from the standpoint of the British Empire, who had more to do with framing this Covenant than any other two men and probably had considerably more to do with framing its general outlines than the President of the United States, although there were certain provisions which the President considered essential, and he was no doubt very largely responsible for their being included, particularly, Article 10. Wihat do they say in their commentary on this article?
In the first instance, it is left to individual states to decide whether or not such a breach has occurred and an act of war against the
League been thereby committed	
It iis the duty of the Council, with the help of its military, naval and air advisers to recommend what effective force each member of the League shall supply; for this purpose, each member from which a contribution is required has a night to attend the Council, with the power of veto during the consideration of its particular case.
I should have thought that that was quite clear without that commentary. I should have thought that that was the proper legal interpretation of the Covenant, but when you have that interpretation, which appears to be the. fair, reasonable and proper interpretation in a commentary issued by the British Government, prepared by the two men who are responsible for the framing of the Covenant and which sets out in unmistakable terms the rights of any member who may be called upon to make a contribution to be present, to vote and to exercise the right of veto, I submit that the matter is not open to serious argument. It appears then that no nation can be called upon to make a military contribution without the consent of that nation given at the Council and with its representative present.

The Senate of the United States evidently think that they will be called upon to make a contribution without being consulted under the terms of the Treaty.
|Mr. ROWELL: I do not think it would be proper for me to express an opinion upon the reasons or motives which may have actuated the American Senate in adopting any particular resolution.
