It is not important and I should not take up the time of the House in discussing the matter, but my hon. friend referred to Sir George Perley suggesting that he had signed the Treaty without having read it. The an-

swer is here on record already that the principal terms of the Treaty were settled while the Prime Minister and his colleagues were in England although the final form and execution were delayed pending the completion of negotiations for the German and Austrian treaties.
My hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) put what he considered to be a poser when he asked what would happen in case one of the nations of the Empire did not desire to ratify the Treaty. It would depend entirely on the conditions under which such a question arose. My hon. friend, if he will recall the facts in connection with our history and our foreign relations, will realize that it is quite a common thing for Great Britain to sign a treaty on her own behalf and not on behalf of the self-governing Dominions. It is quite a common thing for her to ratify a treaty on her own behalf and not on behalf of her Dominions. I have in my desk one of those treaties, which will come before the House. That is the International Opium Convention. That was signed in 1912 but Canada did not have a plenipotentiary present to sign it. The Treaty is signed by the British representatives with the reservation of the following declaration:
The article of the present Convention, if ratified by His Britannic Majesty's Government, shall apply to the Government of British India, Ceylon, the Straits Settlements, Hong Kong, and Wei-hai Wei in every respect in the same way as they shall apply to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland ; but His Britannic Majesty's Government reserve the right of signing or denouncing separately the said convention in the name of any dominion, colony, dependency, or protectorate of His Majesty other than those which have been specified.
The situation would not be a new or novel one if this House declined to approve of an international obligation entered into by the British Empire, even if His Majesty decided to ratify in respect of Great Britain, [DOT]or in respect of. Great Britain and the Dominions that approved it, but did not ratify it in respect of Canada because Canada did not approve. Surely the situation is not difficult to comprehend and I do not understand all this argument which has been addressed to us in reference to the difficulties of such a situation.

That is not the point.
The point is that the *Prime Minister said that if we did not assent we would no longer he considered a part of the British Empiie

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I said in opening it would depend entirely on the conditions under which it arose. If my hon. friend will read
the whole statement made by the Prime Minister I think it is reasonably clear from [DOT]his statement that this was his view. It depends entirely upon the conditions. We might take action under such conditions that we would be virtually declaring ourselves a separate nation of the Empire, but that would not normally be the result as I have pointed out in the case of this particular contention. My recollection is that the Japanese Treaty was in this form, that it did not bind the Domiiiions until they had expressly assented to it; and that after it had been ratified by His Majesty in respect of Great Britain it was subsequently approved by this House and ratified with respect to Canada. It is not a new matter, it is not a difficult matter. All the troubles that my hon. friends are conjuring up are figments of a somewhat disturbed imagination. They are not serious when you look the situation squarely in the face and recognize our constitutional development and the position in which we stand to-day.
I must say that I could not quite reconcile the statement of the leader of the Opposition, supported-by the hon. member for Beauce, that there was danger of some occult centralizing imperialistic influence at work to destroy our autonomy, and the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) that this Government was proceeding along the lines which were disrupting the British Empire. The two statements cannot be correct.
I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am aware of it, but 1 might ask, has he converted my hon. friend to his views?

speechtext: If the gentleman in question has not met with any success in the case of my hon. friend he has not met with any greater suocess in my case.

speechtext: Perhaps it is not fair to allude to my hon. friend in that connection because he did, at the last session, offer the conspicuous example of a member of the Opposition who supported the views of the Government in reference to Canada's position. Therefore my remarks do not apply to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). I am very glad to see that the rest of the hon. gentlemen opposite have got back to the good Liberal position on Canada's status stated in my address of seven years ago and re-stated in my address on this Treaty, and which I found when I entered the Government was the good Conservative position also. I found that the Prime Minister and his Conservative colleagues were just as strong in maintaining Canada's right to full autonomy and self-government and her status within the British Empire as any Liberals with whom I have been associated. I found we were all agreed on that issue, and that has made our association in this important work in connection with Treaties of Peace of the most harmonious kind.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And even my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) to-day comes in behind our position supporting it and standing for that idea. "While the lamp holds out to burn" -there is an opportunity for my hon. friend.
We will be standing with the leader of the Opposition long after you are gone.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend
from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) said that we were not only creating some trouble between the United States and ourselves but there was danger of our creating trouble between Great Britain and ourselves. I was interested in the authority my hon. friend was quoting for that statement. Where did he go to get authority for. the statement that we were creating trouble between Canada and Great Britain? My hon. friend went to one of the plenipotentiaries of the United States. The hon. gentleman by his position not only gives comfort to those who are opposing Canada's status, but he draws his inspiration from a representative of the United States not

from a representative of Canada or Great Britain to attack our position here. If my hon. friend wants to find- out the position of the British Government, there is no difficulty in doing so from the members of the British Government themselves. No man could have made a clearer statement, of the necessity and determination of the British Government to stand behind Canada in maintaining her status than did Lord Grey in that famous letter of his, in which he said that there could be no departure from the principle of the representation of the Dominions.
My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's said he could understand what was meant by independence-he did not agree with that view but he could understand what it meant. He also said that he could quite understand what the old colonial relation meant-he did not agree with that view either but he could understand it. He did not, however, understand what we meant by the present position, the wonderful things that were to be accomplished at this constitutional conference. Well, I did not say that any wonderful things were going to be accomplished at the Constitutional Conference, and I do not think it is difficult to understand the position which this Government takes, which the Government of Great Britain takes, and which the Government of each of the self-governing Dominions takes as the present constitutional relations of the different nations of the Empire. It is this: Although the self-governing Dominions have had the rights of self-government for a long period they have occupied a more or less dependent relation to the Mother Country. They have been steadily growing more independent of the Mother Country in the sense that they have been exercising a larger measure of sovereignty over their own affairs, and the time has come when the Mother says to these Daughter States: "Well, you have been in a measure dependent upon me in the past. I now recognize you as my equals. We stand on an equality as nations of the British family of nations" or "the galaxy of British nations," ,as -Sir Wilfrid Laurier termed it. Is that difficult to understand? A father may have his boys with him in business. They may not be partners although they may be managing various branches of it. The time comes when the father says "I will take you into partnership. You shall be equal with me in your status in the business, although you may not have as much interest, you may not have as much power." The father may retain the majority

interest in the business but the sons are partners, they have the status of partners, there is ajn equality of status. That illustrates the idea although of course it is not an analogy because you cannot apply the same rule to states. I only used the illustration as indicating -what is meant by equality of status. What is the object of a Constitutional Conference? It is to provide improved machinery for consultation and co-operation in matters of common concern. Up to this present time Great Britain has been acting as trustee for all the other nations of the Empire in almost all matters of foreign policy. The time has come when actual participation in matters of foreign policy affecting the Dominions should be enjoyed by the Dominions, and some method of co-operation and consultation must be worked out to this end.
Mr. Speaker, the position of the Government is clear and unequivocal. I thought the position of the Opposition was also clear and unequivocal when my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, defined ,it this afternoon, but it has become somewhat clouded by the speeches delivered to-night. However, I would rather close the debate under the impression that the leader of the Opposition did speak for all his followers, and that the remarks made this evening which differed from his were but temporary lapses. I am glad to think that the House is unanimous in support of this resolution and of the principles embodied in it as set forth by me when I moved the resolution on Thursday last.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. ANDREWS (Centre Winnipeg) moved:
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the provision made for re-establishing in civil life the members of His Majesty's forces who served in the late war has in many cases proved inadequate, and that it is desirable that a special committee of this House be appointed to consider what provision can be made to meet such cases, the committee to have power to call for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath and to report from time to time.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it has been said that it is not so much what a man says as what he does that counts. Also, it has been said that by a man's service to his country his citizenship is proven. Also, "By their works ye shall know' them." I do not claim that all the men who proceeded overseas were citizens of the highest possible type; they were not all plaster saints or high-born financiers, but I do claim that the great, overwhelming majority were amongst the best'citizens of Canada prior to the war.
Amongst them were the flower and youth of Canada. In spite of the fact that all were not possibly of the highest type, I claim that they were second to none in all . those great qualities of self-sacrifice, discipline, courage, fortitude under punishment, and stability of character, which made victory possible. Perhaps I may be permitted as an Englishman to say that I believe there is something in the climate of this northern land of ours that produces men of great virility of character. Well do I remejnber as a new comer thirty years ago listening to the yarns of the old-timers about early days in Canada. Amongst the tales of endurance of the old settlers one story in particular occurs to my mind. It was told that a young man set out in the North country with a load of furs drawn by his dogs. He ran into heavy weather, lost all his food, his fish was all gone, but he made his way ' across the lake against heavy storms and at last, by the utmost perseverance and endurance succeeded in reaching the timber land. Here he built himself a fire, and being without food proceeded to cut off the tails of his poor dogs. He made soup from the tails, drank the soup, fed the bones to the dogs, and eventually arrived at the settlement. When he reached the trading post they [DOT]'aid: "Hello boy, how did you get through?" And he replied: "A little short of tails but otherwise everything was jake." That, I think, illustrates the true spirit of our Canadians-absolutely unafraid in the face of danger, and full of initiative. The distinguishing characteristic of the Canadian forces overseas was the spirit of endurance and absolute determination to conquer or die.
The war has been an education. Men are thinking to-day as they never thought before, and as a result of their thinking these returned soldiers, who are amongst the very best citizens that we have, are organizing, falling into line, linking up for what is commonly known as "a square deal." My hon. friends may well ask: What do you mean by " a square deal?" It is pretty hard perhaps to describe it, because it means something different to almost every man. If hon gentlemen will accompany me for one day in the life of one of these men perhaps they will get a better realization of what a square deal means than in any other way I can suggest.
You will imagine, Mr. Speaker, that it is a June morning, after a more or less strenuous night of shell fire. The sun is just mounting above the horizon, and at this very moment-s-sh! a bigxshell is heard

coming, and it lands about a hundred yards tp your rear. There is a lull and then again is heard-s-sh !-and another big shell lands about one hundred yards short of where you are standing in a little bit of a ditch, really a captured German communication trench. Another delay, and once again-s-sh!-followed by an explosion. The German gunners have the range and the trouble commences in earnest. From that moment, Mr. Speaker, for eight mortal hours everything in the way of shell fire, big and little, comes roaring into that trench. Your comrades are blown up, the trenches are obliterated, and becomes a shambles of dead and wounded. A runner comes from behind and the orders are to hang on at all costs- a German counter attack is expected the moment the shell fire ceases. It does cease after eight mortal hours during which time men face death a thousand times. Then each man stands up not only with his own rifle but with all the rifles that he can grab from his dead friends to repel the counter attack. In this particular case it never comes. But the strain is there-the men are waiting, waiting, waiting. A little later comes an order that the battalion will be relieved to clean up. That means, bury the dead; and our boy amongst others is told off for this purpose. He helps to dig a trench, and collect the dead, and on this particular day they number twenty-one. While the men are stretched there waiting, the officer comes up to read the burial service. He says, "Attention, men. Greater love hath no man than this, that he give up his life for his friend." The officer salutes and carries on. The dead are buried, and the job is nicely finished, when there is another strafe from the Germans, and the graves of the dead are uncovered. The job of burial has to be done once more. It is finally completed, and our man gets back into his little front line and waits to be relieved. It is while he is waiting there that he looks up aloft and sees the stars shining calmly down as they have shone for a million years. The tension of this terrible day relaxes, and he says, " My God, what is it all about? Who is to blame for this Hell? He asks, was it the men that he helped to bury-were they the cause of war? Was it-his company officer? Was it the men across in the German trench, or the German gunners, who were responsible? They had no more to do with the war than we had. He knows it. Was it the brigadier? No, he is under orders. Was it the corps commander who was responsible? No. Was it the Government? If so, our friend makes up 
his mind, that if he is spared by the grace of God to get back, from that day forward he will take a hand in the government of his country. If he is a thinking man, Mr. Speaker, as hundreds and thousands of the men were, and an educated man, he does not stop with the Government, because he knows that the possession of wealth and the control of government can never be separated. Who supplied the party funds? Who came down in delegations from boards of trade and interviewed the Government without ever consulting their local representatives? Were these men the cause of the war and are they to blame? For a while he thinks, yes. But his mind is open, his mind is free, and he sees clearly. He realizes that rich men's sons lie in the grave that he helped to dig that afternoon. He realizes that the Military Service Act played no favourites- it took the rich man's son as well as the poor man's son. Then who is to blame? Ii he is of a socialistic turn of mind, he might think that it. is time the economic power which is now held by a few men in all the countries of the world, which stands behind all governments and must ever stand behind them, was taken out of the hands of these men and placed with the representatives of the people. But that will not satisfy his mind because he knows that individuals compose the nation. What causes war between individuals? Is it lust for power and selfishness, Mr. Speaker? Is that the cause of war, the cause of strife,-selfishness and lust for power? If so, what is the opposite of selfishness? It is love, doing unto other men as they would be done by-the words of the white Christ, the "square deal." The square deal means much or nothing to many minds, but it is a slogan, almost a crusade, to-day with the fifteen millions of men that fought in this war. Nothing less will do. And, Mr. Speaker, the behaviour of our officers, non-commissioned officers, and men in this great fight was so splendid that I have come out with an abiding faith in the decency of human nature. It has been said " as a man sows so shall he also reap." That is true of countries, likewise, I am perfectly satisfied that the great majority of our men who fought, and the great majority of our people who stayed at home, were filled with the spirit of self-sacrifice. Otherwise, we. would never have won the war. As we sow, so shall we reap. If this is not true, Mr. Speaker, it means that there is no justice in this world; it means that our 'civilization is a lie; it means anarchy-red anarchy,-back to nature,-red in tooth and in claw;-that is what it means.

So far as I can learn, Mr. Speaker, it was never the desire of our people that the war should be made a political issue. There may have been differences of opinion as to how the men should be recruited and in respect to other details, but never, so far as I can learn, was it the desire of our people that the war should be made a political issue. And so far as I can learn it is not now their will that the re-establishment of the men and women who suffered through the war should become a political issue. Therefore I appeal to hon. members to tackle this problem in the same spirit which animated our men in France and at home and which helped them to win the war.
Mr. CYRUS W. PECK (Skeena):	Mr. Speaker, I am seconding the motion of my hon. friend in order to get this question before the House. I am quite convinced that the Government is going to give us an opportunity for discussion. But I do not know that I agree with my hon. friend as to the method by which we can best attain the purpose he has in view. The only people I can see any chance of helping us are the Government, because none of the parties opposite have ever said what they are going to do for the returned soldiers.
If this. question is brought up I think it should deal with all matters pertaining to the returned soldier in the following order: Pensions, re-establishment, gratuities. I am going to say right here that I do not for a moment pretend that I shall- support the extreme demands for gratuities that have been made upon the Government. I have told my people that. At the same time, I think we should go into the whole question again, and have it properly ventilated, before, and fully investigated by, a committee sincere in, trying to get to the bottom of it. I have every confidence that the Government is sympathetic, but if they are not I do not see any one else who will help us. Therefore I am going to depend upon' the Government; I am sure they will not let us down.	,
Mr. RICHARD C. COOPER (Vancouver South): Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to discuss in any detail the motion brought forward by my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews), but I do seriously ask the Government to appoint either a new committee similar to the Committee on Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment which we had last session, or give added powers to the Pensions Committee to deal with this ques-33	'
tion. There are still many questions of vital interest to the returned men that have not yet been satisfied. There is only one I intend to mention, it is one that was dealt with by the Committee on Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment last session. I refer to life insurance. >A recommendation was made to the Government that action should be taken to see what could be done in the matter. So far as I know nothing further has been done. It has been discussed already this session, and in my opinion it is one of the most serious questions we have to consider in the future in connection with the man who served in the front line trenches. There are very few men, who, even if not actually wounded, have not received soipe physical or mental disability, and they will have to be considered and helped so far as life insurance is concerned.
I heartily support my hon. friend's motion, and I sincerely trust that the Government will not waste any further time in stating their intention of referring the subject matter to a committee to be thoroughly gone into.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the resolution were pressed to a vote I would support it. At the same time I think it unfortunate that the mover has not given a larger number of cases which this committee is supposed to deal with. In any event, I wish to say, if we are obliged to-day to call upon a committee to further study matters relating to our returned soldiers, it is due largely to the administration of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. A number of the questions which were settled for them by the committee last year could have been settled by a deputy or a minister. The fact remains, Sir,-and my information is not only from friends in the House but from the soldiers themselves-that the deputy is a man whom they do not care to go to because he is not a soldier; he has nothing in common with them, although he may be sympathetic. The minister of the department is also, they say, hard to approach and does not. give ~them the sympathy which they feel they ought to receive.
If it were not for the fact that I possess information that this department must necessarily cease its work very shortly, I would move an amendment to this resolution that, instead of having a committee of the House appointed to further inquire how matters may be dealt with, a minister should be appointed who is a soldier, and that his deputy should also be a soldier, so that the returned soldiers could tell their



grievances frankly and fully to men of their own kind who would be able to understand exactly what was required.
If it is not too late I would suggest that a deputy minister be appointed who is a soldier, so that these men may get a lot of their grievances redressed without coming before this proposed committee. A committee of this House is not satisfactory; it was not satisfactory last year. The report was unsatisfactory, and it may be that, the report of the proposed committee will be also unsatisfactory.
Mr. JOHN H. BURNHAM (West Peterborough) : Mr. Speaker, I sent a copy of this resolution to Peterborough, where the convention of the Great War Veterans of the province is now being held. I asked them to pronounce upon it, and they said they would do so. As the convention is still proceeding I should like to ask the member for Centre Winnipeg if it would be possible for him to adjourn the debate. As we are all aware, the committee appointed to look into this matter last session brought in a report, but as that report in several respects did not quite satisfy the soldiers, and the House, it. was held open, and after a somewhat strenuous debate it was agreed that the Government would hear whatever further complaints the soldiers had to make. I understood the report would be brought back to the House and be adopted in the usual way, but I have heard nothing about it since, nor have I heard what additional complaints have been preferred or what has been done with regard to the matter.
It would appear to me that the proposition contained in this resolution conflicts directly with the work of the committee already in existence, because, so far as I know, that committee has.not yet been released. Perhaps the Government will tell us what additional work has been done in this respect since that debate of last session. It might meet the purpose of this resolution if the assurance could be given that while the work of that committee has not been brought to a conclusion, it is on the way to it.
Mr. A. B. McCOIG (Kent, Ontd:	Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my approval of the resolution proposed by the member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews). It is proper and just that a committee of this House should be appointed with a view to bringing about a more speedy re-establishment of the returned soldier into civil life. I know a number of cases in my section of the country where returned men who have been desirous of locating on farms and of
['Mr. Mackie.]
taking up farming work as a profession have been held back for months and do not know whether or not they can get land for the spring operations. In some cases the men have been assured that farms would be allotted to them, but in the meantime the prices of agricultural implements and equipment have increased to such an extent that those who want to equip their farms for the crop of 1920 will be under the painful necessity of paying from 20 to 25 per cent more for implements and equipment than they would have had to pay had they got the land earlier. It would have been better if a committee had been appointed at an earlier day, but certainly the Government should now appoint this committee and see that all possible assistance is rendered to those returned men who are desirous of locating on farms, as well as those who wish to re-establish themselves in other occupations.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I
desire to support this resolution and to join with the member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) in his intentiofi not to support extreme demands made either in this House or out of it. I am not unmindful of the great service that has been done by this House to the returned soldier. The greatest service they did them or could have done them was the affording of sufficient support at the front. The gratuity which was given to the men on their return was a good one and one which they ought to be grateful for. I think that the great bulk of the'men are grateful for it. But the first thing that this House and this country have to do is to look after the crippled, the widows, and the orphans. I cannot honestly say that that task has yet been fairly done. I hope that the Government will see its way clear to appoint a committee whose sole function will be to inquire into the matter of pensions. I do not say that the pensions have not been fairly well administered or that the scale of pensions is not reasonably high. Undoubtedly our pension scale is the highest in the world, and that is something for which our country ought to get credit. But in the actual administration of the pensions it happens that dependents, and the wounded and the crippled are in many cases not given enough money to live on. That, after all, is the main thing. The question is not whether our pension scale is the highest or the lowest; it is whether those to whom pensions are payable are receiving enough to enable them to live under present conditions. I think that a great deal of the difficulty ifi this re-

gard could be overcome through administrative acts. But after two years' experience in dealing with many of these cases I am thoroughly convinced that the medical man is one of the greatest sources of trouble. I would like the House to grasp that point. The Pension Board has to work under a disability which they cannot override; in many cases they are subject to the decisions of medical men who are not in touch with the returned soldier and whose judgments and opinions vary considerably in different cases. I could cite cases of men who alre disabled to the extent of being unable to do any work at all and who are drawing only $12 to $15 a month by way of pension. I am not blaming the Government or the Pension Board for that; I believe that the three members of the board are efficient men who take a sympathie attitude and who are anxious to do justice to the soldiers and to the widows and orphans who are pensioners of this country. But as I have said, the board,are too much bound by regulations; they have not enough freedom, and the medical examiner is not in sufficiently close contact with the applicant for pensions.
Closely associated with this matter is the matter of life insurance. Many men who have been disabled during the war were unable to obtain the benefit of life insurance because of the fact that the companies levied a rate higher than they were able to pay, and to-day they are unable to get [DOT]the insurance. The Government will not be doing justice to these men until it puts them in the position they would have been in had they incurred no war disability. The first thing we have to do is to look after the disabled and the war dependents; the next thing is to look after insurance; and the third-in connection with which, I realize, there are great difficulties-is to re-establish the men in civil life. I am not in sympathy, and never was, with the demand for a $2,000 gratuity. I do not believe that any man who gave his services voluntarily, as most of our men did, has a right to come back here and make a demand like that upon his country. I go further and say that, ninety per cent of the -[DOT]men are not making such a demand; I have not had five men come to me and ask me to support it. But a large number of returned men are finding it difficult to get back into civil life, and many of those who are becoming re-established are doing so under great disabilities and with much hardship. I can cite cases of bank clerks, for instance, who hpon their return from the front were offered their former positions 33J
at the same salary that they were receiving when they left them five years ago, while those who had remained at home had [DOT]got increases of perhaps $100 a year, making a difference of $400 or $500. Then there is the great student body; I think that a greater claim could be made out for them than any other class. Students are drawn from all classes of society, from the poor as. well as from the rich. I am not in favour *of differentiating at all; I believe that one man's effort is as good as another's and should be dealt with accordingly. Many oi these students have suffered great hardships and met with great difficulty in getting re-established in civil life. The problem is a difficult one, I know; it is one to-which the best thought of men in this House and out of it has been given. But I do hope that the Government will appoint a committee to go into this question, and this question alone, because I think it is big enough to engage the attention of a committee. The Pension Committee will have plenty of work on their hands. Let us try to do what we can to be fair and just to everybody. I would be the last man, I think, to ask in this House for anything that is unreasonable or unfair; but .1 think that Canada cannot afford to have it said that we did not at least endeavour to do justice to the men who have served this country for the last four or five years.
Mr. THOMAS W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton, N.B.): Mr. Speaker, I wish to put myself on record as being in favour of the motion that a special committee be appointed to inquire into the re-establishment of returned men. One of the speakers on the other side has rather found fault that the mover of the resolution did not cite many branches of the service that should be investigated by this committee. I may be able to give some. I do not wish to cover the whole ground, but there are some cases that came under my immediate notice in our province and that I would like to bring to the attention of the House at this time. One is in regard to the matter of pensions which I think the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) mentioned a few moments ago. The hon. member spoke of the medical men- being tied down by regulations; he said that they did not have free enough scope in deciding as to pensions. Another thing he said,- and I heartily agree with him-was that the medical examiner is not brought into close enough touch with the soldier who is applying for a pension. I have the papers here in regard to a man about whom

si spoke briefly, on Monday, who was granted a disability pension in July, having been in the military hospital for something like three months or more before this pension was granted to him. The physician who 'examined him for the pension was the physician who had attended him during those three months. I visited the man in the hospital during that period, and for a certain length of time he was allowed to walk out only fifteen minutes in the forenoon and fifteen minutes in the afternoon. Later on, he was allowed to walk out for thirty minutes in the forenoon and thirty minutes in the afternoon. So, it will be understood that this man was in rather a weak condition. At the end of about three months in the hospital he was granted a full disability pension, this being the finding of the doctors at that time:
JBoard of Pension Commissioners for Canada.
43 Canada Life Bldg.,
St. John, N.B., July 18, 1919.
Sir;

i have the honour by direction to inform you that this office has given full and careful consideration to the proceedings of the Medical Board which examined you prior to your discharge from the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and to the other documents and information on your file. It has been decided to recommend that you be awarded a Class 1 pension at the rate of $600 per annum. If you are married, you will be entitled to a further $96 per annum. If you have children you will also be entitled to a further $144 per annum for the first child, $120 per annum for the second child and $96 per annum for each additional child. Your pension commences on July 5, 1919.
This man had three children, and he was paid this pension, from the 7th day of July , until the end of August. You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that he was granted this full disability pension after careful consideration had been given to the proceedings of the Medical Board and on the examination of a physician who had been attending him for at least three months in the hospital. On November 3, this man received the following notice, and I understand this latter [DOT]decision was made by a physician who never saw the soldier. This is from the Pension Commissioners at Ottawa:
JBoard of Pension Commissioners for Canada.
Ottawa, November 3, 1919.
Sir:-I have the honour to inform you that *very careful consideration has been given to the recommendation that you be awarded pension covering total disability as the result of tuberculosis.
It is noted that you were discharged in 1918 as the result of over age and debility. Several [DOT]examinations in the course of the next two years showed that you had no disability other than a slight difficulty in walking as a result [DOT]of gunshot wound of the leg.
[Mr. Caldwell. 1
Almost three years after discharge you were taken on the strength of the Department of Soldiers' Re-establishment for sanatorium treatment, and upon discharge it is shown that very sparse and scant signs of tuberculosis exist, and such as are at present would no-t appear to be in any way related to your military service, after careful perusal of the history of your case.
Future payments on your account will, therefore, be made at the rate in force prior to your commencing treatment with the D.iS.C.R., covering the disability shown to exist to the extent of five per cent.
Your obedient servant,
Stanley B. Coristine,
The Secretary, Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada.
Rer. M.
This soldier is receiving for this five per cent disability $3 a month; for his wife, 75 cents a month; and $1.75 a month for his three children. Notwithstanding the fact that the doctor who had been attending him for three months pronounced him totally disabled, the doctor who,s I understand, never saw the case, after giving careful consideration, not to the case but to the history of the case, decided that the man was only five per cent disabled. As I pointed out to the House on Monday, this family applied in January, 1920, for aid from the Patriotic Fund, and Dr. Rankine, the doctor whom the military authorities had appointed in Woodstock-and I may tell the House that this gentleman is one of the foremost doctors in our province, a man of the highest integrity, a man whose honour has never been questioned-signed this man's application for aid from the Patriotic Fund and declared him to be one hundred per cent disabled. This doctor had also been attending this man, as I think can be proved by looking up the records in the Pension Bureau at Ottawa where it will be found that the Pension Commis-
3 p.m. sion paid this man's doctor bill tor treatment at the man's own residence. They also paid, or have agreed to pay, Dr. Grant for attending this man in his own home. Dr. Grant also signed this man's supplication for aid from the Patriotic Fund and declared him to be one hundred per cent disabled. There is something wrong with our pension law or with the putting of it into operation, and I should be inclined to think that there was something wrong with both phases.
There is one other matter in regard to soldier's re-establishment about which I wish to speak, and that is the settling of returned men on the land. I am perhaps in as good a position to speak of thfe facts as any other hon. member, having been in

close touch with that work in our province since it was first organized,I was the Chairman of the Agricultural Qualification Committee from the time it was first organized until I had to resign to accept the nomination to run in the by-election last October.
I was also a member of the Loan Committee, and in this way I was in very close touch with the work in our province. I do not wish to criticise the Soldiers' Settlement Act unnecessarily, because I believe it is a good Act and was designed for a good purpose, and is largely fulfilling that purpose. I do -not, however, think that it is going to increase production in the eastern provinces, although it may do so in the western provinces where there is virgin prairie land on which they can settle these men. In New Brunswick and perhaps all the other eastern provinces there is very little such land. Nearly all the virgin lands in the East are -wooded, and such lands can be worked best by men who have had experience in these conditions of cultivation. I do not think production will be increased by putting on such a farm a total stranger to conditions in the particular district. I have no fault to find with the purpose of the Act; I think it a very wise thing to establish these men in one of the noblest callings of the present day, that is, the production of the food necessary to feed the starving millions of the world. I think, however, that the terms of the Soldiers' Settlement Act require modifying in some respects. As hon. members are aware, these men have twenty-five years to pay for the farm on the amortization plan; they have six years to pay off the loan for stock and equipment, beginning with the third year, -they do not pay anything for the first two years on the stock and equipment loan, and that, I think, is a very good provision. I think the time for paying off the loan for stock and equipment should be extended for a longer period, and I will show the House a little later on how I arrive at this conclusion. Every man who was associated with me in that work in New Brunswick-and I do not think I am violating anyone's confidence in saying this-during the past summer and the previous winter, held the same view that I hold, namely, that it will be utterly impossible for these men to make their payments the third, fourth, fifth and sixth years. We had a detail d report made of what the cleared land was worth per acre, as well as the wooded land, together with a value of the buildings. We also secured a statement of the last two crops raised on the
farm, and if it was impossible to get this we asked our inspector to make an estimate-of the possible crop production of the farm. We took first the price asked for the farm and estimated what the man's yearly payments would be for the farm with stock and equipment necessary to operate it. From the total crop production of the farm we then had to deduct the actual cost of producing the crop, in which were included the man's living expenses for himself and his family for the year, and other indispensable expenditures. We were then in a position to know precisely what the man . would have left at the end of the year to make his payments. Let us take the case of a soldier receiving the maximum loan- and in this connection I desire to express my conviction that there is another room for improvement in the Act. The maximum loan, in my opinion, is too small to be of any practical advantage to the borrower, for you cannot buy a very extensive farm with proper buildings for $5,000. Any hon. member in this House who has ever engaged in farming will realize that a farmer must work a certain portion of his land for the keep of himself and his family. If you- double the acreage, the net profit from the added portion is far greater than from the first. It would nearly take a hundred acre farm to support an ordinary family. The man getting the maximum loan of $8,000 would pay $5,000 for the farm,. $2,000 for stock and equipment and $1,000 for permanent improvements. His payments yearly for 25 years on the farm would be $390. On the third, fourth, fifth and sixth years his payments on stock and equipment would be $564 a year. And on a farm of this kind his tax would be in the neighborhood of $60 and his insurance $20. His total payments -would therefore be $1,034 a year for these four years, which would take almost 13 per cent of a net profit on the whole investment of $8,COO. In figuring up the purchases which we made during the summer-we had about one hundred applications per month in New Brunswick alone-we found that very few of the farms would return a net profit-after allowing for actual cost of production not including wages for the man and his family-apart from actual living expenses. We learned that very few of these farms would bring a net profit of more than ten per cent, and some less. I believe, however, that if the time were extended for payment of the loan for stock and equipment to twenty-five years beginning at the third year it would be possible for the borrower to meet

his payments. If we allowed twenty-five years for the whole payment of the loan his payments would be $544 yearly and his taxes and insurance $80, making a yearly payment of $624 a year for twenty-five years, or nearly 8 per cent on the total investment. Of course, one objection that might be raised to the extension of time in regard to stock and equipment would be that the stock and equipment would not be good security after six years. But if I understand the Act correctly, and I think I do, everything that the man ever owns, farm, stock and equipment, including increase of his stock or any equipment he may acquire later, will still be held as security for the land; and as he cannot keep on farming without replacing his equipment when it wears out he will necessarily always have complete equipment of machinery on the farm, as well as stock. The man would be farming under Government supervision so that it would be impossible for him to allow his stock or equipment to deteriorate without the board being immediately aware of it. The field supervisors are supposed to pay these men monthly visits. Let us suppose that a man were given twenty-five years in which to make his payment; we shall see what the Government's security would be like at the end of six years. In the first place, he has to pay down 10 per cent of the purchase price- in the case assumed, this payment would be $500-before he gets possession of the farm. At the end of six years he would have paid $390 a year on his farm, or a payment of $2,340, and $154 a year, or within a fraction of that sum, for the third, fourth, fifth and sixth years on the stock and equipment loan. Thus at the end of six years he would have paid $3,456. This would make this property a better security to the Government than it -was at the outset. For if the man has to pay out every last dollar that he can rake and scrape in order to meet his payments he will not be able to replace his stock and equipment; but if he is given a sufficiently long time in which to pay he will be able to make replacements when necessary. There is also a provision in the Act permitting soldiers to make payments more quickly if they see fit and are able to do so, and my belief is that these men would be only too anxious to make their payments as. quickly as possible, because the more they pay yearly the less their interest charges. These men have no equity in the land and no credit with any one. They are not able to do business the same as other men until their fMr. Caldwell.]'
loan is fully paid. During the present session I have received a number of letters from those who were settled last summer inquiring as to what method they should adopt to secure fertilizer for the coming spring's planting. The fertilizer dealers will not advance them any fertilizer because these farmers have no security to offer; you cannot collect a cent from them unless they are willing to pay, their property being held by the board until the loan is paid. This is right, because, I admit, the board must protect itself. I desire to read that section of the Act dealing with repayment to show why it is necessary to make it possible for the men to meet the payments when they fall due;
AH sales of property, real, personal or other, made pursuant to the provisions of this order and whereon any balance of the sale price shall remain payable by instalments, shall be evidenced by agreement of sale, which shall fully set forth the terms of sale. If any instalment mentioned in any such agreement of sale ds not punctually made, or if default is made in respect to any other provision of such agreement of sale, the .Board shall be at liberty, without any formal re-entry or re-taking, and without resort to proceedings in equity or at law, to rescind such agreement, to cancel such agreement of sale and to recall the property, real, personal or other, to another settler. The effect of such rescission and cancellation shall be to vest such property in the Board absolutely free and discharged of all rights and claims of the settler and of all persons claiming or entitled to claim through or under him for any estate in, or lien, charge or encumbrance upon or against such property. If and when such property is resold by the Board any surplus remains in its hands beyond the amount owing to it as balance of the sale price and interest at five per cent per annum and expenses of taking over and reselling the property, the Board may pay such surplus- to the settler, but if, instead, a deficiency arises, that deficiency shall be paid by the settler to the Board, which shall have a right of action against him therefore. Before exercising the rights by this section given the Board shall give to the settler notice of its intention so to do, which notice shall be deemed duly given if mailed in any post office by registered letter addressed to the settler at his last address known to the Board thirty clear days before the Board acts thereunder.
There is another feature of the Act to which I think some attention should be given. The man's wife does not have any right of dower in the land until the loan is fully paid, and no judgment bill of sale or any other lien can be executed against the property pending that time. Even his crop cannot be seized for debt. I do not find fault with these provisions; they are absolutely necessary, I think, to protect the Soldiers' Settlement Board. On the other hand, I think it will be realized that, it is imperative that the Government should not pass any regulation the terms and condi-

tions of which it will be impossible for these soldier settlers to comply with and I think I have made it clear to the House that it is practically impossible for these men to meet their payments in the third, fourth, fifth arid sixth years under the Act as it is at present.
There is one other feature of soldiers' reestablishment that I would like to speak of *as briefly as I can-because I" think there is a feeling in the country that the time of the House is wasted in long speeches and I do not want to be among those who transgress. What I desire to say has reference to university students who enlisted and went overseas. The p*ension laiy, 1 believe, makes provision for a man who comes back disabled and not able to t$ke up his vocation where he left off. He is given training in some other department that he may wish to take up. While these students may come back absolutely fit physically, they are not in a position to take up anything and become earning entities in the country. They will have to spend two, three or four years before they are in a position to take their places in the world and even to earn their daily bread. I believe these men should be granted something by -way of gift or loan. I am not very much in favour of a gift to anybody, and I do >
not believe that any money given in that way can be considered as a gift or charity at all. I do not want to be misunderstood in that respect. . I be-lieye they are asking for a gratuity in order to educate themselves. I think they should haye some assistance along these lines in the way of a gratuity and that they should be granted the balance of the money they need by way of loan to enable them to finish their education.

The reason for this concurrence was that the provisions for the re-establishment of the soldier was not adequate. Surely if those provisions are not adequate now, they were not adequate then, when we were on the threshold of a very hard winter. What astonishes me is to hear the leader of the Government-whose attitude I assume, is supported by members of the Government and also by hon. gentlemen on the other side who have spoken as well as some who have not spoken-say now: " It is quite true that the provisions for the re-establishment of the soldier are not adequate. Last year they were adequate: We had to vote $40,000,000 without delay; we had no time to study the matter further." But now, four months afterwards, when some of the men who needed the money then may have since starved,-I know some provision was made for necessitous cases, but a great many of the necessitous cases did not apply for pubic

Mr. Speaker, I support the motion of the member for Centre Winnipeg, but I hope that the adoption of the suggestion embodied in this resolution-and I say this without desiring to make any reflections upon my hon. friend (Mr. Andrews)-will not be used by the guilty parties-by the members of the Government and hon. gentlemen opposite who are guilty of having said to the soldier: " We will do this and we will do that for you," but have neglected to fulfil their promises;-I hope, I say, that this committee will not be used as a camouflage to be presented to the Great War Veterans' Convention which is to meet in Montreal next week. I support this motion because I think that a thorough investigation should be made into the land settlement scheme, but not by such a committee as the Re-establishment Committee of last year, which was largely composed of city men. For instance, I was on the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Committee of last .year, and when the question of land settlement came up I was in the' position of not knowing a plough from a harrow. I did not know anything about land settlement, and I am sure that other members of the committee were similarly situated. The Government will be well advised-this is by way of advice, not of criticism-to pick out those particular phases of re-establishment which really need to be looked into .and have them dealt with by separate committees, each made up of men competent to judge of what should be done. So far as land settlement is concerned, I would recommend that the Government address themselves to our worthy friends of the former cross benches who now sit on my left; I am quite sure that the Government could obtain considerable information from them.
The question of insurance was left in abeyance last year. That is a subject which really requires a special committee; an ordinary committee cannot possibly go into such a question as that of sub-standard insurance, the technical term, I understand, for the kind of insurance demanded by the member for Muskoka (Mr. Peter McGib-bon). On such a committee there should be technical men, men trained in the profession of insurance, men who know something about, the matter.

Vocational training is another sphere of activity in connection with soldiers' civil reestablishment. I understand that in February of this year vocational training ceased and that work is no longer being carried on. If the committee is to be a committee such as we had last year and is to bring in recommendations similar to those brought in last year, I cannot for the life of me see the utility of it. If we are going to take up separately new subjects, subjects that have not been so far treated, thbn the committee will be doing good work and I congratulate the Government on having on this late date granted this committee. If it is to repeat again recommendations which we gave last year and act on them as we acted on last year's recommendations, then we might as well not appoint a committee; w-e do not want it. The whole thing amounts to this; the first principal question which should be treated with regard to the re-establishment of the soldier is this, that the soldier be treated and looked after by soldiers. The first advice I shall give to the Government is: Dismiss your Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. The second word of advice is: Dismiss your Deputy Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and the third word of advice is: When you appoint another minister, let us have him in this House where we can see him and talk to him. I am willing to wager that 50 per cent of the members of this House or of the people throughout the country hardly know the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment.

The hon. gentleman mentions a member of the other chamber who is not the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. Had he been Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, there would, perhaps, have been a reason for his presence in the Cabinet as at any rate he was a soldier; he was at the front; but I maintain that such an important department as that of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment should certainly have a minister in this House.
In conclusion, in supporting the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg Centre (Mr. Andrews), and in supporting the suggestion of the leader of the Government (Sir George Foster) I hope this committee will have some definite results. Let us divide it

the way we like, but let us have such results that we can say to the soldier: "At last, after all our promises, after telling you that we would do everything for you when you returned; that nothing was too good for the man who, shed his blood for us on the plains of Flanders, this is the concrete thing we are going to do for you; we promise you no more; we are going to do this; we will not put you off with more promises; this is what you have; either be satisfied with it or not, we cannot do any more; we find that impossible, our funds will not permit us to do any more; our willingness will not permit us to do any more; something will not permit us to do any more." At any rate let us be frank with the soldier, and tell him: "We will give you this, and we will give you nothing else, or we will not give you this," so that the soldier may know exactly where he stands and every one of them will be thankful to this Government and his representative if the soldier is ever placed into that happy position.

speechtext:
On the contrary, I must say that the work of the commitee of last year was very efficient, and that the work of the hon. gentleman himself was, perhaps, more efficient than that of some of the others.
Mr. DANIEL D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria): Mr. Speaker, this question is by no means a new one; we have been dealing with soldiers' re-establishment and soldiers' questions for some time. I am sure I need not tell the hon. member for Winnipeg Centre (Mr. Andrews) that I thoroughly agree with what he says about the deserving returned soldier; nor need I tell him that I agree with him as to the excellent work that was done and the bravery exhibited by our men overseas. We all concur in that. But I think the soldier, who patiently fought in the trenches and who was looking forward from day to day to the end of the war, had his patience pretty well exhausted in operations of that kind without being put to the extreme test of waiting until this Government would do something by way of relief. The war was tedious enough, but the tediousness of the war is not to be compared with the dilatoriness and the "tediosity," if there be such a word, of this Government. This institution, this very excellent Government,
who in turn put up one after another of their best speakers-and they have some good speakers-to praise themselves and to tell of the excellent things they have done and the excellent things they intend to do -had decided this question almost a year ago without obtaining any evidence. We had the exhibition in this House of the Minister of (Justice (Mr. Doherty) standing ,up in his place as the then 4 p.m. leader of the Government and saying that the Government had reached the conclusion that they were not going to do anything along those lines; that the financial condition of the country was such that they could not spepd another dollar, and the argument was that they had done as much or more than any other country and that they could not be expected to go any further along those lines. But if they had stood by that decision, we would have some respect and regard for them, and at all events, felt that they had reached a conclusion and they were prepared to stand by it and to let the people of this country pass judgment upon them as to whether or not they had done what was fair and reasonable in connection with the matter. But there was considerable agitation in the country amongst the returned soldiers, and reports were coming to the ears of the Government that their decision was not popular, and that the returned soldiers, when they had an opportunity, were likely to condemn by theh votes and influence the action of the Government in regard to dealing with their respective cases. A decision was reached in the Government that they would have to do something. That something was the appointment of another committee to inquire into the judgment that they had already passed. I am an old practising barrister, and we have in some courts in this province, at all events in my province, a provision by which a judge may review his own decision. My experience of some twentydive or thirty years is that I never came across any judge who would change a decision which he had already given; he always stood by it. That has been our experience with this Government. The evidence that was collected throughout the country was simply evidence to justify the decision that the Government had already reached. The chairman of that committee, a capable and astute politician, called to the witness stand such persons as would justify the attitude which the Government had taken in saying that the finances of this country were exhausted and that they would not stand any further
i

strain. The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), who is always a ready relief for this Government, was called into the witness box to say that he knew the finances of this country, and that not another dollar could be expended along the line suggested by the soldiers. As might be expected, the chairman of the committee and other friends of the 'Government, and other men who were not friends of the Government, brought in a report confirming the decision that had already been reached that nothing could be done. When that report was brought down, my honoured leader (Mr. Mackenzie King), moved an amendment in this House, after having heard arguments pro and con in respect to the report, and that amendment, as it appears on page 1892 of Hansard for the special session of last year, reads:
That the said motion or amendment be not concurred in, but that the said report now under consideration be sent back to the said committee for further consideration.
When the report of the committee was before the House a great many opinions were expressed by hon. members on both sides, but paiticularly on the Government side and it was suggested that certain means could h,e devised by which money could be raised for the purpose of relieving the soldiers. The hon. gentlemen who are to-day asking for further inquiry, by their votes on that occasion pronounced in a decided manner that no further investigation was necessary and that the report was good enough. We voted against the report on the ground that it was unsatisfactory and we said that one or two of the suggestions should be acted on and an effort-made to find some means by which the soldiers' needs could be met in a way that would be at least fairly satisfactory to these worthy men. It is somewhat surprising, Sir, that hon. gentlemen supporting the Government who were perfectly satisfied with the report and voted for it should to-day come hack and allege that it was unsatisfactory and inadequate and urge that something further should be done. It would be desirable to know when the end of this seemingly endless chain is going to be reached. One report after another is made. Hon. gentlemen opposite who are supporting the Government will vote for a committee and its report, which they will eulogize as being entirely satisfactory, and as soon as it is ascertained that' it is really inadequate and does not meet the requirements of the soldiers, they immediately stand up and ask for another committee and a further investigation. This, Mr. Speaker, is merely tem-

*porizing and offers no relief to the unfortunate soldiers. My good friend, the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government (Sir George Foster) will no doubt appreciate the fact that committees' reports, however beautifully expressed they may be, will not put meal into the pot, or keep it boiling for the poor children of the returned soldiers, who need money in order to obtain the very necessaries of life to support them through the hard times now prevailing in this country. Something tangible should be done. If it is necessary to provide help for the soldiers-and I believe it is-time is of supreme importance, and we should take action at once. Surely if we have had, from the inception of the department down to the present time, a competent minister at the head of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, with facilities for obtaining ample information, he should know by this time what is necessary. The ministers are not overpaid, of course; but shall it be said that we are entrusting them with the control of departments of government, and furnishing them with every necessary staff and equipment, with every means of obtaining any information they may require, and, when anything is to be done, find that they know nothing about the subject with which they have to deal but must call for a committee of the House of Commons, who have never had anything particular to do with that subject, but iwhose duty it must be to inform the ministers upon matters peculiarly within the precincts of their departments? Yet, Sir, that is the condition of things, and I have no other conclusion to reach than that an effort is being made to postpone necessary action from time to time and give to the [DOT]soldiers camouflaged unreality in place of real help, throwing dust in their eyes in the hope of appeasing them. I do not think that anything more will come of this committee. Indeed, I do not believe that a *committee can be appointed which will be better than the last one, or whose report can be more exhaustive; and if the finances of the country could stand no strain last year, I venture to suggest to the present Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) that there is less likelihood now of their being able to do so. I observe that in the month of January, if I read the reports correctly, we plunged into an indebtedness of something like $64,000,000 over and above the income that ought to meet the demands upon the exchequer for that month; and I [DOT] presume that other months since we parted last November were not very much better. Under these circumstances is it proposed

that this n^w committee shall find money and devise means by which it is to be properly distributed for the re-establishment ol *soldiers? 1 submit that this motion is rather indefinite if we are to deal with any special subject. I do not want to find fault with the mover or seconder on that score, for I presume that if the motion is carried steps will be taken to specify more particularly what the subject matter of the inquiry will be. All that we are informed here is that the provisions so far made have proven inadequate.
We have no very great provisions except the Soldiers' Settlement Act, and when time will have developed what takes place under that Act and have fully shown the results, I fear it will be found that the provisions of that Act are unsatisfactory. I am told that the soldier who is put upon the land and to whom money is lent cannot call his soul *his own, and in no respect can he exercise his own judgment. The plough, the horse, [DOT]and the cow he gets is bought for him by emissaries of this Government who are capable of making any amount of graft as middlemen between the farmer and those from whom the articles are bought. They are charged to the farmer, who is supposed to pay for them, but evidently he has nothing to say about the price. The articles are not his; they are branded as Government property and the man has no credit or standing in the country. He has really nothing to say about the property, being as a matter of fact a ward of the Government, and in such a way that his own personality and initiative play no part in the start 'he has in life. I sincerely trust that these men who are re-established on the farms will make a success of their calling, but I think that provision should have been made for those who follow other occupations. When the Act was before the House I urged upon the minister in charge of it the desirability of having a general policy of settling the soldiers besides, establishing them on land. I said that it would not do to frame a policy applicable only to *men who desired to be farmers, but that consideration should be given to lumbermen, miners, fishermen, etc., who might he *anxious to pursue these occupations. The soldiers were drawn from different classes, and there certainly should have been established a general policy embracing men of every calling in life so that the soldiers of every vocation might have an opportunity to resume his work. The 'Government, however, thought proper to single out agriculture as the industry in which to re-establish the men, spending enormous sums of money
on the farms and paying no attention to * the other classes I have mentioned. The results is that we have not only discontented farmers, but discontented lumbermen, fishermen and others, and are experiencing a general dissatisfaction because nothing has been done for those who did not and could not undertake farming. I do not wish to be regarded as unfair to the Government. I know that a great many things have been done, such, for instance, as educating young men in different walks of life, and it would be unjust of me to say that nothing has been undertaken. It is evident from the general discontent from Vancouver to Scutari among the returned soldiers that what should reasonably have been done has not been done.
I voted for a further inquiry last year.
I thought the amendment of the leader of the Opposition should have 'been adopted by the Government and that further inquiry should have been made. For that reason, if there is a motion for the appointing of a committee, I am here to say that any further inquiry that may be necessary should be given. But I would suggest to the Government that a committee sitting in this House is not the best means of inquiring as to what is taking place in British Columbia, the Northwest, Winnipeg or the Maritime Provinces. Of course, we are sick and tired of roving commissions and we are sick and tired of ministers and departments who know nothing about their business. Nevertheless, if a thorough investigation is to be made-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext: These general assertions are sometimes not very pleasant. Instead of including the whole Government among those who know nothing about their business the hon. gentleman should tell us who are the ones who do not know anything about their business. It would be interesting.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
