speechtext:
I rise to a point of order.
Mr, NESBITT: Pardon me, the member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp), the member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) iand several other hon. gentlemen. I sat with those hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House for several years and I know them to be very competent and very upright. The Chairman of the, committee never personally, to my knowledge, asked for any particular evidence to- be submitted to the committee. Various organizations asked to be heard and the chairman put it to the committee whether their request should be granted or not. It was seldom that any 1 evidence was objected to or ruled out excepting rwhen it was proffered ;by organizations connected with the Great War Veterans, and then the committee asked that their evidence might be submitted through that body. I am sure that no committee composed of members of this House ever tried more strenuously to do their duty or attended more closely to that duty than did the committee on the Soldiers' Civil Re-esabli-shment. They sat three times a day for over a month, they listened to t-e-sti-34 *
mony from witnesses from districts ranging from Vancouver to Ha'if ax -and they paid the closest possible attention to that evidence. But they had to take into- consideration 'the interests and financial condition of the -country a,s well as the interests *of the returned -soldier. No man, not excepting -even my hon. friend from North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) could have listened with greater attention to the evidence that was submitted than did the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, and no human being could have given that evidence greater attention than be did, or could have allowed, no matter what exertion he put forth, more evidence to be brought forward unless the committee had sat all last fall in order to listen to it. I repeat that no one could have allowed more evidence or greater latitude or opportunity for evidence to be given, than did the minister -in question. I rose for the purpose of resenting any insinuation that the committee were governed or ruled in -any shape, manner or form by the Government or any -member of it, or that the judgment of the committee was influenced in any manner whatsoever by the Government or any person representing the Government-. Personally I re-sent any insinuation that I was influenced or dominated by anybody it does not matter by whom. The only -authority that has any influence over me in my judgment of any -case that comes before me to be judged- and that influence is directed so that I do not know it-is the Lord. So that I naturally resent any person insinuating that I was elected a member of the committee because it was desired that a certain verdict would be given. The same thing is true of every member of the committee in my humble opinion. Remember that the report of the committee was unanimous; I do not believe that any of the Opposition members on 'the committee who were my strong personal friends were influenced in any degree whatever by any human being; they were influenced -solely by the desire t-o do justice to the returned soldiers as near.as it /was humanly possible to do so.
As to the Land Settlement Board we were not appointed to consider anything with respect to their operations. It did -so happen that we had to secure -some evidence with -respect to the hoard in order to find out what was being done in the re-establishment of the soldier. Now if there is anything wrong in connection with the Land Settlement Board-judging from my experience prior to and since the sittings of the committee-the errors are all on the



side of the soldier and not on the side of the country. The Land Settlement Board is managed with good judgment-the very best judgment I think that could be brought to bear in connection with it- but the proposition is a very difficult one. I listened with a great deal of interest this afternoon to the observations of an hon. gentleman opposite who had been working on the Land Settlement Board in New Brunswick for the reason that the hon. gentleman in question has had experience of, and is familiar with, the question. There is a good deal to be said from his standpoint, but there is also much to be said in opposition to it. It is one of those questions that a committee could sit down quietly and thresh out when the views of the majority of course would prevail.
Just a word about the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. I have had more or less experience in connection with that work, especially since the meetings of the Parliamentary Committee and it is because of that experience that I say that any errors arising in connection with that work have always been in favour of the soldier. And errors are almost impossible to avoid. Not even a man endowed with the wisdom of Solomon could entirely avoid imposition in connection with the. work of the Soldier Settlement Board, and the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and especially the Vocational 'Training BrancH. Even if everything was done that it was humanly possible 'to do I do not think we could escape from imposition, and as I say, any errors that have resulted, according to my experience, have always been in favour of the soldier. It is hardly possible for these departments to escape being imposed upon to a certain extent. I have tried to work out some scheme under which imposition would not occur but it seems to be hopelessly impossible to avoid it altogether.
As to the resolution under discussion it is possible that there are certain things in connection with the re-establishment of the soldier that 'have not yet been investigated. The same may be true with respect to the provision made for the soldiers' dependents. Still while a good many questions have been investigated, I see no reason why, as the leader of the Government pointed out a few minutes ago, a committee could not be* appointed to investigate certain questions relating to the returned soldier that have no\ yet been inquired into and to suggest any remedies where remedies are found to be necessary. Personally I would think that as there

is a motion on the Order Paper for the re-lai.tpo'intment of a committee to inquire into the working of the Pensions Aot, perhaps any other question relating to the returned soldier that has not already been* investigated might be referred to that committee.
During the present session I have listened to several debates dealing more or less with this question, and several hon. members have stated circumstances that seemed very harsh, I did not hear all that was said about pensions this afternoon, but I do know that when the Pensions Committee sat for three years-and I happened to be a member of it from its organization-we inquired into a great many complaints, and I think I can say, without the slightest exaggeration, that in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the committee found the Pensions Board were right. I remember only two instances in those three years where we found the Pensions Board were not correct in their findings in the judgment of the committee; and it must be borne in mind that that committee was composed of members of the House of Commons, whose inclination was, if anything, towards the-complainants.
A great many of these cases appear very hard while you have .heard only one side, but no one knows better than a lawyer that when you eome to hear the other side they may assume a very different aspect. I do not think that complaints-against either the S.'C.R. or the Pensions Board should be aired here by individual members unless they have been inquired into by them personally. I said the other day that after I had inquired into any complaints brought to my notice, if they were within the regulations of the Pensions Act and were capable of adjustment by the Pensions Board, they were immediately adjusted. I can only repeat that statement. Hon. members must bear in mind that the committee of the S.'C.R. and the Pensions Board are governed not by their own ideas but by the provisions of the Statutes controlling them. It would be a fatal thing for those two bodies to act according to their personal inclination, because then we would immediately have complaints of favoritism, and that would be the worst thing that could possibly happen.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would not have taken any part in this debate-in fact, I had no intention of doing so-had not my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) insinuated that the committee-and, by the way, I have seen this stated in the papers before to-

day-that the committee had been handpicked as to some of its members, who were appointed purposely to carry out the will of the Government. I rose to give that statement the most emphatic denial. I see on the other side of the House two or three of my brother committeemen and I leave it to them to say whether any influence was brought to bear to shut out any evidence that should have come before the Committee.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) on the eloquent manner in which he has placed his request before the House, and, secondly, I wrish to state that I shall give my support to the resolution, hoping, as has already been stated by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), that a committee will be given an opportunity of further studying this question.
I do not rise for the purpose of criticising the report of the old committee. The amendment which my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition brought in at the end of last session was that with the further light and knowledge furnished to the House during the discussion the report should be referred to the same committee for further consideration.. Therefore that amendment was not a condemnation of the report or of the personnel of the committee. In speaking briefly on the subject at the time I declared myself favourable to a gratuity- not to the extent which had been asked for before the committee, involving an expenditure of perhaps $800,000,000, but to an extent scarcely reaching twenty or twenty-five per cent of that amount. It is true that at that time the leader of the Government to-day as well as the hon. Minister of the Interior declared to the House and to the country that we were not in a position to grant any further money to the returned soldiers. However, the next day the Government came down with a proposition to acquire the Grand Trunk Railway system, and they did acquire it, and laid on the country an immense amount of further indebtedness. Now my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior having been able to gratify his ambition in that respect, I am sure that his ingenuity is not exhausted, and that he will be able to find the means necessary to give our returned soldiers what they really deserve and what to a great extent they have a right to expect, from the country.	!	1
34J	.
At that time in seconding the resolution of my hon: friend from Winnipeg I had different considerations in view. I felt that the most needy soldier is generally the most humble, and will not go before a committee to receive charity. I know hundreds oi cases in my constituency, Mr. Speaker,- and when I say hundreds of cases, do not think for a moment that I am exaggerating-I repeat, I know hundreds of cases oi returned soldiers suffering in many ways, A returned soldier not able to suit himself according to his ambition will not apply for charity because perhaps he has a brother who will give him a home, or he may be able to go to his paternal home, although-filled with other children. But that is the very soldier who requires the attention of the country. The only fair way is to give something to every soldier. I may be answered that to grant such a gratuity to a great many will be an invitation to waste. 400,000 soldiers are to-day still waiting for re-establishment of the 600,000 who went overseas. The soldier is human, just like any other man, and no doubt a few might waste the money that they got from the country. But the majority of them are sensible men and will re-establish themselves not only with a view to enjoying life, but also with a view to proving the value of their citizenship after the winning of the war.
I represent a lumbering, farming and fishing constituency. I know of a number of cases'of returned men in my constituency who are without the means of following their occupation of fishing. It may be said that $400 or $500 would not be sufficient to-enable a returned man who wanted to engage in the fishing business to buy a sailing vessel or motor boat. That is true, but if he is willing to invest the $400 or $500 in the construction or purchase of a 'sailing vessel or motor boat, some one may easily be found in the locality who will be-willing to trust him with the balance. There might be a tendency not to advance the man the whole amount necessary to establish him in business, because of an apprehension that he might not, having put no money into it himself, be sufficiently industrious and energetic to carry it out successfully. But having invested $400 or $500, he gives a guarantee of his good faith and some person of means in the locality would surely be willing to help him out.
Then, there is'the case of the students. Many young men who vrere on the point of leaving college and entering university went to the wrar and upon their return they

have tried to get the means to attend university. We will say that it would take two or three thousand dollars to put a man through university. Well, if you gave him $400 or $500 he would be enabled to carry on his studies for a certain length of time, and a doctor or a lawyer or other good neighbour in his district would undoubtedly be willing to furnish the means necessary to enable the young man to finish his course, although he might not have been willing to run the risk of advancing the cost of the whole course. I hope, therefore, that the leader of the Government, whose generosity seems to increase year by year since he has acquired a good knowledge of the French language and an appreciation of the sentiment of those who speak it, will, in cooperation with the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) be able to arrange for a committee to look into this matter.
Canada is not bankrupt; Canada can assist her returned soldiers as generously as other countries assist theirs. In fact, Canada has done better for her soldiers than any other country has done. But the Canadian soldiers won a lasting name in the battlefields overseas; his name is of universal repute. When we boast of what the Government or the country has done in relation to the war we must remember that it is the Canadian soldier who did it. It was the Canadian soldiers who saved the Empire at the very beginning of the war; by their courage in maintaining the line until reinforcements came they kept the Germans from breaking through and reaching the sea through France and Belgium. So that I hope that a committee will be appointed which will consider the matter from every angle with a view to doing something to allay the disquiet which prevails throughout the country, particularly on the part of returned soldiers, and to provide generously for the re-establishment of these men into civil life so that they may be enabled to exercise their citizenship in accordance with the true British spirit.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I invite the attention of the House to the wording of the resolution proposed by the member for Winnipeg Centre (Mr. Andrews). It reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the provision made for re-establishing in civil life the members of His Majesty's forces who served in the late war has in many cases proved inadequate, and that it is desirable that a special committee of this House be appointed to consider what provision can be made to meet such cases.
TMr. Turgeon.]
And so on. It will be noted that the first statement in the resolution is that the provision hitherto made for re-establishment of our returned soldiers has proved inadequate. I think we ought to be careful not io allow the impression to go abroad that here is real ground for the contention made by some that the country has grossly neglected the returned soldier. 'Generally speaking, and holding in reserve for the moment special cases to which I shall refer later, I think that Canada has succeeded beyond the hopes of the most optimistic in solving the general problem of re-establishment. Or, to put it in another way, a very large proportion of the returned men are to-day happily reinstated in civil life. In saying that I do not for a moment wish to throw out the inference that the country has discharged its debt of gratitude and otherwise to the returned soldier. That is a debt which we shall never be able to repay, but it is a debt which comparatively few of the men themselves desire to have capitalized in the form of dollars and cents. But that does not alter the fact that I have already mentioned, namely, that in the main the great problem of re-establishment has been most intelligently and fairly successfully dealt with. I am conscious, however, that there are some cases-some classes, if you will-that have not, in my estimation, and I think in the estimation of a large number of the people, been properly dealt with. Indeed, Sir, the right hon. leader of the House (Sir George Foster) this afternoon expressed sentiments which lead me to believe that he himself concurs in that view. I suggest, therefore, that the member for Winnipeg Centre has, perhaps, made the wording of his resolution a little loose, because he generalizes in saying that the re-establishment scheme has proved inadequate and he make's no specific statement of the cases which he desires should go before the committee. Such a committee, appointed under this resolution, would have the whole field to travel over again, d submit that it is inadvisable for this Parliament to appoint another commitee which, .by inviting from different parts of the country witnesses and others who desire to present schemes and cases, will traverse again the wide field which was gone over with such care and in such detail last autumn. I would, however, prefer that either the Government itself by a Cabinet committee, or the House by a special committee, deal in some effective manner with specific cases, some of which I shall present to the House this afternoon, which should be

considered. It is a matter of gratitude to me to note that the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) assured the House that the Pension Committee would take up the matter of pensions. I desire, however, to take this opportunity-as it comes within the purview of this resolution-to refer very briefly to pensions. I am going to give the House two illustrations indicating a principle of administration of the Pension Board, which I desire to characterize here as, in my estimation, iniquitous, to put it mildly. It is a principle indicated by the two cases I shall submit to the House. Five boys of one family went overseas, and three of those boys were killed in. France. The mother was an elderly woman who had married again, so that there .was a step-father. Both of those people were too old to keep themselves, and they were dependent upon those boys for a living. When the three boys were killed, the Pension Board granted a pension of $48 a month to the step-father and the mother. This pension was gratefully received and no complaint was made, they being apparently satisfied with the amount. But this old couple, desirous of reducing the cost of their living, removed from the environs of the city to a place about ten miles outside, secured a small piece of land and built a cottage on it, thereby eliminating rent and raising in their garden some of the sustenance of life. As soon as the Pension iBo^trd learned that this couple had attempted to supplement their meagre pension in this way, they reduced the pension by ten dollars a month on the ground that the couple now had to pay no rent. Can you, Mr. Speaker, and ,hon. members, imagine a more iniquitous practice than that? I give you one other case, and these two are indicative of many more. An elderly lady, a widow, lost her only boy overseas. 'She owned in Vancouver a house which was heavily mortgaged. She received a pension, I think, of $48 a month; it may have been a little more, but it was the ordinary regular pension, with which she was satisfied. In the rear of her lot she had a small building, and she spent $70 in fitting this building up, making it habitable, and she rented it for $15 a month, thus supplementing the meagre pension she was receiving and assisting her to carry on in this life. The Pension Board again seized upon that and reduced her pension by $15 a month, the amount of the pittance she received from this shack in the rear of her lot. Not only did they do that, but they totally ignored the fact that the woman had spent almost a hundred
dollars in fitting up the building. These two cases are sufficient indication of a pernicious regulation being practiced constantly by the Pension Board, and it is such irritating and, 1 consider, utterly unneeded practices as this that cause a great deal of dissatisfaction. I give these illustrations to the House so that we may address ourselves to remedying regulations which are, on the face of them, wrong, unfair, unjust and, as I say, iniquitous, im this case.
I proceed to another phase of the question. I shall not discuss pensions further, because they will go before another committee. We have the claim of the student. I shall not traverse the ground gone over last year in this regard, but the student undoubtedly has a peculiar claim upon this country. This country above all others, and, indeed, in common with the leading countries of the world, realizes that a fair education is a great asset to the community. Indeed, in most of our provinces, we have a law of compulsory education, and why? Simply because we know that a man who has a fair education is a better asset to the country than a man without any education at all. The bulk of these students, particularly in the universities, stopped in the middle of their course and gave their services to the country. Having been for the time being dissociated from their studies, when they come back they find themselves somewhat handicapped, and they are asking that some 'consideration shall be given to them. The only objection to the proposal hitherto has been that it will interfere with other classes; or in other words, there will be other classes of returned soldiers which would claim the same privilege. I at once admit that there is an argument in this; that it is possible that it would cause the Government or the administration having charge of the matter some difficulties and confusion. But if' we are going, as a Parliament, to refuse to do what is eminently just and in the interest of the country simply because it presents difficulties, then we are derelict in our duty to the country, and the sooner Parliament recognizes that it is by adjusting these individual cases that we shall make progress towards social and industrial peace, the better for the country at large. Therefore, I believe the case of the student whose studies were interrupted by the war, is a case worthy of special consideration, irrespective of its relation to other individual cases.
I pass on to another case to which I wish to refer with the utmost brevity, and that

-is the vocational training group, the men 'who are taking vocational training. This is not a criticism of the government; but -as we progress in this hitherto untravelled field, we learn things that we ought, if we are wise, to take advantage of in order to effect remedies. In this particular realm, v it has been discovered that a man will start
*	a course as a bookkeeper, or as a mechanic, [DOT]*or in the motor transport, or as a carpenter, or in some other vocation. He may go on for two or three weeks or a couple of months, and it may be perfectly clear to those in charge that the individual is in the wrong vocation; that he is going to make an utter failure of it; that if we train him for three or six months as the case may be and turn him out, he will be useless and not, in any sense, a credit to the training he has received. It is the .function of Parliament, the duty of the Government and of the department con-[DOT].cerned to formulate such regulations that, when or if it is discovered that a man is .pursuing a course which it is clear he will fail in, he may he changed over to some other course where he may have an opportunity of making a success. That is a real, tangible grievance that should have the consideration of Parliament and of the Gov-
*	ernment.
A good deal has been said regarding the Hand Settlement Board, and I wish to take -this opportunity of paying a tribute to that Board. I am not going to analyze its work in detail, because I have not had an opportunity of studying it very closely; but I have criticised it, as I think, in a constructive manner where I felt I was warranted in doing so. But I must confess to this, that as far and as impartially as I can judge, the Land 'Settlement Board is doing -excellent work in 'Canada. It is administered by a man at the head, Mr. Black, I believe, who is not only doing his best tout enthusiastically devoted to the work. .I do not think a more capable man could foe chosen. What I suggest to hon. members is that we should rather refrain from careless and general criticisms of the Land Settlement Board and seek to point out any specific weakness and take it up directly 'with that Board, or through the Government or, if a committee be appointed, through such a committee. But the point I wish to emphasize is this, that rather than make general and sweeping criticisms, we should particularize and seek to bring out some useful criticism which may offer .an opportunity of a remedy being effected.
.{Mr. Stevens. 1
I wish to say to the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) that I take second place to no man in this House in respect for liis experience in Parliament, but I was seriously disappointed at the attack which he made upon the Government. He, if I remember rightly-and I am subject to correction if I am in error-said that the people were sick and tired of Royal Commissions and that a committee of this House would be useless because it could not understand conditions in British Columbia or the Prairies or the Maritime Provinces. Well, Sir, what in the name of common sense do we want? What justification is there for these sweeping condemnations of the Government? This is an entirely new problem, a new field that has never been trodden before. We are the pioneers in this field, other countries having patterned their vocational training and re-establishment much after the' original steps taken by this Government and this Parliament. 'I say, therefore, that rather than genera] criticisms, rather than sweeping condemnations of the Government, rather than feeding the fires of discontent in this country, the duty we owe to the people, to the returned soldier in particular, and to ourselves, is that, when we bring before Parliament a resolution of this kind, we should attempt to state as specifically as possible what grievance it. is that we are desirous to remedy.
So far as I am concerned, I do not feel that I am at all in duty bound to support the resolution in its present general terms, but I do bring to Parliament, as I have already said, such specific instances as have been laid before me in order to invite attention and correction, although not subscribing in any sense to a general condemnation of the work that has been undertaken, without knowledge or experience, and carried forward, as I believe, with a larger measure of success than has attended any similar work of such gigantic proportions.
Mr. G. B. NICHOLSON (East Algoma);
I desire to say a word or two on the subject that has been introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews). While I agree that it is desirable that Parliament should make further investigation of all the conditions surrounding the problem of re-establishing the returned soldiers in civil life, I do not by any means concur in the statements that have been made to the effect that the work done by the several departments of government which have been dealing with the re-establishment of our men has been inefficient or insincere,

He is not in the most robust state of health, and although he and his wife live in their own home, they, are not in a position substantially to augment their pension of $48. Now, because this man of seventy-five was fortunate enough to secure some light employment during the months of August, September and October last in order that he might earn a meagre pittance, the Pensions Board, after sending an inspector to investigate his case, reduced his pension by half, so that he now receives only $24. One of the reasons adduced for this action is the fact that these people are living in their own home, and do not have to pay-fifteen or twenty dollars a month rent. The other case is that of a widow who lost her only son in Prance, but who has at home three daughters who are domestics.
The Pension Board takes the ground that because these three girls, who are working out as domestics, are in receipt of an income, the mother should not get any pension at all. There is something wrong with regulations that will call upon a board representing the Government and Parliament of Canada to say that because a widowed mother who lost a boy in France has three daughters working out as domestics she is not entitled to some compensation on account of the loss of her son. I say, as I said to the Pension Board, surely these three girls are _ doing all they should be asked to do when they maintain themselves.
In regard to the Department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment and the criticisms that have been levelled against it, I am not here to defend any department particularly but I must say in justice to that department that having had a number of cases of returned men to deal with in my own .district and having been asked by these men to intercede for them, I have never received more sympathetic consideration from any department of Government, nor has any one ever gone further than the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment has gone in every case that has been brought before them. My judgment is that if there is anything wrong with what they are doing, or if their work is not adequate, it is because the machinery has not been made adequate and the responsibility rests upon the House of Commons to see that it is. Therefore, the suggestion made by the right hon. the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) that a committee is to be appointed meets with my absolute approval.
In so far as a cash gratuity to physically fit returned men is concerned I want to
[Mr. Nicholson. 1
make myself absolutely clear to this House as I have to the branches of the Great War Veterans' Association in my own district. I have said to them, and I say to this House, that the responsibility of the country to the disabled men, those who are not fit to go back into civil life or to the same positions that they occupied before they went overseas, and our responsibility to the dependents of the men who fell, will never be properly discharged until we have gone to the limit of the country's resources. I submit that if we dissipate a large part of the country's resources in providing a further cash amount to physically fit men we will be thereby rendering ourselves less able to take care of the physically unfit and the dependents of those who fell. It is not because we would not like to do it. I do not believe there is a man on either side of the House but who would give his last nickel to a returned soldier who needed it. It is not because /Canada does not want to do it but because there is a limit to the resources of the country, and it will tax these resources to the very limit if we take proper care of the widows and orphans of the men who fell and of the men who have come back physically unfit.
I agree heartily with the spirit of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) and with the spirit of the statement made by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster).
I think there should be a committee. My wish would be that the same committee which did such splendid work last year might take hold of the subject again and give the House and the country the benefit of their judgment, as -to the best means of discharging our responsibility to the returned men.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the re-establishment question was before the House last year I did not enter into, the discussion, but I favoured the appointment of a committee. When that Committee brought down a unanimous report I supported its recommendations. I think I can say that I have a mind of my own but at the same time when representative men from bo-th sides sat in committee afternoon, night and sometimes into the morning, men who had served in the trenches, men who have given their sons in the war, men who were acknowledged to possess sound business capacity, and men coming from both political parties,
I felt that I would require some very sound reason before I differed from their recommendations.

If this country could afford it I would like to see divided among the returned soldiers the $200,000,000 that was asked for. But it is impossible to do that. I accepted the report of the committee last year, and I went back home and defended my course. It was not a popular course to defend. 1 was often faced with criticism even by the reasonable men amongst the returned soldiers. When I told them that the committee said it was impossible for Canada to finance some of the schemes that were proposed and that we had to economize on account of the great obligations incurred through the war, they came back at me with statements to the effect that the Government was extravagant, that it was wasting money, that the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment was overmanned and that there was unnecessary expense in connection with it. They had me floored because I was not familiar with the facts in regard to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. If, as the Government claims, the country cannot afford to expend this money, it should be the business of Parliament to see that this Government is not wasting any money. I am not saying that the charge against the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is correct; all I am saying is that the charge was made. We should see that all these institutions controlling the affairs of the returned soldiers are manned sufficiently and economically so that we can convince the returned men that the attitude we are taking in this Parliament is'backed up by actual facts.
There are cases, such as have been mentioned on the floor of the House to-day in which pensions should be provided for at this session of Parliament. I have one complaint to offer to the House and it comes from a great many of the returned men. It is in connection with housing. They have come back from overseas and they are unable to find homes to live in. They cannot avail themselves of any housing scheme in Alberta at any rate. If this Government in some way could help the returned' men to acquire homes of- their own, not by gift but by loan, they would remove a great deal of the criticism that exists.
Again, the suggestion was made last year 

and I think it was left open for consideration-that loans should be extended beyond disabled men. I know it is impossible to grant a loaii to every man who asks for it but it should be possible to consider the merits of a man just as a loan company or
a bank considers them. We should assist such a man in that way provided we were satisfied that he was a gilt edged proposition and would use the money to the advantage of himself and the community in which he lived and, in due course, pay it back. If a loan scheme along this line were adopted I think it would meet the demands of the reasonable men amongst the returned soldiers. We cannot satisfy the extremists in any movement. Even if we can satisfy one reasonable man by a proposal of this kind we should try and do so in any further consideration of the case of the returned men.
I have no objection to the appointment of a Committee to consider further problems in connection with re-establishment provided it deals with the necessities of the moment and deals with questions that it is possible for the country to solve. I am convinced that it is impossible to satisfy the demands of those who are asking from this country more than it is possible for the country to raise. We should be frank and honest enough to say that. But we should attempt to deal with all the reasonable demands which are made and try and solve the question so that we can get rid, if it be possible, of the returned soldier problem, get rid of it for our own satisfaction and get rid of it so that the returned men, or the bulk of the reasonable men amongst the returned soldiers, may be satisfied.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I also would like to say a few words on this resolution. Like the prevoius speaker I understood when I voted for the* adoption of the report of the committee last session that the door would be left open for further discussion of the question of the re-establishment of the returned soldier. There are some matters which I think should be dealt with by any committee which is to be appointed and I hope the committee will be the same as the committee that acted last session. That committee, in my opinion, did excellent work, and there is no reason why they should not be asked to continue their labours and they will have the advantage of the opinions that have been expressed here to-day. I agree with the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) that some assistance should be given to university students. These are mostly youths who went overseas from the courses which they were taking. They are now unable, or perhaps some of them are unwilling, to continue their courses because of the years
5.38

they have spent in service to their country. Now it seems to me that it is in the interest of Canada that these young men should be assisted to continue their courses in the university, and I hope that some means will be found to help them to do so. We must also consider the case of those just over the age of eighteen years who enlisted and served many years in the war and who now find that because they were over eighteen they are not entitled to the assistance which is being given to boys under that age. I think that age limit could very well be increased to twenty-one years, and I hope the committee will take this matter into consideration.
I was pleased to hear from the Acting Prime Minister that the Government was considering bringing in a Bill to cover the question of insurance and I support the stand which the Government is taking in that connection. I believe that a man who was physically fit when he went overseas but who finds himself unable to get insurance when he returns to Canada, should be looked after.
Then there is the question of'better pensions. I believe that the pensions should be increased in amount in a great many cases, and also that the scope of the pensions granted should be enlarged. We have heard to-day of many cases of mothers and wives who should in all justice be entitled to pensions but cannot receive them because of the existing regulations, or because of the law as it stands at the present time.
I do not agree in any way with the criticisms that have been directed against the minister in charge of th^ Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. I have found that minister courteous at all times and invariably willing whenever I have had occasion to speak to him, to do what he could. But in a great many of these cases I have been met with the reply that although the minister thinks they are deserving of consideration, unfortunately owing to the regulations that are in force he can do nothing.
Another matter I would like to refer to is that of the Emergency Fund which was provided for last year. We all know that the returned men did not take advantage of that fund as we expected they would. The reason for that was that they considered it as a dole or a charity and they do not want charity-they want work. What I want to suggest is that the Government should consider opening up public works so as to give the men who are willing to work the opportunity of doing so. 1 do not believe
IMr. McQuarrie. ]
in extravagant expenditures but I do believe that instead of handing out a charity dole this Government should provide work for men who are willing to do it, and in my opinion the great majority of the returned men are willing to work if that work is given to them. I know in my constituency there are a lot of men who are not saying anything, who are not making any complaints, but who are, and have been, unable to obtain employment. 'I hope the Government will give that matter serious consideration. I would like to go further than some hon. gentlemen have done. I would suggest to the committee that is about to be appointed the advisability of considering the granting of some assistance to those who need it if work cannot be given them, I am like all the hon. gentlemen who have spoken here to-day in that I believe first consideration should be given to the disabled men and to the dependents of those gallant fellows who gave up their lives overseas. At the same time I think there are those not classed as disabled men who are entitled to some consideration, and I would impress upon the committee that they should endeavour perhaps to go further in the direction of granting assistance to these men than has yet been attempted.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. ANDREWS FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I shall not detain the House at any length in speaking to the resolution under consideration. Let me begin by saying that I am a man of peace and not a man of war. I am not disposed to pay compliments to hon. gentlemen opposite because of the advice of a very old politician who once told me that it was a bad practice to compliment the other man for he would not believe you anyway. However, if such a thing were at all permissable! to one who is so much younger I would like to say that in listening to the words of the leader of the Government-when he spoke with all the earnestness that he possesses upon this subject and said that he was doing his best -I did feel he meant every word he said. After a long life given by the right hon. gentleman to the public service of the country in all the departments he was called to administer I feel that his administration of those departments has been characterized by that thrift which, I am sure, every citizen in this country will recognize.	<
A complaint was made as to the work of the committees of the House. I was a member of the first committee formed to

deal with the subject of pensions, and jl want to say that hon. members on both sides gave to the work of that committee the best that was in them in their endeavour to do full justice by the men who had fought for a righteous cause, while not forgetting that the Administration was the custodian of the taxes of the people. That committee was presided over by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), and occupied a great deal of the members' time, sitting morning, afternoon and evening for weeks, and they only knew what was happening in this Chamber through their perusal of Hansard or the public press. I must confess that last year when asked to again sit upon the committee I did not feel that I could give to the subject all the time that it deserved, and I sympathize with the men who did act, because I know they were intent on doing their duty between the soldier boys and the taxpayers.
I have heard complaints made about the pensions granted. Yes, those pensions might be higher. They were granted after careful study by that committee and were based upon the Workmen's Compensation Acts of various countries and upon the experience of those countries which had pension lists. It was a new incident in this country's history. We had been through a war more gigantic than has ever been seen before in the history of the world. That there should be things lacking I can conceive to be possible, and that those omissions should be remedied I conceive to be a proper stand for the soldiers to take.
I also 'feel, Sir, that the Soldiers' Committee, the Pensions Committee and the other committee formed to deal with the claims of soldiers have reported sufficiently to this House to have the Administration assume to-day the full responsibility of carrying out the recommendations of those committees-improving upon them where improvement is possible, and rectifying any faults that have become apparent- and I think hon. gentlemen to-day who spoke upon this subject from both sides of the House should direct all their energies towards making the Government feel their responsibility in the matter. It should not be shelved on to committees again; the Government is now fully seized of the matter and should be prepared to act.
There was a time, Sir, before the war was over and before demobilization began when we were told that the Government was well advanced in the development of a scheme by which the returned men would
find all that was coming to them on their return home. That time has arrived, and our returned men who fought so bravely and were wounded deserve everything that is coming to them-not alone from the Government but from Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I have heard it stated by some hon. members that the returned men have not been able to obtain employment-
I have heard that complaint on the street, in my office, in my home, on trains, and I have read it in the press. I am not in favour of turning out all civilians in the Government service and putting returned soldiers in their places. I believe, Sir, in the Civil Service being the most efficient that we can have. I believe in the soldier having a fair share in the public service. But what I do believe in more, Sir, is that the widow, the dependent, the student and the other classes who require immediate aid should be granted that aid.
Now, as to such part of the resolution as bea'rs upon what I have said, I am prepared to support it. But I am not prepared to go to the extent of saying that the provision made for re-establishment in civil life of the members of His Majesty's forces who served in the late war has in many cases proved inadequate. Perhaps it has. The hon. member who proposes the resolution is, however-or was until quite recently- more in the secrets of the Government than I am, and if he states there are cases wherein this resolution will help the soldiers- will help them in returning to civil life, will help them in becoming as they were before, good citizens of this Dominion, will help them for the sacrifices which they have made-then, Mr. Speaker, I will without qualification support the motion of the hon. gentleman.
On motion of Mr. H. B. Morphy (North Perth) the debate was adjourned.
